Wheareas in the first Session of o<sup>r</sup> Parliament holden at Westminster, in the first yeare of o<sup>r</sup> Reigne of England ffraunce and Ireland and of Scotland the seaven and thirteth one Acte[^sec-06-fn-124] was made intituled an Acte for the well garbling of Spices wheareby it was ordeyned & enacted that from and after the last day of September then next ensueing the end of that Session of Parliam<sup>te</sup>, All spices wares drugge and other m<sup>r</sup>chandizes garbleable, that is to say Pepp, Cloues, Mace, Nutmegge, Cynamon, Ginger Long Pepper, Wormeseede[^sec-06-fn-125], Comynseede, Annyseede, Colyanderseede, Bynny pepp Almonde [p. 200] Date Galles Gumes of all sorte and kinde garbleable Spikenard Galingath[^sec-06-fn-126] Turmericke, Setweth[^sec-06-fn-127] Cassia fistula Gynny Pepp [p. 201] Senie[^sec-06-fn-128] Barbaries[^sec-06-fn-129] Rise[^sec-06-fn-130] Erius[^sec-06-fn-131] Stavisaker[^sec-06-fn-132], Calamus ffemyquicke[^sec-06-fn-133] Cassia Lignum Graines[^sec-06-fn-134] Carrowaie seede and all other spices drugge wares and other m<sup>r</sup>chandizes that had beene vsuallie garbled, or ought to be garbled clensed seuered sorted or deuided in the Cittie of London and the libties thereof, should for the ffees vsuallie allowed in that behalfe be sufficientlie clensed seuered garbled and deuided, and afterwarde setled[^sec-06-fn-135] by the Garbler therevnto appointed for the tyme being, or by his sufficient Deputie or Deputies servant or servante before that the same or any pte thereof should be sould vpon payne of fforfecture of all and eu<sup>r</sup>y such spices drugge wares or other m<sup>r</sup>chaundizes, or the value thereof w<sup>ch</sup> should be sould as by the said Acte more at lardge appeth. And whereas the true intent and meaneing of the said Acte was that none of the said spices drugge wares and m<sup>r</sup>chandizes brought into this Realme should be vttered or sould to the end to be vsed in meate drinke, or other needfull occasions amongst o<sup>r</sup> subiecte w<sup>th</sup>in this Realme before such tyme as the same were sufficientlie clensed seuered garbled and deuided as is [p. 202] aforesai[d] And the true meaneing of the same Acte did not in any wyse extend to the clensing seu<sup>r</sup>ing garbling and deuiding of any such of the said spices drugg<sup>e</sup> wares and m<sup>r</sup>chandizes, as should be transported out of this Realme in such sorte as they were brought into the same And wheareas yt is found that by some generall word<sup>e</sup> that passed in the said Acte, no wares marchandizes or Fomodities that are garbleable being brought into this Realme can be sould betweene m<sup>r</sup>chaunt and m<sup>r</sup>chaunte vngarbled to the intent to transporte the same into the p<sup>t</sup><sup>e</sup> beyond the seas but the seller therof by the strict lre of the said statute shall thereby be in danger to forfeft all the said spices drugg<sup>e</sup> wares and marchandizes w<sup>c</sup><sup>h</sup> he shall soe sell vngarbled. And wheareas o<sup>r</sup> loueing subiect<sup>e</sup> the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Companie of m<sup>r</sup>chaunt<sup>e</sup> of London trading into the East Indies, haue crediblie informed vs that they haueing latelie brought from the said East Indies into this o<sup>r</sup> Realme a greate quantitie of spice and other wares and comodities garbleable more then can be vttered and spent w<sup>t</sup><sup>h</sup>in this Realme in many yeares, & haue been therefore humble suiters to vs to haue o<sup>r</sup> lycense to sell some of the same spices in grosse to other m<sup>r</sup>chaunt<sup>e</sup> to be transported in grosse into diu<sup>r</sup>s plac<sup>e</sup> beyond the seas w<sup>c</sup><sup>h</sup> by reason of the said Statute they make doubt to doo w<sup>t</sup>hout o<sup>r</sup> spetiall lycense in that behalfe, w<sup>c</sup><sup>h</sup> favo<sup>r</sup> if we graunte them not, and that verie speedelie other m<sup>r</sup>chant<sup>e</sup> of other nañõns will happilie prevent them in serueing those places w<sup>t</sup><sup>h</sup> such like spices & soe theirs shall lye vpon their hand<sup>e</sup> to their greate losse and damadge. Know ye therefore that we gratiouslie tendring the welfare and Comoditie of o<sup>r</sup> said loueing subiect<sup>e</sup> the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Company of m<sup>r</sup>chant<sup>e</sup> of London trading into the East Indies. And to the end they may be the better enabled to maineteyne and Continue their trade and traffique in the said East Indies of o<sup>r</sup> espetiall grace c<sup>r</sup>teine knowledg and mere motion haue geuen and graunted & by theis present<sup>e</sup> for vs o<sup>r</sup> heires and Successo<sup>r</sup><sup>s</sup> doe giue and graunt full and free libtie licence power & authoritie vnto the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> & Company of m<sup>r</sup>chaunt<sup>e</sup> of London tradinge into the East Indies and to their Successo<sup>r</sup><sup>s</sup> that it shall & may be lawfull to & for them & eu<sup>r</sup>y of them hereafter to vtter sell and put to sale any of the said spices drugg<sup>e</sup> wares and m<sup>r</sup>chandizes by them [p. 203] or any of them alreadie brought from any pte of the said East Indies into this Realme or any pte thereof in whole packes sackes or Caskę vnbroken vngarbled & not clensed seu<sup>r</sup>ed sorted or deuided to any m<sup>r</sup>chant or m<sup>r</sup>chauntę aswell o<sup>r</sup> naturall borne subiectę as Aliens Benicens[^sec-06-fn-136] or Straungers that shall w<sup>th</sup>in the space of 3 monnethes next after the date thereof transporte the same in whole packę sackę or Caskę vnbroken as aforesaid into any the pte beyond the Seas w<sup>th</sup>out any damadge losse forfecture and penaltie against the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> & Company of m<sup>r</sup>chauntę of London trading into the East Indies, or against any of them by vs o<sup>r</sup> heires or successo<sup>rs</sup>, or to o<sup>r</sup> or their vse and behoofe to be had lost forfected or incurred or w<sup>th</sup>out any manner let interrupcõn or disturbance of any other pson or psons whatsoeu<sup>r</sup> The said statute or any other thinge to the Contrarie thereof in any wise notw<sup>th</sup>standing. And we doe further for vs o<sup>r</sup> heires and Successo<sup>rs</sup> of o<sup>r</sup> like especiall grace certeine knowledge and mere moc̃on giue and graunte full free and lawfull power & authoritie vnto all and eu<sup>r</sup>y m<sup>r</sup>chant and m<sup>r</sup>chantę whatsoeu<sup>r</sup> aswell o<sup>r</sup> naturall borne subiectę as Aliens Denizens & straungers that they and eu<sup>r</sup>y or any of them shall and lawfullie may bargaine for buy receiue and take of the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Company of marchauntę of London trading into the East Indies and their Successo<sup>rs</sup> for the tyme being, or of any of them, any of the said spices druggę wares and m<sup>r</sup>chandizes in whole sackę packę or Caskę not broken as aforesaid vngarbled and not clensed seu<sup>r</sup>ed sorted or deuided & the same spices Druggę wares & m<sup>r</sup>chandizes soe b̄gayned for, bought receiued & taken & eu<sup>r</sup>y pte and pcell thereof in such and the same sorte as the same shall be bought in whole packę whole sackę or in Caske not broken up w<sup>th</sup>in this o<sup>r</sup> Realme of England or any pte thereof after the same shall be soe sould by the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Companie of m<sup>r</sup>chauntę of London trading into the East Indies as is aforesaid shall and may lawfullie and freelie w<sup>th</sup>in the space of three monnethes next followinge after the said date thereof transporte carrie or Convey out of any porte haven Creeke or other place of [p. 204] lading or vnlading w<sup>th</sup>in o<sup>r</sup> Realme of England into any the parte beyond the seas and theare at their free wills liberties and pleasures vtter sell distribute and dispose the same to their or any of their most proffitt Comoditie and aduantage w<sup>th</sup>out any damadge losse forfecture or penaltie against them or any of them by vs o<sup>r</sup> heires or Successo<sup>rs</sup> or to o<sup>r</sup> or their vse and behoofe to be had lost forfected or incurred and w<sup>th</sup>out any manner lett interrupcõn or disturbance of any other pson or psons whatsoeu<sup>r</sup>, The said statute or any other thinge to the Contrarie thereof in any wise notw<sup>th</sup>standinge Paying vnto vs o<sup>r</sup> heires and Successo<sup>rs</sup> from time to tyme all and eu<sup>r</sup>y such Customes subsidies, somes of money, and other duties as are or ought to be aunsweared and paid vnto vs o<sup>r</sup> heires and successo<sup>rs</sup> for or by reason of the transportacõn of any of the said spices drugge wares and m<sup>r</sup>chandizes so to be transported as aforesaid.

Provided alwaies neu<sup>r</sup>thelesse that if there shall not be from tyme to tyme and at all tymes hereafter sufficient quantitie or store of the said spices drugge wares and Merchandizes to be garbled clensed seuered sorted and deuided left and being w<sup>th</sup>in this o<sup>r</sup> Realme of England & to be vsed spent and occupied by o<sup>r</sup> loueing subiecte w<sup>th</sup>in the same Realme in their meate drinke and other needfull occasions, and the sane to be sould vttered and put to sale to any of o<sup>r</sup> said loueinge subiecte at reasonable and indifferent prices That then and from thence forth aswell the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Companie of m<sup>r</sup>chante of London tradinge into the East Indies shall cease and forbeare to sell and vtter any of the said spices drugge wares and m<sup>r</sup>chandizes vngarbled as is aforesaid as alsoe the said m<sup>r</sup>chante and others shall cease and forbeare to buy receiue and take the same vngarbled any thing before in theis presente to the Contrarie in any wyse notw<sup>th</sup>- standinge.

Although expresse menc̃on of the cleire yearelie value, or c<sup>r</sup>teynetie of the premisses or of any of them or of any other guifte or graunte by vs or any of o<sup>r</sup> progenitors to the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Company of m<sup>r</sup>chante heretofore made in those[^sec-06-fn-137] presente is not made, or any statute Acte Ordinance pvision proclamac̃on or restrainte to the contrarie thereof made ordeyned [p. 205] or prouided or any other thing cause or matter whatsoeur to the contrarie notw<sup>th</sup>standing. In witnes whereof we haue caused theis o<sup>r</sup> lres to be made Patente. Witnes o<sup>r</sup> selfe at Westminster the ix<sup>th</sup> day of August in the fourth yeare of o<sup>r</sup> reigne of England ffraunce & Ireland & of Scotland the xl<sup>th</sup>.[^sec-06-fn-138] p bre de priuato sigillo. Tho: Ravenscrofte.


##### 1606


#### To the kinge most excellent ma<sup>tie</sup>:


##### The humble petic̃on[^sec-06-fn-139] of yo<sup>r</sup> ma<sup>te</sup> faithfull Subiecte the m<sup>r</sup>chante of London trading [into] the East Indies.

> _[Margin: Humblie praying that yor matie wilbe pleased to grant them a *non obstante* vpon the statute for garbling made in the first yeare of yor highnes Reigne for such spices & other mrchandize vngarbled as shall be transported out of the Realme according to their chartr wthout danger of lawe: And for yor mates better satisfaccon & informacon yt this their request is iuste and reasonable, & according to thintent of ye said statute they humblie desier that the consideracon thereof may be by yor highnes referred to the Lo:]_
> _[Margin: cheefe iustice of Eng-land, & the Lord cheef iustice of the comon plees, or such other learned in the lawe as yo<sup>r</sup> ma<sup>tie</sup> shall thinke fitt.]_

MAY it please yo<sup>r</sup> sacred ma<sup>tie</sup>: to be informed that in the first year of yo<sup>r</sup> most happie reigne there passed an Acte against vttering of c<sup>r</sup>teine spice vngarbled vsed in meate drinke and other needfull occasions amongest yo<sup>r</sup> ma<sup>te</sup> Subiecte whereby greate deceite hurte & damadge happened to such as bought and vsed the same: ffor remedie whereof, the said Acte was purposely made & not for garbling such spice as should be transported out of yo<sup>r</sup> Realmes But by some generall worde in the said Acte it is comprized contrarie to the true meaneing thereof that noe comodities brought into this Realme garbleable cann be sould betweene m<sup>r</sup>chaunt and m<sup>r</sup>chaunt vngarbled to thintent the same may be transported into fforreine pte, but the seller thereof, by the strict lre of the said statute is in danger to forfect all the said spice he shall soe sell vngarbled. Now soe it is most Excellent ma<sup>tie</sup>: [p. 206] **That yo<sup>r</sup> m<sup>r</sup>chantę of London trading [into] the** East Indies, haueing latelie brought from thence into this kingdome a greate quantitie of spices more then this land can vtter in manie yeares, or the Garblers can garble in any due tyme fitt for the sale thereof : They are desirous to sell some pte thereof vngarbled to be transported beyond the Seas as by Charter they are allowed : But by reason of the said statute they make doubt to doe the same, for avoieding of danger By meanes whereof the shall be much inabled[^sec-06-fn-140] to furnish the like voyadge againe in any convenient tyme the w<sup>ch</sup> will proue hurtfull vnto yo<sup>r</sup> ma<sup>tie</sup> in yo<sup>r</sup> Customes and to yo<sup>r</sup> people, & a greate discouradgm<sup>t</sup> to yo<sup>r</sup> m<sup>r</sup>chauntę to proceed in the same Trade, whoe in verie truth, hartelie doe desier aboundantlie to supplie the wantę of the land w<sup>th</sup> the best of their spices, at reasonable ratę & not to haue any of the same spent w<sup>th</sup>in yo<sup>r</sup> Realme, but what shall be garbled according to the said statute : But those onelie to be exempt that by way of m<sup>r</sup>chandize shalbe sent beyond the Seas. May it therefore please yo<sup>r</sup> sacred ma<sup>tie</sup> : That for yo<sup>r</sup> highnes better informaăon what was the true intent of the said statute, to referr the Consideraăon thereof to the Lo : cheefe iustice of England & the Lo : cheefe iustice of the comon plees & such other learned in the Law as yo<sup>r</sup> ma<sup>tie</sup> : shall thinke fitt. And if they vpon due examinaăon thereof shall soe hold it reasonable. That yo<sup>r</sup> ma<sup>tie</sup> would then be pleased to graunte vnto yo<sup>r</sup> Peticioners a *non obstante* vpon the said statute for selling of spices & other m<sup>r</sup>chandize vngarbled, soe as the spices be transported, & not retailed or spent w<sup>th</sup>in the Realme. And as most bound we pray God giue yo<sup>r</sup> ma<sup>tie</sup> : a long & most happie reigne ou<sup>r</sup> vs.


##### A reference from his ma<sup>tie</sup> :

The kę ma<sup>tie</sup> is pleased that the Lo : Thrēr & Earle of Salisburie shall vpon conference w<sup>th</sup> the twoe LL cheefe Iustices consider whether this desier of the m<sup>r</sup>chantę be against [the] true intent of the statute, or noe : & whether it be w<sup>th</sup>out p<sup>r</sup>iudice to [p. 207] the Realme that such a *non obstante* vpon the said statute be graunted & if they finde it reasonable to be done that they giue order to his ma<sup>t e</sup> Atturney to drawe such a booke as shall be requisite

Tho: Lake.


#### 1606.[^sec-06-fn-141]


##### To the right Ho: the Lorde of his ma<sup>ties</sup> most Ho: privie Councell.


##### The Petic̃on of the Comp: of m<sup>r</sup>chante trading into the East Indies humblie shewing.

<span class="sc">That</span> wheares by o<sup>r</sup> Charter we are lycensced to carrie for the said Indies eu<sup>r</sup>y voyadge to the some of 30000<sup>li</sup> of all such fforreine Coines as we shall bring into this kingdome soe as 6000<sup>li</sup> theareof be heare first Coyned : Now soe it is right Ho: that the Companie haueing made twoe voyadge w<sup>th</sup> retournes verie comodious to his ma<sup>tie</sup> in his Customes and his Realmes, & haue alsoe now alredie sent forth a 3 voyadg & are in a redines to sett forth a 4<sup>th</sup> voyadge, aswell for those place where they haue form<sup>r</sup>lie beene as for discou<sup>r</sup>y of furder trade in those pte, & are desirous to manadge & carrie their trade as neare as they can rather by the transportac̃on of o<sup>r</sup> Natiue Comoditie [s] then by vsing the benefitt granted them for transportac̃on of fforreine coine as aforesaid: But thinge soe stand that as yett noe trade cann be theare driuen w<sup>th</sup>out some moneys, & espetiallie such fforreine coines as they are acquainted w<sup>th</sup>all. In considerac̃on whereof & forasmuch as in o<sup>r</sup> c<sup>r</sup>teine knowledge diu<sup>r</sup>s of o<sup>r</sup> Company haue latelie brought into this Realmes greate somes of fforreine Coines farr exceeding that w<sup>ch</sup> [p. 208] we now requier: We humblie beseech that by yo<sup>r</sup> ho: good favo<sup>rs</sup> his ma<sup>tie</sup> may be moued to vouchsaffe vs his highnes graunte for transportac̃on in theis o<sup>r</sup> shipps for theast Indies the some of 15000<sup>li</sup> onelie in forreine coines, w<sup>th</sup>out new coyning any pte thereof: & the rather in reguard y<sup>t</sup> forasmuch as we haue form<sup>r</sup>lie had in the first voyadge, much difficultie and losse in such moneys as weare heare coyned by reason those people ar altogether vnacquainted w<sup>th</sup> the stamp of this kingdome, beside the stay of o<sup>r</sup> shipps now for coyning thereof wilbe to thutter ou<sup>r</sup>throw of the voyadge. And we as most bound beseech god to geue yo<sup>r</sup> Lo<sup>ps</sup>: all health and happines.


#### To the right Ho: the Lorde of his ma<sup>ties</sup>: most Ho: priuie councell.


##### The Petic̃on of the Company of m<sup>r</sup>chaunte trading into the East Indies humblie shewinge.

THAT whearas of late vpon o<sup>r</sup> humble Petic̃on it pleased yo<sup>r</sup> lops: for the reasons therein mencioned to conceiue it fitt we should be pmitted to transporte 15000<sup>li</sup> in fforreine Coines of those 30000<sup>li</sup> graunted vs by o<sup>r</sup> Charter, & that w<sup>th</sup>out new coyning any pte thereof. The w<sup>ch</sup> some of 15000<sup>li</sup> vpon better advice & Considerac̃on of o<sup>r</sup> intenc̃on furder to discou<sup>r</sup> & enlardge that trade, we vnderstand will not be be sufficient (notw<sup>th</sup>standing the comodities we now carrie of dyvers sorte) to manadge the same w<sup>th</sup> good order, & for retournes in this present voyadge. We therefore humblie pray that by yo<sup>r</sup> honorable good favo<sup>rs</sup> his ma<sup>tie</sup> may be now moued to vouchsaffe vs his highnes graunte for transportac̃on in theis o<sup>r</sup> ships for the East Indies the some of 20000<sup>li</sup> in forreine Coines in place of the said 15000<sup>li</sup> w<sup>th</sup>out new coyning any pte thereof. And as most bound we pray god giue you all health & happines.


<!-- page: 301 | folio: 209 -->
> _[Margin: ffor apprhencon of such saylers as shall goe away.]_

WHEREAS[^sec-06-fn-142] we haue hired diu<sup>rs</sup> saylo<sup>rs</sup> to goe in o<sup>r</sup> voyadg now intended for the East Indies who haue not onelie subscribed to o<sup>r</sup> Booke, to pforme the same but alsoe haue receiued wage of vs & some ymprest moneys, and yet we may doubt (as in form<sup>r</sup> tyme hath beene vsed) that aswell before the shipps were readie to depte, as at their depture some of such a nomber may be missing not onelie w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> losse, but alsoe tending to the ou<sup>r</sup>throwe of the wholle voyadge : ffor prevencoñ thereof we humblie pray that a warrant may be graunted, or some convenient meanes vsed for app<sup>r</sup>hencõn & ponishm<sup>te</sup> of such as are or shall goe away or depte & absent them selues from their place and service in this present voyadg after they shall be hired and agreed w<sup>th</sup>all.


#### To the Lord High Admirall of England

> _[Margin: A peticon not to presse men from o<sup>r</sup> shipps.]_

WHEREAS we are informed that there now is a presse for men to be sent downe to Chatham & we are in doubt that thereby o<sup>r</sup> men appointed for bringing in one of o<sup>r</sup> shipps into the docke at Debtford may be pressed thither, the w<sup>ch</sup> will proue an exceeding hindrance vnto the voyadge w<sup>ch</sup> we are now in hand to prepare for theast Indies. We humblie pray that yo<sup>r</sup> Lo<sup>p</sup> : wilbe pleased to graunte yo<sup>r</sup> warrant that o<sup>r</sup> men may not be taken from vs in this tyme of necessitie : & soe much the rather as the omitting of this oportunitie of bringing the said shipp now into the Docke may be the ou<sup>r</sup>throw of o<sup>r</sup> said intended voyadge.


<!-- page: 302 | folio: 210 -->

##### To the kinge most excellent ma<sup>tie</sup>:[^sec-06-fn-143]


![Decorative woodcut initial letter T with floral and foliage patterns.](../figures/fig-014_p0302.webp)

> _[Margin: for restraint of bringing in of pepper]_

<span class="sc">Hat</span> wheareas now after a longe & chardgable voyadge such retournes as we made from thence is for the most p̄te pepp̄, & in such quantitie as we shall not be able to vent the same neither at home nor abroade, but w<sup>th</sup> intollerable losse, and discouradgm<sup>t</sup> to follow that trade any furder vnlesse Restraint be made that noe pepp̄ be brought hither from any the p̄te beyond the Seas till we shall be able to haue made sale of o<sup>rs</sup>, and soe much the rather for that how willing soeu<sup>r</sup> we shalbe to afford the same at any lowe rate, yet the Netherlanders studious how to wearie vs out of that trade by prevencons in o<sup>r</sup> sales & retournes both in theast Indies and heare at home, will soe watch their times as they will much hurte vs either by affording to o<sup>r</sup> People bad pepp̄ better Cheepe, to beate downe the prize of o<sup>r</sup> better pepp̄ w<sup>th</sup> the hurte of the comons of this land whoe buie the same for their owne spendinge, or by some other deuice, as by experience we daylie finde. Now forasmuch as we will be eu<sup>r</sup> readie to afford o<sup>r</sup> best pepp̄ at such rate as shall be reasonable not exceeding ij<sup>s</sup> a pounde we most humblie beseech yo<sup>r</sup> sacred ma<sup>tie</sup>: of yo<sup>r</sup> gratious clemencie in considerac̃on hereof, to vouchsaffe vs yo<sup>r</sup> most Princelie warrant for restrayning aswell yo<sup>r</sup> ma<sup>te</sup> subiecte, as any other to bring any pepp̄ into any yo<sup>r</sup> ma<sup>te</sup> dominions from any forreine p̄te for the space of           yeares next ensueing vnles it be by vs from theast Indies. And we as most bound beseech thalmightie God to giue yo<sup>r</sup> ma<sup>tie</sup>: a longe and happie reigne ou<sup>r</sup> vs.


<!-- page: 303 | folio: 211 -->

#### To the right ho: the lorde of his ma<sup>te</sup> most hono: priuie Councell.


##### The peti<span class="sc">c</span>õn of the Company of East India m<sup>r</sup>chante humblie shewing vnto yo<sup>r</sup> Lo<sup>ps</sup>:[^sec-06-fn-144]

> _[Margin: That none but y<sup>e</sup> Company may trade to theast Indies.]_

<span class="sc">THAT</span> wheareas we haue alredie w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> greate chardge & Adventure setled a trade in the East Indies verie pffittable for this comon wealth & for furder enlardgm<sup>t</sup> thereof, are even now prepareing of shipps & other pui<span class="sc">c</span>õns w<sup>th</sup> good hope that the same will proue dailie more & more Comodious aswell for ventinge of o<sup>r</sup> natiue Comodities, as for retournes of thinge verie needfull for this o<sup>r</sup> land at reasonable rate.

Soe it is right Hono: that ptelie by reason of S<sup>r</sup> Edw: Michelbornes hard dealinge in the East Indies[^sec-06-fn-145] by surprising the ships & goode of some such as we haue & of others whome we intend to haue trade w<sup>th</sup>all, vpon p<sup>r</sup>tence they ar Infidells: & ptlie for that there is some reporte that theare are others suiters alsoe for Commission to doe the like: Not onelie the most of the cheefest of the Companie are discouradged to Adventure any more: but alsoe such as haue alreadie sett downe their Adventures begynn to drawe backe whereby vnlesse some good course be taken herein, that trade will whollie decay w<sup>th</sup> the intollerable hurte & dishono<sup>r</sup> of this o<sup>r</sup> land & nation.

> _[Margin: To repell force by force.]_
> _[Margin: That we may carry forreine Coine]_

In considera<span class="sc">c</span>õn whereof & forasmuch as we giueing ou<sup>r</sup> the trade yt will remaine whollie in the hande of the Hollenders: whoe as they haue endevored to bringe the same to passe by diu<sup>r</sup>s kinde of meanes: soe it is not to be doubted but that they will then sell such thinge, as now are, or shalbe brought thence at what Rate them please. Wee humblie beseech: That by yo<sup>r</sup> honorable good meanes some convenient course may be entred into, to take away theis & such like obstacles as may hinder soe good & honorable an endevo<sup>r</sup>: the w<sup>ch</sup> wilbe easilie effected, if that from hencforth noe way be geven to any such Comission and that by some publick edict, all others his ma<sup>te</sup> subiecte be [p. 212] phibited from any manner of trade or dealing in those pte, during the time of o<sup>r</sup> graunte. And further more right ho: it would be agreater incouradgm<sup>t</sup> vnto vs cherefullie to pceed herein yf that for o<sup>r</sup> better saffitie in theis doubtfull occasions, his ma<sup>tie</sup> by yo<sup>r</sup> ho: good favo<sup>rs</sup> would alsoe be moued to graunte vs Comission to repell force by force if the same be offered vs. As alsoe that we may w<sup>th</sup>out doubt of any lett or danger of the statute to send w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> ships soe much forreine Coine as shall be needfull for vs, the w<sup>ch</sup> wilbe now much lesse then formerlie we haue done by vertue of o<sup>r</sup> Charter And furder that in some convenient sorte the states of the Low Countries may be alsoe dealt w<sup>th</sup>all: That notw<sup>th</sup>standing their Peoples contenẽõns w<sup>th</sup> the Portugalls whoe should haue all the trade in those pte we may freelie trade w<sup>th</sup> them in all place theare as neighbo<sup>rs</sup> and ffreinde w<sup>th</sup>out excepẽõn. And &c:


##### A petiẽõn to the Lord Thr̄er.[^sec-06-fn-146]

> _[Margin: The difference for entrie of the Nutmeges to be mediated.]_

**H**UMBLIE declareing vnto yo<sup>r</sup> Lo<sup>p</sup>: That amongst other Cömodities now brought from thence we finding the Nutmegge of such evill Condiẽõn as they are for the greater pte Rumps & noe Nutmegge we thought good to make o<sup>r</sup> entries thereof in the Custome house accordinglie The w<sup>ch</sup> entries the ffarmo<sup>rs</sup> altogether seekinge their owne priuate proffitt w<sup>th</sup>out haueing any reguard to the quallitie of the same or of o<sup>r</sup> longe and chardgable voyadge & Adventure refuce to take: vrging vs to enter them all for Nutmegge the w<sup>ch</sup> paith more then twice the Custome of Rumps, whereas in verie deed 2 pte theareof are Rumps & that of the worst sorte: The w<sup>ch</sup> course seemeth not onelie against the rate sett downe for paym<sup>t</sup> of Custome but alsoe against all comon reason w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> intollerable iniurie. wherefor we humble beseech: that by yo<sup>r</sup> Lo<sup>ps</sup>: good meanes the matter [p. 213] may be soe mediated as that neither we nor [the] ffarmo<sup>rs</sup> may haue any Iniurie or losse herein. And as most bound we pray god giue you all health and happines.


#### To the Right ho: the Lord*e* of his ma<sup>t*e*</sup>: most ho: priuie Councell.[^sec-06-fn-147]

> _[Margin: <span class="sc">Touching S<sup>r</sup> Edw: Michelbornes fact comitted in theast Indies.</span>]_

<span class="sc">Hat</span> whereas we haue w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> greate chardge sought all possible meanes for setling & inlardgeing of a trade in the East Indies, aswell for venting o<sup>r</sup> Natiue Comodities, as for retourne of thing*e* comodious & needfull for this o<sup>r</sup> Realme at reasonable rat*e*. Soe it is Right ho: That even now when we were in a course furder to enlardge the same we vnderstand by łres & Certificate from o<sup>r</sup> ffacto<sup>rs</sup> at Bantam. That S<sup>r</sup> Edward Michelborne hath taken & spoiled some of o<sup>r</sup> freind*e* there, whereby not onelie the vtter ou<sup>r</sup>throwe of the whole trade is much indangered: but alsoe the saffetie of o<sup>r</sup> men & good*e* remayneing in those pte are greatlie to be feared.[^sec-06-fn-148] In tender considera<span class="sc">cõn</span> whereof we humblie beseech y<sup>t</sup> by yo<sup>r</sup> ho: good*e* meanes, some speedie course may be taken herein for o<sup>r</sup> saffetie either by sequestra<span class="sc">cõn</span> of the good*e* w<sup>ch</sup> the said S<sup>r</sup> Edw: Michelborne hath now brought home, or otherwyse, as in yo<sup>r</sup> hono: discre<span class="sc">cõns</span> shall be thought fitt: vntill vpon better informa<span class="sc">cõn</span> the estate and saffetie of o<sup>r</sup> ffacto<sup>rs</sup> & good*e* theare may be furder knowne. ffor at the writeing of the said łres now come, noe c<sup>r</sup>teintie of the takeing of the Guzarat & Cheny Iunck w<sup>ch</sup> the said S<sup>r</sup> Edw: now confesseth: nor some other thing*e* w<sup>ch</sup> are heare now reported, was then there acted, or come to knowledge.


<!-- page: 306 | folio: 214 -->

#### To y<sup>e</sup> Right ho : y<sup>e</sup> Lorde of his ma<sup>te</sup> : most honorable priuie Councell.[^sec-06-fn-149]

> _[Margin: A peticon for transportacon of moneys vncoyned.]_

THAT wheareas by o<sup>r</sup> Charter we are lycenced to carrie for the said Indies eu<sup>r</sup>y voyadge to the some of 30000<sup>li</sup> of all such forreigne Coines as we shall bring into this kingdome soe as 6000<sup>li</sup> thereof be heare first coyned. Now soe it is right hono : That the Company haueing made twoe voyage w<sup>th</sup> retournes verie comodious to his ma<sup>tie</sup> : in his Customes & his Realmes, and haue alsoe now alredie sent forth a 3 voyadge & are in a readines to sett forth a 4<sup>th</sup> voyadge aswell for those places where they haue form<sup>r</sup>lie beene as for discou<sup>r</sup>y of furder trade in those pte, and are desierous to manadge & carrie their trade as neare as they cann, rather by the transportac̃on of o<sup>r</sup> natiue comodities, then by vsing the benefitt graunted them for transportac̃on of forreine Coine as aforesaid : But thinge soe stand that as yet noe trade can be there driuen, w<sup>th</sup>out some moneys, & espetiallie such fforreine coines as they are acquainted w<sup>th</sup>all. In Considerac̃on whereof & forasmuch as in o<sup>r</sup> c<sup>r</sup>teine knowledge diu<sup>r</sup>s of o<sup>r</sup> Company haue latelie brought into this Realme greate somes of forreine Coines, far exceeding that w<sup>ch</sup> we now requier : we humblie beseech that by yo<sup>r</sup> ho : good favo<sup>rs</sup> his ma<sup>tie</sup> may be moued to vouchsaffe vs his highnes graunte for transportac̃on in theis o<sup>r</sup> ships for theast Indies the some onelie of 18000<sup>li</sup> in forreigne coines w<sup>th</sup>out new coyning any pte thereof : and the rather in reguard that forasmuch as we haue form<sup>r</sup>lie had in the first voyadge much difficultie and losse in such moneys as weare heare coyned by reason those people are altogether [p. 215] vnacquainted w<sup>th</sup> the stampe of this kingdome beside the staie of o<sup>r</sup> ships, now for coyning thereof wilbe to the vtter ou<sup>r</sup>throw of this voyadge. And we &c :


##### To the kinge most excellent ma<sup>tie</sup> :[^sec-06-fn-150]

THAT by Charter we are lycensed to carrie for the said Indies in eu<sup>r</sup>y voyadge to the some of 30000<sup>li</sup> of all such forreine Coines or siluer as we shall bringe into this Realme soe as 6000<sup>li</sup> thereof be heare first coyned.

> _[Margin: ffor transportacon of moneys vncoyned.]_

But forasmuch as in the first voyadge to those pte we had much *difficultie & losse* in such moneys as were heare then coyned those People beinge vnacquainted w<sup>th</sup> the stampe of this kingdome : *in reguard Thereof* we haue eu<sup>r</sup> since (vpon o<sup>r</sup> peticõn) beene lycenced to transporte *such* forreine Coines as *we haue sent thither* w<sup>th</sup>out new coyning any p<sup>te</sup> of the same. *In consideracon whereof &* for that in o<sup>r</sup> c<sup>r</sup>teine knowledge diu<sup>r</sup>s of o<sup>r</sup> Company haue latelie brought into this Realme greate somes of fforreine Coines farr exceeding that we shall now haue occasion to vse, *& we are desireous to manadge o<sup>r</sup> trade as nere as wee cann rather by transportacon of o<sup>r</sup> Native comodities then by vsing the benefitt granted vs for transportacon of fforreine Coines as* aforesaid we humblie beseech that yo<sup>r</sup> ma<sup>tie</sup> wilbe now pleased vpon this o<sup>r</sup> peticõn to vouchsaffe vs yo<sup>r</sup> highnes grante as heretofore for transportacõn of such forreine Coines or siluer as we shall send in the shipps now preparing for the said Indies w<sup>th</sup>out new coyning any pte thereof, & the rather for that all the moneys & siluer w<sup>ch</sup> we shall soe now send thither will be vnder the some of 20000<sup>li</sup> in the whole. And we &c :


<!-- page: 308 | folio: 216 -->

##### To the Right Ho : thearle of Salisburie principall Secretarie to his ma<sup>tie</sup> :


##### The petic̃on of the Companie of m<sup>r</sup>chauntę trading into the East Indies humblie shewing.[^sec-06-fn-151]

> _[Margin: To the Lo : of Salisburie for procureing his Mates lres and Comission in the 4<sup>th</sup> voyadge & the Coppie of the former lres in the 3 voyadge to be presented if need be.]_

<span class="sc">That</span> wheareas in Ianuarie last it pleased his ma<sup>tie</sup> : to vouchsaffe vs his highnes lres in o<sup>r</sup> behalfe to diu<sup>r</sup>s Princes in theast Indies[^sec-06-fn-152] the w<sup>ch</sup> lres were then sent by the conveyance of o<sup>r</sup> shipps we prepared at that tyme to goe for those partę : Now soe it is right ho : That we haueing noe meanes as yet to knowe whether the same lres be deliu<sup>r</sup>ed or by any Accident miscaried or deteyned in o<sup>r</sup> mens handę we then sent thither. And being shortlie to send other shipps for furder trade and discou<sup>r</sup>y of those kingdomes. We humblie pray in reguard thereof That yo<sup>r</sup> lo<sup>p</sup> : will be a meanes vnto his ma<sup>tie</sup> : in o<sup>r</sup> behalfe That his highnes will be now againe pleased to vouchsaffe vs his most gratious lres vnto the said Princes to the like effect as before w<sup>th</sup> some addic̃on as shalbe fitt, together w<sup>th</sup> his ma<sup>ties</sup> Comission to such of o<sup>r</sup> ffactor<sup>s</sup> as shall goe now Principall in this voyadge. And as most bound we pray god to giue yo<sup>r</sup> lor<sup>p</sup> : many happie yeares.


##### 12[^sec-06-fn-153] of Decemb̃ 1607

> _[Margin: A lre to S<sup>r</sup> Tho : lake from the lo : Threr to drawe a Bill for his mates signature for]_
> _[Margin: transportacon of 20000<sup>li</sup>. written w<sup>th</sup> my lordes owne hand]_

<span class="sc">S<sup>r</sup> Tho : lake</span>, I haue mooued his Ma<sup>tie</sup> :, That wheareas by Charter the m<sup>r</sup>chauntę trading to theast Indies are allowed to Carrie forth 30000<sup>li</sup> of all such fforraine Coynes as they shall bring into this Realme So as 6000<sup>li</sup> thereof be heare first Coined : But forasmuch as in the first voiadge to those ptę, they affirme that they had much losse, in such money as were then here Coined, those People being vnacquainted w<sup>th</sup> the [p. 217] stampe of this kingdome : & for that euer since, they haue been licenced vppon humble peticõn to traunsporte forraine Coines w<sup>th</sup>out new Coyninge any p<sup>te</sup> of the same And for that as they also affirme diu<sup>r</sup>s of that Companie in their Certaine knowledge haue latelie brought into this Realme greate som̃es of fforraine Coine, farr exceeding that the shall now haue occasion to Carrie forth, being as they saie but 20000<sup>li</sup>, w<sup>ch</sup> is 10000<sup>li</sup> les then by their Charter they may transport. In respect of all w<sup>ch</sup> his ma<sup>tie</sup> hath pleased most gratiouslie to grant their said peticõn vppon my humble sute yesterday made vnto his h<sup>s</sup>. Theis ar therfore to pray yo<sup>u</sup> to cause a Bill redie for his mate signiture to be drawne & to present the same to his ma<sup>tie</sup> : accordinglie, giuinge authoritie vnto me to suffer 20000<sup>li</sup> at this tyme, to be traunsported, notw<sup>th</sup>standinge that noe p<sup>te</sup> thereof be Coyned here. This 21 of decemb̃ 1607

Yo<sup>r</sup> verie louing freind *T Dorset.*[^sec-06-fn-154]


##### To the right ho : the Earle of Salisburie principall Secretarie to the kinge most excellent ma<sup>tie</sup> :


##### The Petic̃on of the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Companie of m<sup>r</sup>chaunte tradinge to the East Indies humblie shewinge

> _[Margin: The some of the saffe Conduct is in fo : 98.[^sec-06-fn-155]]_

THAT we haueing w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> greate chardge & Adventure setled a trade in the East Indies we are desirous to enlardge the same aswell for the ventinge of o<sup>r</sup> natiue Comodities as for retournes of thinge verie needfull for this kingdome at reasonable prices And to that end amongst diu<sup>r</sup>s other Citties and Countries the w<sup>ch</sup> we intend god Willingge to discou<sup>r</sup> in those p<sup>te</sup> we haue and doe purpose to visitt the Citties of Aden and Moccha at the mouth of the red sea & some other place thereaboute vnder the dominion of the Grand signio<sup>r</sup> whose łres of saffe Conducte would be verie helpfull vnto vs in this behalfe. We humblie desier that it will please yo<sup>r</sup> Lo<sup>p</sup> : of yo<sup>r</sup> ho : favo<sup>r</sup> to vouchsaffe vs [p. 218] yo<sup>r</sup> lop<sup>s</sup> łres To S<sup>r</sup> Thomas Glover Ambassador w<sup>th</sup> the Grandsignio<sup>r</sup> at Constantinople comanding him in his ma<sup>ties</sup> : name to doe his best endevo<sup>rs</sup> to obtaine for vs w<sup>th</sup> expedĩcõn such łres of Comendãcõn & saffe Conduct from the Grandsignio<sup>r</sup> as Convenientlie may be by him procured for vs to the effect of that w<sup>thin</sup> written And as most bound we pray god giue yo<sup>r</sup> lo<sup>p</sup>: manie happie Yeares.[^sec-06-fn-156]


#### To the right ho: the Lo: of his ma<sup>ties</sup> most ho: priuie Councell.[^sec-06-fn-157]

WE the Company of the m<sup>r</sup>chauntę of London tradinge theast Indies, most humblie declare vnto yo<sup>r</sup> Lo<sup>ps</sup>: That we haueing now brought a shipps ladinge of Cloues out of those ptę, & findinge the same to be very full of dust & garble by the longe Carriadge thereof, we haue beene enforced to make o<sup>r</sup> entries in the Custome howse accordinglie, otherwyse we should haue beene compelled to pay the Custome of Cloues, onelie for dust & garble of small or noe valew at all. The w<sup>ch</sup> manner of entrie, the ffarmo<sup>rs</sup> (seekinge their owne priuate gaine haueing noe reguard to the quallitie of the same, or of o<sup>r</sup> longe & Chargeable voyadge & Adventure) refuce to take Vrdginge vs to enter them all for Cloues w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> intollerable iniurie. wherefore o<sup>r</sup> humble sute is. That by yo<sup>r</sup> lo<sup>ps</sup> good meanes, this difference betweene us & the ffarmo<sup>rs</sup> may be soe mediated, as that neither we, nor they may be iniured herein, & that we by noe such offers of hard measure may be any way discouraged from that trade soe longe, soe dangerous & chardgeable vnto vs, & beneficiall to this kingdome. And we as most bound beseech god to giue yo<sup>r</sup> Lo<sup>ps</sup>: all health & happines.


<!-- page: 311 | folio: 219 -->

#### To the right ho: the Earle of Salisburie Lord high Thr̄er of England.


##### The humble petic̃on of the m<sup>r</sup>chauntę of London tradeing into the East Indies.[^sec-06-fn-158]

<span class="sc">Umblie</span> shewing That in the yeare 1607. w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> greate chardge & Adventure wee sent three shipps for trade of m<sup>r</sup>chandize into those ptę w<sup>th</sup> order in the way of their passadge thither, to make alsoe trade at Aden, Surate, & vpon the Coaste of Cambaia yf soe convenientlie and [p. 220] peaceablie they might doe the same, where vpon one of o<sup>r</sup> said shipps comeing to Surate noe way in the Actuall possession of the kinge of Spaigne & o<sup>r</sup> men being there kindlie vsed & suffered to trade by those Country people : Notw<sup>th</sup>standing certaine Portugalls Subiecte of the kinge of Spaigne[^sec-06-fn-159] liueinge at Deu and Goa neare to Surate watching their fitt oportunitie w<sup>th</sup>out any offence offered haue vsed such violence against o<sup>r</sup> men there as they haue beene Compelled to flee thence w<sup>th</sup> the losse not onelie of nyneteene men a penasse & alonge Boate but alsoe of a greate quantitie of moneys and goode beside the danger of the losse of o<sup>r</sup> said shipp w<sup>th</sup> her adventure for want of a sufficient nomber of men to saile her As by diu<sup>rs</sup> lres from some of o<sup>r</sup> people then theare taken & since ymprisonned at Lisborne readie to be shewed at lardge appe<sup>th</sup> Our humble suite now is. That in reguard we haue beene & at this present now are at a greate chardge for buildinge shippinge fitt for this trade the w<sup>ch</sup> we doubt not but will proue very proffitable for this kingdome, aswell by venting Comodities vnneedfull as by bringinge home such as are needfull for the vse and benefitt of this o<sup>r</sup> Realme, And that theis place where o<sup>r</sup> men did now trade is not in the actuall possessio[n] of the kinge of Spaigne. That by yo<sup>r</sup> honorable goode meanes his Ma<sup>tie</sup>: will be pleased gratiouslie to enter into some good course for o<sup>r</sup> releefe herein aswell for the freeing of o<sup>r</sup> men theare taken, as for satisfacc̃on of o<sup>r</sup> losses and wronge there sustayned Contrarie to the Amitie and agreem<sup>t</sup> betweene his ma<sup>tie</sup>: & the kinge of Spaigne as we humblie vnderstand yt. And as most bound we beseech God to giue yo<sup>r</sup> Lo<sup>p</sup>: all health and happines.

> _[Margin: The Condicon of a Pursar y<sup>t</sup> tyeth him selfe for c<sup>r</sup>teine yeres & further service. in 200<sup>li</sup> w<sup>th</sup> suerties[^sec-06-fn-161]]_

THE Condic̃on[^sec-06-fn-160] of this Obligac̃on is such That wheareas the aboue bounden **A B** is now hired by the aboue named Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Company of m<sup>r</sup>chaunte of London trading into the East Indies to goe as Pursar of the good shipp called the Assenc̃on in this present intended fourth [p. 221] voyadge for the said Indies and yet neu<sup>r</sup>thelesse hath agreed to serve the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Companie & their successo<sup>rs</sup> as their Couenante servant in all and eu<sup>r</sup>y such their busines & affaires whatsoeu<sup>r</sup>, w<sup>ch</sup> they or any by them authorized shall thinke fitt to ymploie him in, aswell at, in, vnto and from the said East Indies as at or in any other place or places whatsoeu<sup>r</sup> during the space of yeares next ensueing the date aboue written, or during soe many and such tyme of the said yeares as the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Company or their successo<sup>rs</sup>, or such as shall be by them authorized shall thinke meete, and for such wagę and Consideracõn as alredie is agreed vpon betweene the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Company and him the said **A B.** as is specified and sett downe in the Courte Booke of the said Company. Yf therefore the said **A B** doe from hencforth during all the said terme of yeares, or soe longe tyme thereof as the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Company or their successo<sup>rs</sup> shall reteine him in their service well trulie and honestlie serve the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Company their successo<sup>rs</sup> and Assignes as their servant in all and eu<sup>r</sup>y their affaires and busines as Pursar or otherwyse whatsoeu<sup>r</sup> as they or such as shalbe by them authorized shall thinke good to ymploie him. & doe his best endevo<sup>r</sup> for pformaunce & execucõn of what he shall be sett aboute or ymployed in as aforesaid for the proffitt and good service of the said Companie. And according to the chardge he is now ymployed in as a Pursar doe keepe a true and pfect Accompt by Inventorie of all such provision tackle municõn furniture, victualls and other necessaries w<sup>ch</sup> are or shall be during the said voyadge brought abourd the said shipp or prouided for thuse of the same. And alsoe an Inventorie of all the goode wares & m<sup>r</sup>chandize as shalbe brought into or caried out of the said shipp, aswell belonging vnto the said Companie as any other. And doe likewise keepe an Inventorie & Accompt of the expence & bestowinge of all such provision tackle municõn furniture and other necessaries w<sup>ch</sup> shall be brought into or caried out of the said shipp & of the remainder thereof. And doe at all tymes being therevnto required deliu<sup>r</sup> vp a true [p. 222] Accompt of the same or any other his ymploym<sup>t</sup> to the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> of the said m<sup>r</sup>chauntę or his Deputie, or to such as shall be authorized thereunto by the said Companie: And doe not in this or any other voyadge or voyadgę of the said Company vse any private trade or traffique in m<sup>r</sup>chandize for his owne propper Accompt or Adventure, or Colo<sup>r</sup> the private trade of any other. That then &c:

> _[Margin: The Condicon of hired servantes to be imployed in any place bound in 200<sup>li</sup> wth suerties.]_

THE Condicõn of this obliga​cõn is such. That wheareas the aboue bound Samuell Broadshawe[^sec-06-fn-162] is now hired by the aboue named Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> & Company of m<sup>r</sup>chauntę of London trading into the East Indies & hath agreed to serue the said Company & their successo<sup>rs</sup> as their Couenante servant in all & eu<sup>r</sup>y such busines and affaires whatsoeu<sup>r</sup> w<sup>ch</sup> they or any by them authorized shall thinke fitt to ymploy him in, aswell at in vnto and from the East Indies as at or in any other place or places whatsoeu<sup>r</sup> during the space of yeares next ensueing the date aboue written, or during soe many and such tyme of the said yeares as the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> & Company or their successo<sup>rs</sup>, or such as shalbe by them authorized shall thinke meete & for such wages & Consideracõn as alreadie is agreed vpon betweene the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> & Company & him the [p. 223] said **A B** as is specified and sett downe in the Courte Booke of the said Company. Yf therefore the said Samuell Broadshawe doe from hencforth during all the said terme of		yeares or soe long tyme thereof as the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Companie or their successo<sup>rs</sup> shall reteyne him in their service well trulie & honestlie serve the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> & Company their successo<sup>rs</sup> and Assignes as their servan[t] in all and eu<sup>r</sup>y their affaires and busines whatsoeu<sup>r</sup> w<sup>ch</sup> they or such as shall be by them authorized shall thinke good to ymploy him and doe his best endevo<sup>r</sup> for p̄formance & execuc̃on of what he shall be sett aboute or ymployed in as aforesaid for the proffitt and good service of the said Companie. And according to the chardg he is or shall be ymployed in doe keepe a true & p̄fect accompt of all such thinge as is or shalbe Comitted to his chardge And doe at all tymes being theare vnto required deliu<sup>r</sup> vp atrue Accompte of the same his ymploym<sup>t</sup> to the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> of the said m<sup>r</sup>chaunte or his deputie or to such as shalbe authorized therevnto by the said Company And doe not in this or any other voyadge or voyage of the said Company vse any private trade or traffique in m<sup>r</sup>chandize for his owne propp Accompt or Adventure or Colo<sup>r</sup> the private trade of any other. That then &c:

> _[Margin: The Preacher bound in to performe this Condicon.]_
> _[Margin: A Condic̃on that the Pursar or other shall saue harmles his suertie.]_

THE Condic̃on of this Obligac̃on is such That wheareas the aboue bound ffrancis Shapton is hired and agreed w<sup>th</sup>all[^sec-06-fn-163] by the aboue named Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Companie of m<sup>r</sup>chaunte of London trading into the East Indies to goe as Preacher in this their present intended 4<sup>th</sup> voyadge to those pte. Yf therefore the said ffrancis Shapton doe not absent himselfe but willinglie goe in the said voyadge & therein according to his best skill & knowledge doe his vttermost endevo<sup>r</sup> diligentlie to teach and instruct o<sup>r</sup> people by all loueing & godlie admonitions. And doe not during the said voyadge vse any private trade or [p. 224] traffique in m<span class="sc"><sup>r</sup></span>chandizeing for his owne prop<span class="sc">p</span> Accompt or Adventure, or Colo<span class="sc"><sup>r</sup></span> the private trade of any other. That then this &c: <span class="sc">the</span> Condic̃on of this &c: That wheareas the aboue named **A B.** at the spetiall request and intreatie of the aboue bound **T S**[^sec-06-fn-164] by his obliga<span class="sc">c̃</span>on of the date aboue written standeth firmlie held and bound vnto S<span class="sc"><sup>r</sup></span> Thomas Smyth knight & Will̃m Greenwell to thuse of the Companie of m<span class="sc"><sup>r</sup></span>chauntę of London trading to the East Indies in the some and penaltie of 200<sup>li</sup> of lawfull &c: w<sup>th</sup> Condic̃on therevnto for the faithfull service of the said **T S** vnto the foresaid Companie and pformaunce of c<span class="sc"><sup>r</sup></span>teine other Condic̃ons and thingę therein mencioned and expressed as thereby at lardge appe<span class="sc">t</span>h. If therefore the said **T S.** his Execū or Ađs doe at all tymes heereafter and from tyme to tyme sufficientlie saue and keepe harmlesse & indempnified the said **A B** his Heires Executor<sup>s</sup> and Admĩstrator<sup>s</sup> of for and conc<span class="sc"><sup>r</sup></span>ninge the said Obliga<span class="sc">c̃</span>on wherein the saied **A B** standeth bound as is aforesaid. And of for and from all arrestę Ac<span class="sc">c̃</span>ons suitę Iudgm<span class="sc"><sup>t</sup></span>ę execuc̃ons troubles chardgę and damadgę whatsoeu<span class="sc"><sup>r</sup></span> w<span class="sc"><sup>ch</sup></span> he the said **A B** his heires Execū or Ađs shall thereby susteyne and incurr. That then this &c:

> _[Margin: A Lycence for transportacoñ of moneys vncoyned 1607.]_

<span class="sc">James</span>[^sec-06-fn-165] by the grace of god kinge of England Scotland ffraunce and Ireland defendo<span class="sc"><sup>r</sup></span> of the faith, &c: To all to whome theis pñtę shall come Greeteing. Wheareas o<span class="sc"><sup>r</sup></span> late deere sister Queene Elizabeth by her tres Patente vnder the greate seale of England beareing [p. 225] date at Westminster the one & thirteth daie of Decemb̃ in the three and forteth yeare of her reigne vpon petic̃on made vnto her by diuʳs her loueing subiectę for her royall Assent and lycense to be granted vnto them. That they at their owne Adventure Costę and chardges aswell for the honoʳ of this Realme of England as for the increase of Nauigac̃on and Advancemᵗ of trade of mʳchandize wᵗʰin the same might Adventure and sett forth cʳteine voyage wᵗʰ a Convenient nomber of shipps & Pynnaces by way of traffique & mʳchandize into the East Indies in the Countries and Portę of Asia & Affrica did incorporate the said petitionʳs into a Bodie politique by the name of the Gouʳnoʳ and Companie of mʳchauntę of London trading into the East Indies. To haue hould and inioy the sole benefitt of the trade & traffique of the said East Indies for the space of fyfteene yeares from the birth of oʳ lord god then last past before the date of the said łres Patentę. And wheareas by the said łres Patentę lycence was granted to the said Gouʳnoʳ and Company of mʳchauntę of London trading into the East Indies to transporte out of this Realme into the said Indies in euʳy of their voyadgę during the said terme of ffyfteene yeares All such forreine Coyne of Silver, Spanish or other forreine sylver, or bullion of sylver as they should during the said terme bring or cause to be brought into this Realme of England from the partę beyond the Seas, either in the same kinde, stampe, sorte or fashion wᶜʰ it should haue when they brought it in or any other forme stampe or fashion Coyned in the mynte wᵗʰin the Tower of London soe as the whole quantities of Coyne or moneys by them to be transported in any of their said voyadgę during the said terme should not exceed the value of Thirtie Thowsand poundę in any one voyadge and soe as the some of eight[^sec-06-fn-166] Thowsand poundę at the least pcell of the said some or value 30000<sup>li</sup> to be transported as aforesaid should be first coyned wᵗʰin the said Tower of London before the tyme[^sec-06-fn-167] might be transported in any of the said voyadgę as by the said łres Patentę more at lardge appeth. Now forasmuch as the said Gouʳnoʳ and Companie of the said mʳchauntę since the said łres Patentę to them granted [p. 226] made twoe seu<sup>r</sup>all voyadge into the said East Indies and retourned their shipps from thence laden w<sup>th</sup> sundrie kinde of m<sup>r</sup>chandizes proffitable for o<sup>r</sup> kingdomes, and haue alreadie sett forth the last yeare a third voyage & are now in a redines to sett forth a fourth voyadge into the said East Indies, and haue humblie besought by Petic̃on & shewed vnto vs that by experience they haue form<sup>r</sup>lie found that they could not w<sup>th</sup>out greate difficultie and losse vnto them in the value of their moneys new coyned make trade for their m<sup>r</sup>chandize into the said East Indies because they were not such as the People of those pte were acquainted w<sup>th</sup>all, but stamped w<sup>th</sup> an Imadge or supscripc̃on strange and vnknowne vnto them And that they haue beene and are desierous by all good meanes to manadge and carie their said trade as neere as they can for the benefitt of o<sup>r</sup> kingdomes & domynions, rather by the transportac̃on of the natiue Comodities of the same, & by bartring & exchandge of them for forraine Comodities, w<sup>ch</sup> now they purpose more lardglie to attempt & haue good hope to accomplish then by vsing the whole libtie granted to them by the said tres Patente for carying out of the full some of Thirtie thowsand pounde in eu<sup>r</sup>y voyadge in mann<sup>r</sup> aforesaid, And that they will content themselues in this their now intended fourth voyadge to the said Indies w<sup>th</sup> the libtie of Transporting Twentie thowsand pounde onelie in forreine Coines or forreine sylver w<sup>th</sup>out other Coyne bullion or Silver. In reguard wheareof they did humblie pray in their said petic̃on that we would be gratiouslie pleased to graunte them lycence that they may transporte the value of Twentie Thowsand pounde in forreine Coynes or forreine sylver in this their intended fourth voyadge, w<sup>th</sup>out new coyneing the same, or any pte thereof Knowe yee therefore that we favoring the said m<sup>r</sup>chaunte, and being desierous to giue them furtherance and incourradgem<sup>t</sup> to proceede and goe forward in their trade, of o<sup>r</sup> espetiall grace c<sup>r</sup>teine knowledge & meere motion haue geven and granted and by theis presente for vs o<sup>r</sup> heires and Successo<sup>rs</sup> doe giue and graunte lycence vnto the said Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Companie of m<sup>r</sup>chaunte of London trading into the East Indies that it shall and may be lawfull for them their facto<sup>rs</sup> and Assignes in this now intended fourth voyadge into the East Indies, to transporte out of this o<sup>r</sup> Realme of England all such forreine Coyne or silver, either Spanish or other forreine silver as they haue prepared [p. 227] procured or gotten or shall p<sup>r</sup>pare procure or gett being alreadie brought or to be brought from the parte beyond the seas, before the depture of their shipps out of the River of Thames soe as the whole quantitie of the Coyne moneys & silver by them soe to be transported in this their present intended fourth voyadge towarde the said East Indies doe not exceede the value of Twentie thowsand pounde the same to be transported in the same kinde, sorte, stampe, or fashion as they said moneys or silver are or shall be procured gotten or brought into this Realme of England, & that w<sup>th</sup>out any new coyneing or altering the said forreine monies or silver, or any p<sup>t</sup>e thereof Any statute restrainte or prohibition in that behalfe made to the Contrary in any wise notw<sup>th</sup>standing. In witnes whereof we haue caused theis o<sup>r</sup> łres to be made Patente Witnes o<sup>r</sup> selfe at westm̄ the eight day of ffebruarie in the fifte yeare of o<sup>r</sup> Reigne of England ffraunce and Ireland & of Scotland the one and forteth.

p łre de privato sigillo *Coppin.*


![Decorative woodcut historiated initial I with foliate scrollwork.](../figures/fig-015_p0319.webp)

> _[Margin: A spetiall Comission granted vnto Alexander Sharpie Generall & Richard Rowles Leieutenant genrall 1607.]_

<span class="sc">Ames</span>[^sec-06-fn-168] by the grace of God kinge of England Scotland ffraunce and Ireland defendo<sup>r</sup> of the faith &c: To o<sup>r</sup> trustie and welbeloued Alexander Sharpie and Richard Rowles Greeting Whereas diu<sup>r</sup>s of o<sup>r</sup> loueing subiecte at their owne Adventures coste and chardge aswell for the hono<sup>r</sup> of this o<sup>r</sup> Realme of England as for the increase and advancem<sup>t</sup> of trade of m<sup>r</sup>chandize w<sup>th</sup>in the same haue form<sup>r</sup>lie sett forth three voyadge to the East Indies w<sup>th</sup> c<sup>r</sup>teine shipps & Pinnace by way of m<sup>r</sup>chandizeing by w<sup>ch</sup> shipps and Pinnace they haueing discou<sup>r</sup>ed [p. 228] and begunn to settle a trade in some pte of the said East Indies & their shipps being retourned in twoe of their form<sup>r</sup> voyadge from thence laden w<sup>th</sup> sundrie m<sup>r</sup>chandize brought from those pte, they the said m<sup>r</sup>chaunte intending to frequent those Countries of the East Indies by Contynuing the trade alreadie discou<sup>r</sup>ed and begonn and indevoring further discou<sup>r</sup>y of trade of those pte for the more ample vent of the natiue Comodities of o<sup>r</sup> kingdomes, and retourning from the places of their discou<sup>r</sup>y such necessarie Commodities as shalbe of spetiall vse and benefitt both to vs and o<sup>r</sup> subiecte, and haue now prepared c<sup>r</sup>teine shipps to the said East Indies. And whereas the said m<sup>r</sup>chaunte haue Chosen you the said Alexander Sharpey to be principall Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> or Gen<sup>r</sup>all of all the m<sup>r</sup>chaunte Mariners and other o<sup>r</sup> subiecte w<sup>ch</sup> are or shalbe shipped in any of the said shipps. And you the said Richard Rowles to be Leiutenant gen<sup>r</sup>all of all the m<sup>r</sup>chaunte Marin<sup>r</sup>s & other o<sup>r</sup> subiete w<sup>ch</sup> are or shall be shipped in any of the said shipps, Wee gratiouslie favoring their intended voyadge and approueing and allowing of their choise of you [to] the same Gou<sup>r</sup>nm<sup>t</sup> being desierous to furnish you w<sup>th</sup> all fitt and Convenient power and authoritie to rule and gou<sup>r</sup>ne all & eu<sup>r</sup>y o<sup>r</sup> subiecte ymployed in this voyadge by a due obedience to be by them yealded vnto you in the obserueing & executeing of all such [p. 229] good orders and Constitucõns as you shall thinke Convenient to ordaine and appointe for the furtherance of the said voyadge to the honor of vs and or kingdomes, and for the advancemt of The said trade doe hereby straightlie chardge and Comand all and eury pson and psonns ymployed vsed or shipped in this voyadge in any of the said shipps to giue all due obedience and respect vnto you during the said voyadge, and to beare themselues one towarde another in all good order and quietnes for avoieding any occasion that might breed mutiny quarrells or dissencoñ amongst them to the hindrance of the good successe wch is to be hoped for by Gode providence of the said intended voyadge, and in defaulte of such dutie & obedience to be pformed towarde you for the Correccõn and quenching of all such mutiny quarrells or dissencoñ that shall or may be moued by the disorder evill disposition or pversnes of any the said psonns. Wee doe hereby authorize you the said Alexander Sharpie during the said voyadge or during soe long tyme as you shall lyve in the said voyadge to chastice correct and ponish all Offendors and transgressors in that behalfe according to the qualitie of their Offences wth such ponishmte as are comonlie vsed in all Armies by Sea when they are not Capitall, And for Capitall Offences as for wilfull murther wch is hatefull in the sight of god, or muteny wch is an offence that may tend to the ourthrowe of the said voyadge the same being trulie and iustlie proved against any of the pson or psonns aforesaid. We doe hereby giue vnto you the said Alexander Sharpie during all the tyme of the said voyadge or during soe long tyme as you shall liue in the same full power and authoritie to vse and put in execucõn or lawe called Marshall lawe in that behalfe. And in case of yor decease wch god forbid we doe then likewise hereby authorize you the said Richard Rowles to execute the power and authoritie by this or Comission granted to the said Alexander Sharpey in as ample mannr as is herein before expressed, and in such sorte as the said Alexander Sharpey did or might doe by vertue hereof. and theis or lres shalbe vnto you and either of you sufficient warrant and dischardge for the doing and executeing of all and singuler the premisses. And forasmuch as at this present tyme we are in amitie wth all Christian Princes and are vnwilling that any or subiecte should giue occasion of breache or hindrance of that league [p. 230] or amitie w<sup>ch</sup> we hould w<sup>th</sup> any o<sup>r</sup> Confederate freinde or Allies. And because we are not ignorant of the emulac̃on and envie that doth accompanie the discou<sup>r</sup>y of Countries and trade and of the quarrells and Contenc̃ons w<sup>ch</sup> doe many tymes fall out betweene the subiecte of diu<sup>r</sup>s Princes that meete the one w<sup>th</sup> the other in forreine and farr remote Countries in the Course & psecuteing of their discou<sup>r</sup>ies, and being desierous that o<sup>r</sup> subiecte should forbeare to moue or beginn any quarrell or Contenc̃on vpon the subiecte of o<sup>r</sup> Confederate freinde or Allies either in their pceeding or retourne vpon or from any of their voyadge. We therefore doe hereby straightlie chardge and Comand you the said Alexander Sharpie, and you the said Richard Rowles and all other vnder yo<sup>r</sup> gou<sup>r</sup>nm<sup>t</sup> that neither in yo<sup>r</sup> voyadge outward or homewarde or in any Countrie Iland Porte or place where you shall abide or come during the time of yo<sup>r</sup> being abroad out of o<sup>r</sup> kingdomes or dominions where you meete w<sup>th</sup> any the subiecte of the kinge of Spaine or of any other o<sup>r</sup> Confederate freinde or allies, or of any other nac̃on or people, their shipps vessells goode or m<sup>r</sup>chandize you doe attempt or goe aboute to sett vpon take or surprize their psons shipps Vessells goode or m<sup>r</sup>chandizes or offer any iniurie or discourtesie vnto them vnlesse you shall be by them first therevnto iustlie prouoked or driven either in the iust defence of yo<sup>r</sup> owne psonns yo<sup>r</sup> ships vessells goode or m<sup>r</sup>chandize either by any other their disturbance or hindrance whatsoeu<sup>r</sup> in yo<sup>r</sup> quiett course of trade either for recompence or recou<sup>r</sup>y of the psonns goode or m<sup>r</sup>chandize of any o<sup>r</sup> subiecte that are alreadie in or neare the East Indies or otherwise for any iust cause of yo<sup>r</sup> defence as you will awnsweare the Contrarie at yo<sup>r</sup> vttermost pills. In Witnes whereof we haue caused theis o<sup>r</sup> lres to be made Patente Witnes o<sup>r</sup> selfe at Westm̄ the eight day of ffebruarie in the fifte yeare of o<sup>r</sup> Reigne of England ffraunce & Ireland & of Scotland the xxxxj<sup>th</sup>[^sec-06-fn-169]

*Coppin.*

p̄ b̄re de priuato sigillo


### Notes

[^sec-06-fn-001]: (1) This is the famous first Charter of the Company, granted by Queen Elizabeth on the last day of the sixteenth century. In the absence of the original (of the fate of which nothing is known) the above is the oldest and most authoritative version in the India Office collection. There is another manuscript copy among the "Parchment Records" (No. 2), but it is of later date, and, so far as can be judged, of inferior [p. 164] accuracy. As, however, it is evidently taken from an independent source, the two have been carefully compared, and the differences noted, where at all important. Besides these, there is a very early copy, in excellent preservation, in vol. 306 of the *Harleian MSS.* in the British Museum; this also has been collated with the present text, and all variations (except where the difference is merely one of spelling) have been recorded in the footnotes. Finally, the version printed by Purchas has been consulted in cases where the others disagree; and thus, it is hoped, the materials for a fairly reliable text of this most important document have been obtained and placed on record.

He was a large subscriber to the early voyages of the Company, and one of the first committees (see page 169).

[^sec-06-fn-009]: (8) Maurice Abbott, brother of George, Archbishop of Canterbury, and of Robert, Bishop of Salisbury. In 1615 he visited the East Indies; and on his return was made deputy governor of the Company, to which post he was re-elected 8 times. He was one of those appointed to treat with the Dutch Commissioners in London in 1619, and in the following year was sent, with Sir Dudley Digges, on a special [p. 165] embassy to Holland on the same business. He became governor of the Company in March, 1624, and held that post until some time in 1638 or 1639, the period of his mayoralty. He was a member of parliament for several years, and spoke often in defence of the Company. He was knighted on the accession of Charles I., who, some 14 years later, made him "king's lieutenant" of London and suburbs during his Majesty's absence in the expedition against the Scots. He died 10th Jan., 1641/2.

[^sec-06-fn-035]: (10) Richard Wright was the first secretary of the Company, mention being made of him in that capacity on the 8th Oct., 1600, and he was still secretary in July, 1602. The loss of the second Court Book prevents us from saying how long he held this post, but there is reason to think that it could not have been to a later date than July, 1606. In 1615 he married the widow of John Stockley, who had been also a freeman of the Company, and a committee in 1608-10. Mrs. Stockley seems to have been a woman of some wealth, for at her husband's funeral the governor, deputy and committees were invited to dinner (*Court Minutes*, 29th Jan., 1614), and in the same year she adventured £1200 in the Company's stock (*Ibid.*, 18th Feb., 1614). On 13th May, 1618, "Lyonell, son of Richard Wright, of Walthamstow," was admitted to the freedom of the Company, and as the admission was by patrimony, this entry probably relates to a son of the whilom secretary.

It would seem (see note 2 on next page) that wormseed was at this time occasionally included under the term "Zedoary."

[^sec-06-fn-127]: (2) Obviously the copyist's corruption of *Setwall*, the "cetewale" and "setewale" of Chaucer and "setuale" of Spenser, corruptions of the Low Latin *zedoaria*, a corruption of the Arabo-Persian *djedwar*, a denomination which in the mediæval commerce of Europe with India originally included Zedoaria rotunda, the tuber of *Curcuma Zedoaria*, Zedoaria longa, the tuber of *Curcuma Zerumbet*, Zedoaria flava, or Cassumanar, the tuber of *Zingiber Cassumanar*, and Zerumbet, the tuber of *Zingiber Zerumbet*, the last trade denomination being a corruption of the Arabo-Persian *zurumbad*. Chaucer and Spenser, however, by Setwall probably meant either the "Common Valerian" (*Valeriana officinalis*) or "Spanish Valerian" (*V. pyrenaica*); and our English botanists of the seventeenth century also included under the term the drug Spikenard, the *sumbul* or *jatamansi* of the bazaars of India, the fleshy rhizome of the "Himalayan Valerian" (*Nardostachys Jatamansi*), the νάρδος πιστίκος of the Gospels of St. Mark and St. John, where the qualifying adjective (meaning in Greek "faithful," "genuine") obviously came to be attached to the substantive νάρδος (the Persian *nard* from the Sanskrit *nar*, "a perfume") from its phonetic resemblance to the Sanskrit *pisita*, "fleshy." As, however, "Spikenard" is separately denominated in the previous line of the present list of drugs, while "Setweth" is named after "Galingath" and "Turmericke," it is clear that in the early trade of the Company, Setwall still continued to stand for one or more of the varieties of Zedoary above enumerated.

    "A chambir had he in that hostillerye\
    Alone, withouten eny compaignye,\
    Ful fetisly i-dight with herbes soote,\
    And he himself as swete as is the roote\
    Of lokorys, or eny cetewale."

    Chaucer: *Milleres Tale*.

    "Ther was eke wexing many a spice,\
    As clowe-gelofre, and lycorice,\
    Gyngevre, and greyn de Parys,\
    Canelle, and setewale of prys."

    Chaucer: *Romaunt of the Rose*.

    "Embathed Balme and chearfull Galingale\
    • • • • •\
    Dull Poppy and drink quenching Setuale."

    Spenser: *Muiopotmos*.

    "Went forth when May was in her prime (O: S:)\
    To get sweet Setywale."

    Drayton: *Pastorals*, Ec: IV.

    See also John Gerarde's *Herball or Generall Historie of Plantes* (London, 1633); and the *Nomenclator* of Adrianus Junius (London, 1585), in which the entry regarding Zedoary is:—"Zadura *vulgo* Zedoaria. Cretonart. Zedoarie, or [as some say] [p. 201] wormseede." In Florio's *Worlde of Wordes* (London, 1598), it is :—" Zedoaria, the herbe Zederie, or wormeseede ;" and in Skinner's *Etymologicon* (London, 1671) : —" Setwall, Valeriana sic dicta vel quod seratur circa Muros, vel quod Muros sponte sua obsideat." The term " Cretonart " in the above quotation from the *Nomenclator* of Adrianus Junius I find again only in Vansleb's *Present State of Egypt* (London, 1678), where it follows Ginger, in the list of druggists' roots exported from Egypt in the seventeenth century.

The *Hector*, a "ship of London, trading to Surat, where she arrived in August last, intercepted by "four Portugal frigates 3rd October following and taken prize, and the men prisoners "for using commerce within their conquest without the King of Spain's licence; "value of the goods, 2,000*l*; 19 prisoners carried to Goa, three brought to Lisbon, "the rest at Goa.     "Was alsoe red twoe lres the one from Anthonie Marlowe thother from ffrancis "Bucke the Companies servauntes dated at Lisborne the 15<sup>th</sup> of Iulie last, Alsoe w<sup>th</sup> "a discourse of their goinge to Surate & of their takeinge & mishapps therein: & of "their ymprisonment at Lisborne &c: And their request to the Companie for their "inlardgm<sup>t</sup> ........ Upon Consideracon whereof ...... it was thought fitt That "w<sup>th</sup> all expedicon the Lord Threr be made acquainted w<sup>th</sup> theis their lres, w<sup>th</sup> "request of his honorable favo<sup>r</sup> to his ma<sup>tie</sup>: for releefe theirin, for diuers respectes "mentioned, *As by the peticon in the Register at lardge appereth*. And for the effectinge "of this busines m<sup>r</sup> Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup>, m<sup>r</sup> Deputie, m<sup>r</sup> Harrison, m<sup>r</sup> Iohnson, & m<sup>r</sup> Hamersley "were intreated w<sup>th</sup> all Convenient speede to repaier vnto the Lord Threr at "Salisburie, or where his Lo<sup>p</sup>: may be found, to acquainte his Lo<sup>p</sup>: therew<sup>th</sup>, & w<sup>th</sup> "what ells they shall thinke fitt for the good & speedie dispatch hereof." (*Court Minutes*, 8th Aug., 1609.)

    "Att this Courte m<sup>r</sup> Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> declared how kindlie he & those appointed to goe "w<sup>th</sup> him to the Courte were intreated by the Lord Threr whoe promyseth to haue "a spetiall care of their sute vnto his Ma<sup>tie</sup>: & at his Lo<sup>ps</sup>: retourne to London w<sup>ch</sup> "would be w<sup>th</sup>in Tenn daies, he would giue them further satisfaccon touchinge their "sute." (*Ibid.*, 14th Aug., 1609.)

    A further letter on this subject will be found on page 306. It would appear that the prisoners were set at liberty at the end of 1610 or the beginning of 1611, through the good offices of the English ambassador in Spain.

[^sec-06-fn-162]: (1) Samuel Bradshaw or Broadshawe was engaged by the Company on 15th Dec., 1607, for service “at home or abroad, as they see fit, at 16*l*. per annum.” On the 29th of the following month, he was told off to attend Mr. Rowles, the lieutenant-general of the voyage. Later on (26th Feb.) he is referred to as a factor. We learn from *Purchas* that, on the murder in Madagascar of Rowles and his companions, Bradshaw took the command of the vessel for the rest of the voyage. It will be remembered that on the way home the ship was lost off the coast of Brittany; and as Bradshaw is not mentioned among the survivors, it may be presumed that he went down with the ship.

    There is an entry in the *Cal. S. P., East Indies*, 1513-1616, of a letter from Samuel Bradshaw at Tecco, under date 10th Feb., 1613; but from an examination of the document to which it relates (*O. C.* 104), it seems clear that the date given is that on which the *copy* (for it is only a copy) was made, and that the original must have been the letter from Bradshaw of 11th March 1609/10, to which reference is made in Moris's letter from Bantam of 14th Sept., 1610, printed in *Purchas*, Lib. III., c. 9, § 3.

[^sec-06-fn-168]: (1) A Commission to the commanders of the *Fourth Voyage*, the most disastrous of all the early ventures of the Company. The expedition consisted of two vessels, viz. the *Assention*, which had been previously employed in the *First* and *Second Voyages*, and the *Union*, which was specially bought for the occasion. Alexander Sharpie, the General of the expedition, was in command of the *Assention*, and Richard Rowles took charge of the *Union*. The two ships got separated after leaving Saldanha Bay. The *Assention*, after some delay on the African coast, and visits to Aden (where [p. 228] Sharpie was for some time kept prisoner by the governor) and Mocha, shaped her course for Surat. On the 29th August, she ran on a shoal in the bay of Cambay, and three days later became a total wreck. The crew made their way in their boats into the Gandevi River, some thirty miles south of Surat. Here they were hospitably treated by the natives and passed on to Surat, whence Sharpie and a large number of the men started for Agra. Sharpie and others were left sick on the route; others died or straggled from the company; and finally only three men reached their destination, and reported the state of affairs to Captain Hawkins, who was then in the city as the representative of the Company. In Oct., 1611, Sharpie embarked on the *Trades Increase* at Surat, and accompanied Sir Henry Middleton, who seems to have entertained a high opinion of him, to Mocha and Bantam. Captain Downton, writing in June, 1613, mentions Sharpie as being then absent from Bantam, and this is the last notice of him that can be traced.

    The *Union*, as has already been mentioned on page 222, note, after losing her commander and several of her men at Madagascar, proceeded to Acheen and procured a cargo, but on her way home, was wrecked off Audierne, on the coast of Brittany, with the loss of nearly all her crew.

    There is a docquet of this commission in the Public Record Office (*see Cal. Dom. State Papers*, 1603-1610, p. 400).

### What łres were written from his ma<sup>tie</sup> to the Princes in the East Indies in ffebruarie 1607.[^sec-07-fn-001]

> _[Margin: In all 12 łres were now sent in Spaignish as before.[^sec-07-fn-003]]_

<span class="sc">That</span> was the form<sup>r</sup> 7 łres *folio.* 41.[^sec-07-fn-002] Viz to Suratt Aden Tedore Nere Lunter Iava Maior, Molloccos, & the łre of the Teno<sup>r</sup> of that to Surate purposed for Callicutt, written from his ma<sup>tie</sup>: to those Princes Anno 1606. were now all againe of new written from his ma<sup>tie</sup>: to those Princes in Anno 1607 w<sup>th</sup> this Addic̃on to each onelie That is. Although we sent vnto you the last yeare after the retourne of o<sup>r</sup> Subiectę from those pte & sent you a Present yet for that we doubt whether those łres be come to yo<sup>r</sup> hande, we haue thought good to Visitt you againe w<sup>th</sup> new łres & w<sup>th</sup> a new present, And to lett you vnderstand that the Contente of o<sup>r</sup> former łres were to this purpose That &c: as in the m<sup>r</sup>gent of the foresaid łre to the Molloccos.[^sec-07-fn-004]

Lykewise ffower łres more were now written from his ma<sup>tie</sup>: to the Princes & Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>rs</sup> in those parts Viz 2 of the Teno<sup>r</sup> of that of Suratt w<sup>th</sup> generall salutačons in the inside & on the outside left Blancke for o<sup>r</sup> ffacto<sup>rs</sup> to sett downe the names and titles of such Princes there as they shall see good to deliu<sup>r</sup> them vnto, w<sup>th</sup> Presentę alsoe in their discrec̃ons.
