In the name of God Amen the 14<sup>th</sup> day of Aprill Anno dn̄i 1609. A Comission agreed vpon and sett downe by us the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> Deputy and Comittees of the Marchaunt*e* of London tradeinge to the East Indies, [p. 296] aswell for the better direccoñ of o<sup>r</sup> loueinge freind, and principall ffactor Captaine David Middleton, As for all other ffacto<sup>rs</sup>, Master, Pylott, Pursers Mariners, and other Officers or psonns goeinge in this o<sup>r</sup> present intended Voyadge to the East Indies in the good shipp named the Expedicoñ: w<sup>ch</sup> we humbly beseech Almightie God, to blesse w<sup>th</sup> a happy successe and Conclucoñ.[^sec-07-fn-102]

> _[Margin: **1**]_

<span class="sc">Nprimis</span> whereas we the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> Deputie Comittees & Marchaunte aforesaid have to o<sup>r</sup> greate chardge prepared the said shipp named the Expedicoñ of the burthen of 240 Tonnes, wherein Edmund Musgraue goeth m<sup>r</sup> for a voyadge by Godę grace to be made to the East Indies, And haue furnished the same sufficientlie and in plentifull manner, w<sup>th</sup> men, tackle, victualles and all other needfull puisions for such a voyadge, of a spetiall trust and Confidence, w<sup>ch</sup> we haue in the integritie and iust carriadge of o<sup>r</sup> said loueinge freinde David Middleton; we doe appointe and authorize him Captaine to goe in the same shipp, and to Comand all the menn therein, haueinge pcured him sufficient authoritie from o<sup>r</sup> Sou<sup>r</sup>eigne lord the kinge mat<sup>ie</sup>: in that behalfe: Not doubtinge but that he will soe behaue himselfe, as he may be both feared and loued. And that he will w<sup>th</sup> all his dilligence and endeavors prosequute o<sup>r</sup> designes & labour to bringe this o<sup>r</sup> voyadge to a happie end.

2 Item for that Religious gou<sup>r</sup>nm<sup>t</sup> and exercise, doth best bynde menn to pforme their Duties: We doe appointe and order: That prayers be said Morneinge & eveninge in the shipp, And the whole Company called therevnto, That all ioinctlie may w<sup>th</sup> reverence & humility pray vnto Almightie God to blesse & preserue them from all dangers in this longe and tedious voyadge: And for better pformance thereof we haue deliu<sup>r</sup>ed a Bible vnto the Pursar.

3 Item that noe blasphemeinge of God sweareinge thefte drunckennes or other lyke misdemeanors be vsed, But that the same be sevearelie punnished, And that noe diceinge, or other unlawfull games be pmitted, ffor that the same ar most [p. 297] comolie the begyninge of quarrells & many tymes murther a iust occasion of Godę wrath and vengeance from w<sup>ch</sup> the Lord deliver vs all : wherefore we doe order That there shall be ponishmente prouided sett vpp and published in the said shipp for such Offences, whereby eu<sup>r</sup>y man may take notice what he ought to avoied.

4 Item That noe liquor be spilt in the Ballast of the shipp or filthines be left w<sup>th</sup>in bourde, w<sup>ch</sup> in heate breadeth noysome smells and infecc̃õn : But that the overlopps and other place of the shipp, be kept cleane and sweete w<sup>ch</sup> is a notable preservac̃õn of health.

5 Item That Contynuall and true Iournalls, be kept of eu<sup>r</sup>y daies course, and Navigac̃õn duringe the whole voyadge, w<sup>th</sup> a true relac̃õn of eu<sup>r</sup>y thinge that passeth : And this to be done seu<sup>r</sup>ally by Captaine, Master, Pilott, the Marchaunt Masters mate and pursar and they at Convenient tymes to Conferr togither aboute the same, To thend that yf any of them haue forgotten what an other hath obserued the same may be added whereby a pfect discourse may be sett downe to be presented to the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Company when God shall graunte the said shipp safe retourne and to be kept for better direcc̃õn of posteritie.

6 Item That the Company & M<sup>r</sup> take due notice of the seu<sup>r</sup>all provisions, deliu<sup>r</sup>ed to the said shipp, and to settle the same in the chardge of the Officers appointed for that purpose. And that the same be entred in the Pursars booke vnderwritten by the said Officers, To thend that such thingę as are puided, for their needfull supplies, may not be ymbecilled, And that nothinge thereof, be ymployed for any vse whatsoeuer, w<sup>th</sup>out warrant vnder the hand of the Captaine, directed to the Officer that hath such chardge w<sup>ch</sup> warrant shall serue for his dischardge in his accompte otherwyse to be awnswearable for the same w<sup>th</sup> his wagę, And eu<sup>r</sup>y such warrant to be registred in the pursars booke, The day of the monneth & the occasion, And this to be done alsoe by the Pursar vpon forfecture of soe much out of his wages.

7 Item That at eu<sup>r</sup>y place where yo<sup>u</sup> shall water and refresh yo<sup>r</sup> selues yo<sup>u</sup> shall call the whole Company together giueinge them most stricte & straight chardge and warneinge not to [p. 298] straggle but to behaue them selues peaceably & Civillie towarde the people of that place (yf any be there) the better to <span class="sc">p</span>cure their freindshipp towarde the supply of yo<sup>r</sup> wante, And the like to be done and vsed, in eu<sup>r</sup>y place where yo<sup>u</sup> come, least the losse of yo<sup>r</sup> liues and ou<sup>r</sup>throwe of o<sup>r</sup> voyadge, pay for yo<sup>r</sup> disorders, beside an vtter discredditt to o<sup>r</sup> Nac̃õn : And that yo<sup>r</sup> men doe vse, a discreete meane in eateinge of fruite, fresh victualls, or drinkeinge of water least they surfett, and fall into diseases, whereof we haue had too much experience : And the better to restraine vnrulie appetite : We thinke fit That yo<sup>u</sup> the Captaine doe appointe some of the discreetest in yo<sup>r</sup> Company to <span class="sc">p</span>cure and prouide in such places, what yo<sup>u</sup> want : And the same to be first brought vnto yo<sup>u</sup>, and yo<sup>u</sup> to repte the same to yo<sup>r</sup> Company as yo<sup>u</sup> shall see good and needfull, And that none presume to doe contrary w<sup>th</sup>out seveare ponishment : Alsoe that yo<sup>u</sup> haue a spetiall care, to see the sicke releeued w<sup>th</sup> such fresh meate and other Comfortable thinges, wherew<sup>th</sup> we haue furnished the said shipp for that purpose : And that the same be not otherwyse spent in Ryott & banquettinge, and soe the sicke <span class="sc">p</span>ishe for want of thinge needfull.

8\. Item when yo<sup>u</sup> haue refreshed yo<sup>r</sup> selues at Saldania or elswhere thereaboute, where yo<sup>u</sup> shall thinke most convenient and good for harbor, & plentie of victualls : yo<sup>u</sup> shall apply yo<sup>r</sup> selues, and w<sup>th</sup> all possible speede endevour yo<sup>r</sup> course for Bantam, And being arriued there, yo<sup>u</sup> shall Conferr and take aduise of o<sup>r</sup> ffactors for or Conc<sup>r</sup>ninge yo<sup>r</sup> voyadge to the Molluccos or Banda : And shall take alonge w<sup>th</sup> you thither such of o<sup>r</sup> said ffactors there as yo<sup>u</sup> shall thinke good, espetially Syddall for his experience as alsoe Spaldinge whome we hould the fittest psonns in that behalfe : But yf that yo<sup>u</sup> cannott <span class="sc">p</span>cure yo<sup>r</sup> ladeinge at the Molluccoes and Banda : Then we leaue the same to yo<sup>r</sup> discrec̃õn, to be done at Bantam, or any other place where yo<sup>u</sup> shall thinke will be most for o<sup>r</sup> proffitte.

9 Item yo<sup>u</sup> shall espetiallie foresee, and take care, That in ladeinge either Cloues Nutmegge or Mace yo<sup>u</sup> cleanes them as much as yo<sup>u</sup> cann from dust and Rumps, That the shipp be not stuffed w<sup>th</sup> such vnproffitable ware as is not worth the Custome, And soe we loose all o<sup>r</sup> chardge : wherefore rather burne the [p. 299] same, then[^sec-07-fn-103] lade it in the shipp And be carefull to buy dry Cloues and not such as are greene.

10 Item That yo<sup>u</sup> be very carefull to haue yo<sup>r</sup> due and full weight and the same putt into bagge nombred and marked and sent abourd the shipp w<sup>th</sup> some ffactor or other trustie psonn, w<sup>th</sup> a łre Conteyneinge the pticular of eu<sup>r</sup>y bagge vnder the nomber, The same łre to be deliuered to the pursar, whome we chardge to weigh eu<sup>r</sup>y bagge, at the takeing of yt into the shipp, whereby he may see that the weight is accordinge to the łre receiued, keepinge eu<sup>r</sup>y łre and entringe the Contente in his booke whereby yf any error happen yt may be found out, w<sup>ch</sup> we wish yo<sup>u</sup> the Captaine to examyne eu<sup>r</sup>y nighte That there growe noe abuse.

11 Item That the purser be Contynually aboorde the shipp and take true notice of all thinge whatsoeu<sup>r</sup> are brought into the shipp or carried out eyther by the Captaine Marchaunt ffactor Master Mariner, the pursar himselfe or any other whosoeuer, And to enter the same in his booke vnder the name of the Owner that eu<sup>r</sup>y one may haue his due at the returne, As the pursar will awnsweare yt w<sup>th</sup> the losse of his wage : And yo<sup>u</sup> the Captaine to giue the pursar stricte chardge in this behalfe.

12 Item, That there be but one hatch open (yf yt may be) at the ladeinge of the shipp, and thother hatches to be locked vp, and that the master or his Mate and the purser to stand by the open hatche when any goode are shott into hould lockeinge the same vpp when they haue left worke, and the key to be giuen to the Capteine to keepe.

13 Item That nothinge be bought, but what is espetiall good And that yo<sup>u</sup> doe not overwett the Cloues,[^sec-07-fn-104] badd nutmegge and mace haue taught vs to advise o<sup>r</sup> ffactors to be more carefull.

14 Item, for that voyadge of this Condic̃on and chardge cannott admitt any priuate trade our will is, And we doe expreslie order That neither yo<sup>u</sup> the Captaine, nor any other, vpon any pticuler, or other accompte, then the generall and ioincte stocke doe lade, or deale w<sup>th</sup> any of the Comodities herevnder expressed (Vizt) pepp, Cloues, Nutmegge, Mace, Synamon, Ginger Indico Callicoes Ambergreece, Muske Alloes Beniamyn Gumlacka Rawe & sleeue silke Pearles Dyamonde [p. 300] Bezar stones: And that yf any shall soe doe the same shall be applyed to thaccompt of the Company as o<sup>r</sup> owne propꝑ goode  It beinge noe way reasonable That wee should pay them their wages w<sup>th</sup> meate and drinke, And they lade those thinge in o<sup>r</sup> shipp, w<sup>ch</sup> should defray o<sup>r</sup> chardge.

15\. Item That in eu<sup>r</sup>y place where yo<sup>u</sup> come and trade yo<sup>u</sup> shall compare their waighte & measures w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>rs</sup> before yo<sup>u</sup> buye To thend yo<sup>u</sup> may knowe the Better what to doe And howe to make yo<sup>r</sup> rekeninge, ffor w<sup>ch</sup> purpose we haue putt a Chest w<sup>th</sup> weighte into our said Shippe.

16\. Item we straightlie chardge That the best and sufficientest of o<sup>r</sup> ffactors be appointed to wey, what is bought by weight on the land  And to keepe a p̄fect Booke thereof that the same may be nightlie conferred w<sup>th</sup> the pursars booke, whereby errors or abuses may be the better found out.

17  Item we straightlie chardge that noe excessiue drinkeinge feastinge or banquettinge, or shooteinge of of Gonnes be at any tyme made or vsed either aboorde the Shipp att Sea, or on land, The same beinge a greate waste and Consumpc̃on of victualls, wyne and powder & the cause of many diseases & disorders in the Company  And therefore to be spent w<sup>th</sup> discrec̃on and spareinge.

18  Item That yo<sup>u</sup> matt the inside of the shipp before yo<sup>u</sup> put or lade any spice in her, espetiallie where yo<sup>u</sup> lade Cloues Pepp Nutmegge & Mace, And that yo<sup>u</sup> make choise of such Nutmegge, as be lardge and sounde, And att the ladeinge thereof not to lyme them too much, for that doth burne them,  Alsoe that in any Case, yo<sup>u</sup> lay the Mace in Canisters in some fitt place by yt selfe, That yt be not spoyled by the heate of the other spice, takeinge good heede to buy that w<sup>ch</sup> is bright, & not wythered nor red, nor darke browne Colored  And lykewyse for Cloues to buy such as shall be free of dust, The w<sup>ch</sup> those people doe vse to putt amongst them for their advantage in the waight.

19  Item That yf necessitie drawe yo<sup>u</sup> at the ladeinge of any Cloues for better setlinge of them, to cast water vpon them, lett yt be but asprinkelinge w<sup>th</sup> some thinge for the purpose like a wateringe pott, for that too much wett in o<sup>r</sup> Cloues in other voyadge, hath brought vs greate damadge.

20  Item That yf o<sup>r</sup> ould Cloth w<sup>ch</sup> was left at Bantam, be [p. 301] not sould, Then yo<sup>u</sup> shall Conferr and aduyse w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> ffactors there howe the same shall or may be vented, either by sendinge yt to Banda : or by leaueinge (yf neede be) a ffactory at Banda w<sup>th</sup> the same and addinge therevnto some money and some other Comodities as yo<sup>u</sup> shall thinke fitt.

21 Item That yo<sup>u</sup> the Captaine doe giue often notice to all ꝑsons goeinge w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> in the shipp, what they are to obserue by this o<sup>r</sup> Comission & direcc̃ons, And that yo<sup>u</sup> giue espetiall chardge to all o<sup>r</sup> ffactors. That they make diligent inquiry what Comodities are to be bought or bartered for in eu<sup>r</sup>y Island, or place where they shall come or arriue And what English m<sup>r</sup>chandize may be there vented And of what kinde & Color most vendible

22 Item That yo<sup>u</sup> remember, aduise & putt o<sup>r</sup> ffactors at Bantam in mynde that they doe their best endevo<sup>rs</sup> to procure the Chineses to bringe from Chiney sleve and soweinge silkes of the Colo<sup>r</sup> and sizes we haue now deliu<sup>r</sup>ed vnto yo<sup>u</sup> As alsoe some Rawe silke that we may fall into some trade w<sup>th</sup> them, And see yf they can sell any of our English Cloth vnto them whereby to bringe them to the vse thereof.

23 Item, That yo<sup>u</sup> remember to doe yo<sup>r</sup> best endevo<sup>r</sup> to bringe for the Lo : Thr̄er some parratte Munkeys Marmesates, or other strange beaste and fowles, That yo<sup>u</sup> esteeme rare and delightfull.[^sec-07-fn-105]

24 Item, That for the quantities of moneys & m<sup>r</sup>chandize putt into this our said shipp, we referr yo<sup>u</sup> to o<sup>r</sup> invoise deliu<sup>r</sup>ed vnto yo<sup>u</sup> herew<sup>th</sup>, togither w<sup>th</sup> the ꝑticular sorte Collors and prices, w<sup>th</sup> patternes of all sorte, whereby to make sale.

25 Item whereas heretofore the Company haue receiued greate wronge by the Generalls Captaines Masters and Mariners admittance of voluntary men to goe in o<sup>r</sup> shipps : We therefore hereby straightlie chardge yo<sup>u</sup> the Captaine Master & other Officers, That yo<sup>u</sup> suffer none such to goe alonge w<sup>th</sup> you w<sup>ch</sup> putt the Company to greate chardge beside many other Inconvenience, Nor any but such as are, or shall be allowed of by o<sup>r</sup> direcc̃on and whose names are entered into o<sup>r</sup> Booke.

26 Item, for that yt is vnfitt, and inconvenient, That o<sup>r</sup> trade [p. 302] be ympted vnto any, but to o<sup>r</sup> generall Company we doe hereby expreslie order & appointe, That yo<sup>u</sup> chardge all o<sup>r</sup> ffactor<sup>s</sup>, not to write or aduise any their pticular freinde or others of the prices of any Comodities, either there bought or sould But onelie in their generall łres to the Gou<sup>r</sup>nor and Company.

27   Item That yo<sup>u</sup> the Captaine at yo<sup>r</sup> returne from Bantam for England doe bringe w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> vnto vs from thence an Inventory of all o<sup>r</sup> goode debte and moneys then remayneinge in those parte. And that yo<sup>u</sup> putt to o<sup>r</sup> generall accompte all guifte presente & gratificačons w<sup>ch</sup> shall be giuen by any forreine prince, potentate or others, to whome we haue hertofore giuen or sent any presente, or to whome there shall be nowe any given.

28   *Item*, That by agenerall Consent of yo<sup>u</sup> the Captaine ffactor Master Pilott & Mariners, some good order be by yo<sup>u</sup> sett downe in writeinge, soe soone as yo<sup>u</sup> come to Sea, conc<sup>r</sup>ninge the dispotičon of dead mens goode in the voyadge by sale at the maste, or otherwyse for buyeinge, sellinge borroweinge and lendinge one an other, And orderinge what Sallary shall be allowed the pursar, vpon eu<sup>r</sup>y pound, for keepinge accompte thereof to avoied Controu<sup>r</sup>sie and question heereafter, And eu<sup>r</sup>y Mariner and others in the shipp to sett their hand or marke vnto the same order: But yf any ffactor shall happen to dye, Then his goode booke accompte & other thinge are to be safelie preserued and brought home for England.

29   *Item*, that for better preservačon of health, yo<sup>u</sup> doe from tyme to tyme, as the water Caske shall be emptied of fresh water, cause the same to be forthw<sup>th</sup> filled againe w<sup>th</sup> salt water for prevenčon of leakeinge & mustines w<sup>ch</sup> must be often shifted.

30   *Item*, touchinge the facte Comitted in the Indies by S<sup>r</sup> Edward Michelborne thoughe we knowe o<sup>r</sup> selues to be meerelie innocent therein, yett yf by any meanes, we or o<sup>r</sup> goode should be dampnified thereby, we doe wish yo<sup>u</sup> to seeke to that kinge & Magistrate for redresse & recompence thereof, The w<sup>ch</sup> yf you cannot obtaine, Then o<sup>r</sup> will and order is that you vse the benefitt of o<sup>r</sup> kinge ma<sup>te</sup> Comission giuen yo<sup>u</sup> in that behalfe.

31   *Item*, That yf the said David Middleton Captaine shall happen to dye goeinge outwarde in this present voyadge (w<sup>ch</sup> God forbid) then we will & appointe That Thomas Emmesworth [p. 303] m<sup>r</sup>chaunt & ffactor<sup>r</sup> in this present voyadge shall succeede in his place, and be principall Comander in the said shipp vntill shee come to Bantam: And that yf the said David Middleton shall happen to dye at Bantam, That then yo<sup>u</sup> the Master Pilott and other cheefe Officers, w<sup>ch</sup> shall arive att Bantam shall Conferr and advise w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> ffactors at Bantam, w<sup>ch</sup> of them there shall be held & esteemed the fittest psonn to succeede in his place & roome: And therevpon he w<sup>ch</sup> they shall soe thinke fittest, our will is, shall pcure the ladeinge of o<sup>r</sup> said shipp, and retourne as principall Comander therein for England.

32 Item, for that we finde best proffitt, by the lardge sorte of pepp, both for the prices w<sup>ch</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> pay aswell for thone as for thoter, we will that in any case yo<sup>u</sup> buy of the lardgest sorte, And lett the same be putt by yt selfe into the shipp, That yt be not mingled w<sup>th</sup> any other: yett o<sup>r</sup> desire is not to haue any pepp except yt be to saue dead fraight.

33\. Item we doe appointe and expreslie order, That yo<sup>u</sup> the Captaine w<sup>th</sup> Thomas Emmesworth, the pursar & such others as yo<sup>u</sup> the Captaine shall thinke meete to call vnto yo<sup>u</sup>, doe dulie examyn the dealeinge of all or any of o<sup>r</sup> ffactors at Bantam, either in or for o<sup>r</sup> generall accompte or otherwyse or of all or any of their priuate trade or trades, since their goeinge thither: And that yf yo<sup>u</sup> shall therevpon finde all or any of them, to haue dealt or traded for them selfes, or to haue willfullie or cuningelie abused and wronged vs therein, or to haue demeaned them selues contrary to o<sup>r</sup> expresse order formerly giuen vnto them in that behalfe: Then we will that yo<sup>u</sup> take notice of their misdemeanors, and to admonish them, for reformac̃on thereof, As alsoe to c<sup>r</sup>tifie vnto vs the pticuler abuses by them or any of them Comitted.

34\. Item, Lastlie but w<sup>th</sup> the first to be remembred: We chardge and pray yo<sup>u</sup> all, To haue an espetiall care and reguard: And to haue yo<sup>r</sup> Eyes open to all devises & practices w<sup>ch</sup> may be wrought against yo<sup>u</sup>, or[^sec-07-fn-106] shipp, or goode in eu<sup>r</sup>ry or any place where yo<sup>u</sup> come or shall ariue keepinge a Contynuall watch whereby yo<sup>u</sup> may be ready to prevent any mischeefe intended against you, suspect all howe freindlie soeu<sup>r</sup> they seeme: Be [p. 304] ready still and stand vpon yo<sup>r</sup> guarde, Trust not yo<sup>r</sup> saffety to the carelesse attendance of the Comon Mariners whoe will not loose their present pleasures or ease, though the losse of their liues or[^sec-07-fn-107] shipp and goode depend vpon yt: And albeyt we haue sett downe eu<sup>r</sup>y thinge w<sup>ch</sup> we remember & desier to be done in pticular yett yf you the Captaine David Middleton the said Thomas Emmesworth Edmund Musgraue M<sup>r</sup>, Iohn Davis Pilott & Thomas Cleyburne[^sec-07-fn-108] shall vpon due Considerac̃on and Consultac̃on together finde cause to alter any thinge before yo<sup>u</sup> come vnto Bantam w<sup>ch</sup> we haue herein sett downe as aforesaid havinge w<sup>th</sup> good advise resolued therevpon, We referr the same to yo<sup>r</sup> discrec̃ons: And for better assistaunce and more wary pceedinge in all courses, vpon all occac̃ons, & in all o<sup>r</sup> affaires and busines for or conc<sup>r</sup>ninge this present voyadge: We will & appoint the said Thomas Emmesworth (soe longe as he shall contynew w<sup>th</sup> you) and Edmund Musgraue Iohn Davis & Thomas Cleyburne to advise & Consulte w<sup>th</sup> you the Captaine of and aboute all thinge w<sup>ch</sup> shall be needfull therein, whome we wish yo<sup>u</sup> to ymbrace and vse w<sup>th</sup> a loueinge respect & freindly & diligently to hearken to their Councells puttinge in execution, what shall w<sup>th</sup> good deliberac̃on be soe, by yo<sup>u</sup> & them agreed vpon together, ffor the better avoiedinge of such Contenc̃ons as were the last voyadge in the Consent. And thus not doubtinge of yo<sup>r</sup> faithfull care & diligence herein: we comend yo<sup>u</sup> and your endevo<sup>rs</sup> to Gode providence, whome we hartilie pray to blesse you all & o<sup>r</sup> affaires, And to guide yo<sup>u</sup> w<sup>th</sup> his feare & defend yo<sup>u</sup> from all dangers *Amen.* London the 14<sup>th</sup> day of Aprill 1609.

p me David Middleton

Sealed & deliu<sup>r</sup>ed in the p<sup>r</sup>sence of Richard Mountney[^sec-07-fn-109]

Richard Atkinson.


<!-- page: 397 | folio: 305 -->
To o<sup>r</sup> loueinge freinde m<sup>r</sup> W<sup>m</sup> Kealinge, m<sup>r</sup> W<sup>m</sup> : Hawkins & to all other o<sup>r</sup> Officers & servante in any o<sup>r</sup> Ships Comeinge out of the East Indies.[^sec-07-fn-110]


![Decorated woodcut initial A with leafy foliage.](../figures/fig-017_p0397.webp)

> _[Margin: 4 of this Tenor deliured to m<sup>r</sup> Worstenholme]_

AFTER o<sup>r</sup> hartie Comendations &c : Whereas the Officers of his ma<sup>t e</sup> Customes doe vsuallie send some of their servaunte abourde all shipps comeinge to any pte of this Realme to haue care that by noe meanes his ma<sup>t e</sup> Customes may be defrauded, to avoyde all blame to o<sup>r</sup> selues and yo<sup>u</sup>, we haue thought good to requier yo<sup>u</sup> that yf any of their said servante shall come abourde of any of ou Shipps that yo<sup>u</sup> doe intertaine them in kinde and loueing manner for the better execution of their place & his ma<sup>t e</sup> service. And further accordinge to o<sup>r</sup> instruccõns formerlie giuen yo<sup>u</sup>, we earnestly wish & requier yo<sup>u</sup> carefullie to keepe and reserue for his ma<sup>tie</sup> : & the Lorde all such rare fowles beaste or other thinge as are by you, or any of yo<sup>r</sup> Company brought from those pte, and to vse such meanes as none of them be sould or giuen away before they come to o<sup>r</sup> hande, for the comeinge thereof to the hande of his ma<sup>tie</sup> : or the Councell or any other by any other meanes then from vs, will be some disgrace & discontent to the Company. And thus not doubtinge of yo<sup>r</sup> care herein we bid you farewell London the 14<sup>th</sup> of August 1609.

Yo<sup>r</sup> loueing freinde the Company of Marchaunte of London tradeinge to the East Indies.


<!-- page: 398 | folio: 306 -->

#### To o<sup>r</sup> loueinge freinde Anthony Marlowe & ffrancis Bucke or either of them at Lisborne[^sec-07-fn-111]

> _[Margin: one of this Tenor deliured to m<sup>r</sup> Eldred]_

AFTER o<sup>r</sup> hartie Comendac̃ons &c: yo<sup>r</sup> łres dated in Lisborne the 15<sup>th</sup> of Iulie last we haue receiued whereby as we are verrie sorrie to heare of yo<sup>r</sup> hard mishapps, soe we haue done & will vse all possible and speedie meanes that in vs lieth for yo<sup>r</sup> releefe and inlardgm<sup>t</sup>, & will be readie to pforme what other thinge yo<sup>u</sup> doe requier of vs by yo<sup>r</sup> said łres: In the meane season we haue thought good by this occasion not onelie to make knowne vnto yo<sup>u</sup> o<sup>r</sup> greefe for this yo<sup>r</sup> distresse, but alsoe to advertice yo<sup>u</sup> that for yo<sup>r</sup> better releefe & Comfort we haue dealt w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> good freind m<sup>r</sup> Iohn Eldred,[^sec-07-fn-112] to giue order to his servant W<sup>m</sup>: Squier remayneinge at Lisborne, to furnish yo<sup>u</sup> for yo<sup>r</sup> present necessities w<sup>th</sup> the some of Twoe hundred Duckette yf yo<sup>u</sup> shall need soe much & further (yf need be) w<sup>th</sup> the some of three or fower hundred Duckette more, yf for the same yo<sup>u</sup> cann assuredlie by any good meanes there, worke yo<sup>r</sup> inlardgm<sup>t</sup>: Wherein yo<sup>u</sup> are to be well aduiced & be of some c<sup>r</sup>teine grownde before yo<sup>u</sup> parte w<sup>th</sup> any money & thus wishinge yo<sup>u</sup> to Comforte yo<sup>r</sup> selues in the lord whoe will bringe theis yo<sup>r</sup> troubles to a blessed yssewe in his good tyme as may make most to his glorie & yo<sup>r</sup> Comforte in hast we end as we begunn the 14th of August 1609. Yo<sup>r</sup> loueing freinde the Company of Marchaunte of London tradeinge to the East Indies.


<!-- page: 399 | folio: 307 -->
To the right wo<sup>ll</sup>: my very loueinge freinde S<sup>r</sup>: Thomas Walsingham knight & other his Ma<sup>te</sup>: Iustices of the Peace Assembled at Crayford in Kent or elswheare.[^sec-07-fn-113]

AFTER my hartiest Comendacõns &c: Wheareas Anthonie Emerson and [ *blank* ] shipwrighte latelie hired by the East India Company & by them ymployed about the builedinge of their Shipps at Deptford, doe notw<sup>th</sup>standinge their said agreem<sup>t</sup> now absent them selues from the said worke to the greate hindraunce thereof, and evill example vnto others. I ame in the name of the said Companie to intreate yo<sup>r</sup> favo<sup>rs</sup> herein, espetiallie beinge a Case of greate ymportaunce for the hono<sup>r</sup> and proffitt of this kingdome Whereby they may be soe ponished accordinge to the statute in that respect puided, as yt be a warninge vnto them and others to abstaine from the like. And thus not doubtinge of yo<sup>r</sup> kinde favo<sup>rs</sup> herein I Comitt yo<sup>u</sup> to the Tuicõn of Thalmightie. London the 25<sup>th</sup> of Septemƀ . 1609.

Yo<sup>r</sup> loueinge freind *Tho: Smyth.*

To the right wo<sup>ll</sup>: my very loueinge freinde S<sup>r</sup> Robert Mansfeild knight one of the principall Officers of his Ma<sup>te</sup>: Navy.[^sec-07-fn-114]

S<sup>R</sup> The East India Companie haueinge caused certaine Iron Ordinance to be made readie for their shipps now abuildinge at Deptford, haue not as yett any Convenient place for the stowadge thereof. Wherefore I hartelie pray yo<sup>u</sup> to affoorde them soe much favo<sup>r</sup> as to giue yo<sup>r</sup> order that the said Iron Ordinance may be suffered to be laid on his Ma<sup>te</sup> [p. 308] Wharfe at Deptford there to remaine for some shorte space vntill the Shipps be lanched. The w<sup>ch</sup> yo<sup>r</sup> favo<sup>r</sup> the Companie will be readie to requite in the best manner they May: And I remaine

Yo<sup>r</sup> very loueinge freinde

London the 25<sup>th</sup> of Septemb̃ 1609.

*Tho: Smyth:*

> _[Margin: A Commission to m<sup>r</sup> Barber to see that nothinge be carried out of the Dragon w<sup>th</sup>out order.]_

THEIS[^sec-07-fn-115] are to Certifie all those whome yt may Concerne That we the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> and Companie of the Marchaunte of London tradinge into the East Indies haue appointed the Bearer hereof Barber w<sup>th</sup> all expedi<span class="sc">c</span>õn to make his repaier abourd o<sup>r</sup> Shipp called the Dragon latelie come from the Indies, and there to remayne to foresee and vse all meanes for preven<span class="sc">c</span>õn that noe goode of what kinde soever be conveyed or carried out of the said Shipp w<sup>th</sup>out the warrant of the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> of the said Company in writeinge accordinge to the Teno<sup>r</sup> of a l̃re from the Lo: highe Thr̃er of England, whearevnto we doe authorize him by this o<sup>r</sup> Comission. In witnes whereof I the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> of the said Companie haue hearevnto sett my hand the 15<sup>th</sup> of *Nouember* 1609.

*Tho : Smyth.*

London the of March 1609.[^sec-07-fn-116]

> _[Margin: <span class="sc">Rich</span>: Reaue <span class="sc">W</span>m: Revett Iohn Iourden Phillip Glascocke Ieofferey Carleile <span class="sc">Rich</span>: Weekes and others.]_

ALBEYT we haue receiued noe l̃res from yo<sup>u</sup>, nor yo<sup>r</sup> Generall since yo<sup>r</sup> depture, nor otherwyse heard from yo<sup>u</sup>, but by some vncertaine reporte from Cairo, whereby wee vnderstand yo<sup>u</sup> haue traded at Mocho neere Aden, both in sellinge o<sup>r</sup> English and buyinge those [p. 309] Country Comodities, whereof we hope yo<sup>u</sup> haue by the Carivan of Aleppo, and by the way of Cairo written vnto vs as alsoe haue sent Iohn Iourden overland accordinge to yo<sup>r</sup> Comission,[^sec-07-fn-117] w<sup>ch</sup> yf yo<sup>u</sup> haue neglected yo<sup>u</sup> are worthy much blame, for yt may much preiudice the Company, and be the occasion of yo<sup>r</sup> owne wauntꝭ, for that we knowe not whither to direct either shippinge or lres vnto yo<sup>u</sup>: yett such is the care we haue of yo<sup>r</sup> good that haueinge now sent out three Ships to say the Tradesincrease of 1000 Tuns,[^sec-07-fn-118] the Pepp Corne of 240 Tuns and the Little Darlynge of 100 Tuns whereof is Admirall S<sup>r</sup> Henrie Middleton[^sec-07-fn-119] and m<sup>r</sup> Lawrence ffeemell[^sec-07-fn-120] principall ffactor: we haue not onelie by them sent yo<sup>u</sup> theis lres but alsoe haue giuen them chardge in their Comission, that wheresoever they shall finde any of yo<sup>u</sup> they shewe you all loue and kindnes whereof we doubt not.

Our pleasure therefore is that all such stocke as is (for o<sup>r</sup> accompt of the fourth voyadge) in all or any of yo<sup>r</sup> Custodies or w<sup>ch</sup> you may receiue, yo<sup>u</sup> doe as M<sup>r</sup> ffemell shall aduise yo<sup>u</sup> (yf already yo<sup>u</sup> haue not) speedilie tourne into such Comodities as are best and most proffitable for theis partꝭ, and w<sup>ch</sup> will take least bulke, as good rawe silke, fine booke Callicoes yf they be cheepe, rich Indico, good druggꝭ, cloues, or maces well chosen for we must pay freight for them to the accompt of the Sixt voyadge, yett doe we not soe tye yo<sup>u</sup> to the saveinge of freight but that yo<sup>u</sup> should send such Comodities whereof alsoe wee may make most proffitt, & the same to packe vpp very safe from wettinge markeinge them both vpon the Inner & outer surplus w<sup>th</sup> a distincte marke & n<sup>o</sup>: whereby the same may be distinguished from goodꝭ of any other voyadge.


<!-- page: 402 | folio: 310 -->
And Concerninge yo<sup>r</sup> selues whether yo<sup>u</sup> shall stay in those parte or not, we haue referred that vnto S<sup>r</sup> Henry Middleton M<sup>r</sup> ffemell and Captaine Hawkins to deale w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> vpon tearmes of stayinge and to contynue the same wages w<sup>ch</sup> we formerlie agreed w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> for, that soe the chardge of soe many as shall there remaine may be put to the accompt of this Sixt voyadge, and the rest to come home in the first Shipp that retourneth for England. Yo<sup>u</sup> shall alsoe vnderstand that in this Sixt voyadge we giue o<sup>r</sup> ffactor<sup>s</sup>, noe liberty for any priuate trade but for soe much as they putt into the generall stocke, wee are contented to accept thereof bindinge them from priuate traffique directly or indirectlie, and for such wages as we are agreed vpon, they or their Assignes shall yearlie receiue the same in England, soe that they are not to receiue any wages in the Indies, exceptinge onlie some x<sup>li</sup> yearelie to buy them apprell, and that to be paid them in Ryalls of 8 at 5<sup>s</sup> ꝑ peece w<sup>ch</sup> we knowe to be a reasonable rate consideringe they cost us here 4<sup>s</sup>—6<sup>d</sup> ꝑ Ryall beside the venture and forbearance.

Now therefore soe many of yo<sup>u</sup> as shall be elected to stay there and shall be contented w<sup>th</sup> theis Condicõns, giueinge Bond for the true ꝑformance thereof shall be assured to haue yo<sup>r</sup> wages according to agreement.

And because yo<sup>u</sup> had some liberty granted by the fourth voyadge to adventure some small matter in priuate we are content that such as stay behinde as ffactor<sup>s</sup> (in payinge freight) shall send home such stocke as they haue gathered, vnto m<sup>r</sup> Governo<sup>r</sup> and Company w<sup>ch</sup> shall be sould for their most aduantage, and yf they shall desyre the proceede thereof to be sent backe in the generall stocke, their request therein shall be ꝑformed, but hencforth noe priuate adventure to any ffacto<sup>r</sup> will be ꝑmitted.

And yf any of you dislike of the restrainte of yo<sup>r</sup> priuate trade, wee haue giuen order that yo<sup>u</sup> may retourne in theis Shipps: but yf you shall be willinge to stay, yo<sup>u</sup> may expect the Company will noe lesse Consider of yo<sup>r</sup> deserueinges then yo<sup>r</sup> care and diligence shall giue them iust occasion, for hitherto they haue never beene vngratefull vnto any that haue well deserued.


<!-- page: 403 | folio: 311 -->

#### London the         of March 1609.[^sec-07-fn-121]

> _[Margin: To m<sup>r</sup> Sharpey & m<sup>r</sup> Rowles]_

<span class="sc">Forasmuch</span> as since yo<sup>r</sup> depture we haue receiued noe łres from yo<sup>u</sup>, nor M<sup>r</sup> Rowles and yett haue hard by łres written from Cairo home (thoughe vncertaine intelligence) that yo<sup>u</sup> haue had good traffique at Mocho both in sellinge o<sup>r</sup> English Comodities and byinge Indico and other m<sup>r</sup>chandize whereof we hope (though we haue not receiued them) yo<sup>u</sup> haue written łres by the Carivans and sent Iohn Iourden over land according to yo<sup>r</sup> Comission, w<sup>ch</sup> yf yo<sup>u</sup> haue not done will argue greate remisnes & may not onlie greatelie hinder the Company, but alsoe discouradge such ffacto<sup>rs</sup> as yo<sup>u</sup> haue lefte in those parte, for want of supplies Wherefore we haue by S<sup>r</sup> Henry Middleton Generall of this o<sup>r</sup> sixt voyadge not onlie written theis few lines vnto yo<sup>u</sup> but alsoe by him sent łres vnto any such ffactory as yo<sup>u</sup> may in any place haue planted praying yf by the prouidence of God yo<sup>u</sup> shall meete together that vpon receipt of this o<sup>r</sup> łre yo<sup>u</sup> would relate vnto S<sup>r</sup> Hen: Middleton, [or] his viceadmirall one m<sup>r</sup> ffeemell the whole proceedinge of yo<sup>r</sup> voyadge and to aduise him where yo<sup>u</sup> haue traded, where yo<sup>u</sup> finde least danger, & most apparance of proffitt, As alsoe yf yo<sup>u</sup> haue lefte any of o<sup>r</sup> stocke behinde, where, and at whose hande yt may be demanded to thend he may accordinge to order giuen him send or bringe home the same when he retourneth.

ffurther we desier yo<sup>u</sup> to assist him and m<sup>r</sup> Lawrance ffeemell w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>r</sup> best advice not onlie w<sup>ch</sup> of those ffacto<sup>rs</sup> yo<sup>r</sup> selfe haue placed in that Country, but alsoe w<sup>ch</sup> amongst all the ffacto<sup>rs</sup> that wee haue either at Aden, Suratt, Bantam, or ells where w<sup>th</sup> whome yo<sup>u</sup> may haue conversed are the fittest men to be ymployed in o<sup>r</sup> service both in reguard of their honest carriadge, and sufficient knowledge of that Country Comodities.


<!-- page: 404 | folio: 312 -->

### London y<sup>e</sup> 19<sup>th</sup> of March. 1609.

> _[Margin: Iohn Hearne Robert Browne Henry Sydall Bantam]_

BY the Dragon w<sup>ch</sup> God be praysed arryved at Plymouth the middle of Septembƀ last we receiued lres twoe from yo<sup>u</sup> Iohn Hearne one from Roƀt Browne one from Iohn Sarys & one from Henry Sydall: By Iohn Hearnes łre the third of Septembƀ we haue aduise what pepp, Alloes, white Benyamin and silke was sent for o<sup>r</sup> accompt all w<sup>ch</sup> we haue receiued by Godę favo<sup>r</sup> althoughe the Ship was very leakye and came weaklie home, in soe yll case as that we durst scarce adventure her (after she was lightened aboue 100 Tonns []) to come for London notw<sup>th</sup>standinge we finde avery greate want of the pepp yo<sup>u</sup> write was put abourd, to the full want as yt appeth to vs to be, Aboue twentie Tuns each Tun cont 2000 waight :[^sec-07-fn-122] w<sup>ch</sup> seemeth the more strange vnto vs in that the pepp yo<sup>u</sup> laded at Bantam had lyen soe longe and dryed soe much, that of 7489 sackę, there was lost 238 there, all w<sup>ch</sup> Considered together maketh vs thinke that o<sup>r</sup> busines was not well husbanded neither w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> nor in the Shipp comeinge home: Therefore we pray yo<sup>u</sup> that hereafter nothinge be bought nor sould privatelie but that yo<sup>r</sup> Iournall or booke Couchant may contynually lay open for eu<sup>r</sup>y one that is o<sup>r</sup> ffacto<sup>r</sup> to looke vpon, for wee hould yt noe way fitt, that he that is o<sup>r</sup> cheefe ffacto<sup>r</sup>, should carrie all the accomptę close to him selfe in such sorte that those whoe are w<sup>th</sup> him can giue noe reason howe o<sup>r</sup> Comodities are lessened, guiftę given, nor howe the wantę doe happen as some of yo<sup>r</sup> selues haue written vnto vs in theis yo<sup>r</sup> łres, that yo<sup>u</sup> can yeald vs noe reason w<sup>ch</sup> way the foresaid 238 baggę of pepp should be lost :

We are sorry that there hath not beene a Contynuall booke kept there that we might thereby haue discerned in good sorte howe o<sup>r</sup> busines hath beene carried. ffor we are giuen to vnderstand that m<sup>r</sup> Scott brought away his owne accomptę as alsoe m<sup>r</sup> Towerson did the lyke and lefte noe Coppies of them w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>u</sup>. It had beene fittinge for such as are the Companies servantę to haue kept a booke for the Company, there to haue remaned, and haue brought home a Coppy thereof for their owne vse, or at least so much thereof as might concerne them. ffor an amendm<sup>t</sup> [p. 313] whereof we haue sent yo<sup>u</sup> a lardge booke to be a Contynuall Couchant soe longe as yt shall last, willinge yo<sup>u</sup> the principall ffactor<sup>r</sup> and those that shall succeede yo<sup>u</sup>, that from hencforth yo<sup>u</sup> suffer those that are factors<sup>rs</sup> w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> to be priuie to all thinge bought and sould or otherwyse to be disposed of As alsoe that yo<sup>r</sup> booke and accompte may be publique and comon to all the rest of o<sup>r</sup> ffactors<sup>rs</sup>, w<sup>ch</sup> shall be good for yo<sup>r</sup> selfe to avoyed scandall or suspi<span class="sc">c</span>õn : And will be alsoe agood informa<span class="sc">c</span>õn vnto the rest of the ffactors<sup>rs</sup> vnder yo<sup>u</sup>, and bringe contentm<sup>t</sup> vnto vs, to free vs from suspi<span class="sc">c</span>õn of any practizes when yo<sup>u</sup> shall carry yo<sup>r</sup> busines publiquelie.

Wee write vnto yo<sup>u</sup> twoe yeares past by the *Assencõn* and *Vnion* as alsoe by the *Expedicõn*, Captaine, David Middleton, the Coppies of w<sup>ch</sup> łres we doe herew<sup>th</sup>all send yo<sup>u</sup>.[^sec-07-fn-123]

Albeyt we haue heretofore suffered yo<sup>u</sup> to haue private trade, yett the Company hath now vpon speciall considera<span class="sc">c</span>õn resolued, Not to pmitt yt any longer, for that we finde that those whoe haue had the manadgeinge of o<sup>r</sup> busines, haue had more care to inrich them selues, then to seeke o<sup>r</sup> proffitt, for yf they had not soe done they might haue ymployed o<sup>r</sup> stocke (w<sup>ch</sup> they haue had in their hande since S<sup>r</sup> Iames Lancaster came from thence) soe as the benefitt thereof might haue borne the chardges of o<sup>r</sup> howse at Bantam at the least.

We wrote vuto yo<sup>u</sup> by Captaine David Middleton that yo<sup>u</sup> should noe more pay yo<sup>r</sup> selues yo<sup>r</sup> wages by Royalls of 8 at iiij<sup>s</sup> the peece but att such a moderate rate, as might be indifferent:[^sec-07-fn-124] yett now vpon better considera<span class="sc">c</span>õn the Company haue concluded, and giue yo<sup>u</sup> direct order to pay noe more wages at all there, then may be needfull for the comelie apprellinge of any of o<sup>r</sup> ffactors<sup>rs</sup> w<sup>ch</sup> we deeme to be x<sup>li</sup> or 20 m<sup>r</sup>ke at the most p̄ Annū and the rest to be paid here in England, either to be adventured in the generall stocke or to such of yo<sup>r</sup> freinde, as yo<sup>u</sup> shall assigne the Company to pay yt vnto. And w<sup>th</sup>all such wages as yo<sup>u</sup> shall pay to lett the Ryall of 8 for fyve shillinge.

Alsoe we signifie vnto yo<sup>u</sup> all, that althoughe any of yo<sup>u</sup> shall [p. 314] succeede such as were before yo<sup>u</sup> in place yett there shall be noe succession of increase of wages allowed vnto yo<sup>u</sup> except yt be by spetiall order & direc̃cõn from the Governo<sup>r</sup> and Company. Wee haue appointed S<sup>r</sup> Henry Middleton to be o<sup>r</sup> Generall, vnto whome we wish yo<sup>u</sup> to shewe yo<sup>r</sup> selues obedient, and to doe as he shall ymploy yo<sup>u</sup> whether yt be by tarieinge there, or goeinge to any other place whether he shall see occasion to carry yo<sup>u</sup>.

Althoughe we had giuen order heretofore that noe man should bringe home any goode in o<sup>r</sup> Shipps of the nature and kinde that we o<sup>r</sup> selues doe lade, yett the greatest nomber in the Dragon brought home store of pepp, w<sup>ch</sup> causeth vs to thinke that the same was stolne from vs and occasioned the want we found of o<sup>r</sup> pepp in the said Shipp. ffor prevencõn whereof hereafter we haue reiterated the same Comandement, and wish eu<sup>r</sup>y one of yo<sup>u</sup> that shall either be at the cleiringe of any of o<sup>r</sup> Shipps away from thence, or come home in any of them, that yo<sup>u</sup> see and make diligent inquirie amongst the Company of the said Shipp publiquelie, whether any of them haue any goode of such kinde yea or noe. yf they haue and can make due proofe that they bought yt there, then yo<sup>u</sup> are to pay them for yt & shoote yt into the hould: yf they haue none signifie soe much vnto vs, that they denied to haue any there.

We haue alsoe taken order, that whosoeu<sup>r</sup> shall lade any goode in o<sup>r</sup> Shipps and shall not register the same w<sup>th</sup> the Pursar shall haue yt taken from him. And we requier eu<sup>r</sup>y one of yo<sup>u</sup> to doe yo<sup>r</sup> best that the same may be dulie pformed.

We will doe o<sup>r</sup> best endevo<sup>rs</sup> to prevent that none such as S<sup>r</sup> Edward Michelborne was, should disturbe yo<sup>r</sup> quiett whoe dyed a yeare since hopinge that tyme will weare out the remembrance of his deede.

fforasmuch as we haue found greate inconvenyence by lettinge of yo<sup>r</sup> money there at 2 or 3 for one to be paid heare, whereby diu<sup>r</sup>s of the Mariners and their wyues and Children after their deathes haue beene ympou<sup>r</sup>ished we doe therefore thinke yt fitt, that noe such Exchandge be suffered or pmitted for the avoidinge of scandall both from yo<sup>u</sup> and vs.

It appeth by the Accompte sent home that yo<sup>u</sup> haue drawne yo<sup>r</sup> wages after iiij<sup>s</sup> the Ryall of 8 from the first of October 1605 [p. 315] to the 31<sup>th</sup> of October 1608, w<sup>ch</sup> being accompted after iiij<sup>s</sup> vj<sup>d</sup> the Ryall as yt costeth vs beside the adventure we finde you haue allowed yo<sup>r</sup> selues 470 Ryalls of 8 more then is yo<sup>r</sup> due w<sup>ch</sup> we expect to haue restored by yo<sup>u</sup> that haue receiued the same, as alsoe that from the 31<sup>th</sup> of Octoƀ 1608 yo<sup>u</sup> receiue the Ryall of 8 at 5<sup>s</sup> and not otherwyse.

Thomas Harwood the Gunner of the Dragon giueth vs in accompt 20 barrells of powlder lefte w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> Iohn Hearne, whereof as of all thinge ells lefte vnder yo<sup>r</sup> chardge we expect a good accompt.

There is one W<sup>m</sup>: Lanwell lefte at Bantam whoe standeth indebted in the Pursars booke of the Dragon iij<sup>li</sup>—iiij<sup>s</sup>—x<sup>d</sup> w<sup>ch</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> are to defaulke out of his wages there and make the Company Creditor for the same.


#### London the 15<sup>th</sup> of March 1609.

> _[Margin: To m<sup>r</sup> Hawkins and the rest of o<sup>r</sup> ffactors att Suratt &c:]_

<span class="sc">Our</span> harty Comendačōns remembred &c: yo<sup>r</sup> łres of the fourth of Octoƀ 1608[^sec-07-fn-125] we receiued p Moloneux m<sup>r</sup> of the Dragon whoe by Gode assistaunce aryued saffelie at Plymouth in Septemƀ last being 1609 subscribed by W<sup>m</sup>: Hawkins and W<sup>m</sup>: ffinche, together w<sup>th</sup> a note from W<sup>m</sup>: ffinche of wares aswell there to be bought as sould w<sup>th</sup> waighte measures valuačōns of moneys & other pticular intelligences to good purpose and w<sup>ch</sup> we cannot but Comend wishinge the lyke carefullnes to be contynued in yo<sup>u</sup> all. Wee vnderstand of yo<sup>r</sup> saffe arriuall at the Barr of Suratt and of landinge yo<sup>r</sup> goode, together w<sup>th</sup> that vnhappie surprize of yo<sup>r</sup> men & goode by the Portugalls,[^sec-07-fn-126] we doe vnderstand alsoe of the season of the yeare and of the depthes of o<sup>r</sup> Shipps for that place, of all w<sup>ch</sup> aduise we doubt not but to make good vse hereafter. Yett we cannot but blame yo<sup>u</sup>, for sendinge so much goode and moneys a shore, before yo<sup>u</sup> had bought or laden any goode backe againe, and alsoe for adventuringe the ymploym<sup>t</sup> of all yo<sup>r</sup> moneys in one bote, yt [p. 316] beinge the first that yo<sup>u</sup> sent from the shore to the Shipp, whereas yf you had sent lesse at once w<sup>th</sup> good caution, yo<sup>u</sup> might haue prevented o<sup>r</sup> losses of goode and men in greate measure yf not altogether, And howsoeu<sup>r</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> excuse yt, that yo<sup>r</sup> men were fainte hearted and yealded w<sup>th</sup>out resistaunce, yett we are informed by Bucke and Marlowe now prisoners in Lisbone that they were destitute of powder and other meanes to defend them selues, w<sup>ch</sup> was a greate neglect in yo<sup>u</sup> to be soe secure,[^sec-07-fn-127] as not to arme and animate yo<sup>r</sup> men thorowlie, beinge in the Middest of dangers, and comittinge soe much goode to their chardge, we are informed by some of the Dragons Company that yo<sup>u</sup> had sould much of yo<sup>r</sup> lead and other english Comodities at Suratt, but in your łres yo<sup>u</sup> mention onlie the disbursem<sup>te</sup> of all yo<sup>r</sup> monie, yo<sup>u</sup> write vs alsoe of greate Elaphauntę teeth bought by the way but not what they cost, such thingę yo<sup>u</sup> doe not well to omytt we hope that o<sup>r</sup> twoe shipps that we sett out hence in April 1608 . the *Vnion* and the *Assencõn* haue visited yo<sup>u</sup> as we gaue them Comission, And that by makeinge saile of yo<sup>r</sup> english Comodities yo<sup>u</sup> did furnish yo<sup>r</sup> selues w<sup>th</sup> Indico & other Cambaia goode in due tyme, yo<sup>u</sup> giue vs good incourradgm<sup>t</sup> touchinge the easinesse and the greate benefitt of placeinge a factory in Suratt and other places neare Cambaia, w<sup>ch</sup> we alwaies soe conceaued, & cheeflie aymed at yt, to w<sup>ch</sup> end beside all other meanes wherew<sup>th</sup> we did furnishe yo<sup>u</sup> thether we gaue yo<sup>u</sup> direcčõns, łres, and presentę, wherew<sup>th</sup> soe soone as you should be landed to addresse yo<sup>r</sup> selues to visitt the greate Magoll, that by his protecčõn yo<sup>r</sup> residence and ffactory at Suratt, might be more safelie setled before any further violence or treacherie of the Portugalls plottinge there, might be put in execučõn against yo<sup>u</sup>, w<sup>ch</sup> we greatlie feare yo<sup>u</sup> did not hasten to prevent, till yt was too late, neither can we gather by yo<sup>r</sup> łres that yo<sup>u</sup> did land any of yo<sup>r</sup> presentę for the kinge, and therefore we cannot but feare that yo<sup>r</sup> interteynem<sup>t</sup> w<sup>th</sup> him will be accordinglie, and moreover in that spetiall other Cawtion w<sup>ch</sup> we gaue you to beware and not to trust the Portugalls, we finde to o<sup>r</sup> Coste that yo<sup>u</sup> were too carelesse, all w<sup>ch</sup> Considered thoughe we hope the best, yett we cannott but [p. 317] rest very doubtfull both of yo<sup>r</sup> saffetie and of o<sup>r</sup> goode, till wee doe heare further, we haue furnished in theis shipps for Suratt Elaphaunte teeth, Quicksylver, and other Marchandize, for w<sup>ch</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> gaue vs aduise, and whereof the Cape Marchaunt M<sup>r</sup> ffemell hath the Invoices, w<sup>th</sup> the sales whereof, as alsoe with his direcc̃ons what to send ffor England, he is to make yo<sup>u</sup> acquainted, & therein we requier yo<sup>u</sup> to assist him w<sup>th</sup>all dilligence, and w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>r</sup> best endevo<sup>rs</sup>. Those base thinge as sweete fennell seede, Cum̃yn, longe pepp, and such lyke as are not worth the fraight, we doe not expect nor doe wishe yo<sup>u</sup> to send any: we haue resolued and doe thinke yt fitt M<sup>r</sup> Hawkins, that yo<sup>u</sup> doe in the first of theis three shipps retourne for England w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>r</sup> accounte Iournall, and such other yo<sup>r</sup> obseruac̃ons touchinge the affaires of those Countries, that by yo<sup>r</sup> intelligence we may be the better directed in o<sup>r</sup> further proceedinge to settle in those parte, and in any hand we giue yo<sup>u</sup> straight chardge to foresee and prevent that the Mariners nor any other be suffered to pester the Shipps w<sup>th</sup> luggage, w<sup>ch</sup> abuse had well neare beene the losse of the Dragon in hir nowe comeinge home, beinge pestred for want of gou<sup>r</sup>nm<sup>t</sup> (eu<sup>r</sup>y man doeinge what he listed) w<sup>th</sup> at least one hundred Tuns of Mariners goode more then her burthen.

And forasmuch as we haue heretofore found that the priuate trade of our ffacto<sup>rs</sup> hath beene carefully carryed for their owne Lucar and gaine w<sup>th</sup> the greate neglect of o<sup>rs</sup>, conuertinge all the ritche & pretious thinge to their owne vse & nothinge for the Company but pepp and grosse Comodities, and seeing theis three shipps in this Sixt voyadge, are the begynninge of a new accoumpte, we haue ordered that nowe and hencforth neither o<sup>r</sup> Generalls Marchante ffacto<sup>rs</sup>, nor any other that we ymploye shall be p̄mitted any pryvate dealeinge or trade for them selues and therefore S<sup>r</sup> Hen: Middleton himselfe, M<sup>r</sup> ffemale and all the rest that are now ymployed in this shippinge haue putt their moneys into the generall stocke, and haue giuen their seu<sup>r</sup>all Bonde w<sup>th</sup> suerties as them selues can witnesse not onelie to forbeare all priuate trade directlie or indirectlie for them selues, but alsoe to forbid and hinder all others from the lyke, and therefore soe many of yo<sup>u</sup> of the third voyadge as are now there resident, or shall be lefte there to Contynew still, notw<sup>th</sup>standinge any lib̄tie of priuate [p. 318] trade much or little admitted vnto yo<sup>u</sup> in the said third voyadge & seeinge this voyadge is the begynninge of a new account wherein we intend to carry an even and equall hand to all that we ymploy, we doe therefore lett yo<sup>u</sup> knowe that you are hencforth to forbeare all priuate tradinge for yo<sup>r</sup> selues, & to ymploy yo<sup>r</sup> selues onlie and whollie for the generall stocke giueing bonde to S<sup>r</sup> Henry, M<sup>r</sup> Downton[^sec-07-fn-128] or M<sup>r</sup> ffemale to the Companies vse for the true pformance thereof, onlie for apparrell and such vses yo<sup>u</sup> are to take of yo<sup>r</sup> wages soe much as will suffice soe yt exceed not x<sup>li</sup> p̄ Annū accounteinge the Ryall of 8 at 5<sup>s</sup>, and the rest of yo<sup>r</sup> wages to be paid yo<sup>u</sup> in England, neyther hath the Generall or Cape Marchant any authoritie or power to augment wages w<sup>th</sup> any of yo<sup>u</sup> but we haue power to gratifie any man that we shall thinke to deserue the same, w<sup>ch</sup> may be sufficient incourradgm<sup>t</sup> to styrr vp your best endevo<sup>rs</sup> in o<sup>r</sup> seruice. And we haue giuen order to displace and bringe home all such as by their refusall shall shewe them selues to be otherwyse disposed then in o<sup>r</sup> Comission we haue ordayned. And towchinge S<sup>r</sup> Edward Michelborne (whoe is dead almost a yeare since) howsoeu<sup>r</sup> we suspected him to haue gotten his goode by wrongfull courses yet we knowe not in pticular whome he had wronged. Therefore as yett we can say nothinge to that matter in as much as we receiued not the Captaines łres w<sup>ch</sup> you mention were taken by the Portugalls, that he had directed to o<sup>r</sup> kinge complaineinge of his losses And thus wishinge yo<sup>r</sup> prosperyty and good successe we Comitt yo<sup>u</sup> to God and rest.


### Notes

[^sec-07-fn-001]: (1) At a Court held on the 15th December, 1607, the governor and others “were “intreated to Consider what Comissions and lres aswell from his ma<sup>tie</sup>: as from the “Companie wilbe now convenient to be sent, And therevpon to cause the same, to be “drawne and made readie in due tyme before the departure of the shipps” (*Court Minutes*).
[^sec-07-fn-002]: (2) *i.e.* page 103.
[^sec-07-fn-003]: (3) The last four words have been added by another hand.
[^sec-07-fn-004]: (4) See page 109.
[^sec-07-fn-005]: (5) See page 251, note 2.
[^sec-07-fn-006]: (6) See page 252, note 1.
[^sec-07-fn-007]: (1) Apparently an error for "and."
[^sec-07-fn-008]: (2) In the Company's general instructions for the voyage (*see* page 245), orders were given for the despatch overland of messengers, for whose safety a royal safe conduct (no doubt the present document) had been procured ; and in later letters the Company [p. 233] expressed their strong disapproval that their orders on this point had not been carried out. It would appear that Jourdain and Glascock were the two factors designated for this duty.

    John Jourdain or Jourdan was elected a factor on 7th Dec., 1607, and was assigned to the *Assention*. On the wreck of the vessel he appears to have made his way to Agra, and thence back to Surat, where in Oct., 1611, he embarked on Sir Henry Middleton's ship, and accompanied him in his voyage to the Red Sea and afterwards to Bantam. He seems to have been actively employed during the next few years in trading voyages from Bantam to various parts of the East Indies, and in 1614 we find him “president of the English at Bantam.” He returned to England in 1617, but in the same year entered into an agreement with the Company to serve them for a fresh term of five years; and accordingly by Nov., 1618, he was back again in his old post as President at Bantam. Eight months later he was slain in a skirmish with the Dutch at Patani. His journal, covering the period between his departure from England in March, 1608, and his return in 1617, is now in the British Museum (*Sloane MSS.*, 858).

    Philip Glascock was elected a factor at the same time as Jourdain, but a few days later was rejected in favour of Richard Wickham. On 22nd Jan., 1607/8, he was again elected, and proceeded on the voyage. Nothing of importance can be traced concerning his further career.

[^sec-07-fn-011]: (1) Added by another hand.
[^sec-07-fn-012]: (2) Joseph Salbancke was possibly the original member of the Company of that name, who adventured 240*l.* in the *First Voyage*; and hence, it may be, the consideration with which he was now treated. After the wreck of the *Assention* he proceeded to Agra, and thence started with Covert through Persia and Arabia to make his way overland to England. At Bagdad, however, they met an Englishman named White, who informed them of Middleton's expedition; whereupon Salbancke determined to make for the Red Sea, hoping to meet Middleton, and acquaint him with the particulars of Sharpie's voyage and shipwreck. On his journey he heard a false story of Middleton's capture, whereupon he tried to make his way to Socotra, but fell into the hands of the Portuguese, who carried him to Muscat, thence to Ormuz and Goa, and finally, it would seem, to Lisbon, where he was released and returned to England. In 1612 he went out again as cape merchant in the *Expedition* of the *Twelfth Voyage*. He was at home once more in 1614, but seems to have left again for the Indies in the following spring with Keeling on a voyage on account of the *First Joint Stock*. In [Nov.?] 1616 he writes from Agra, where he seems to have remained for some time. In 1618 he took part in a voyage from Surat to the Red Sea, when a firman was obtained from the Pasha of Sana for trade at Mocha, &c. Nothing can be traced as to the time or place of his death, but it must have been before the end of 1624, as by Jan., 1625, his widow had married again.

[^sec-07-fn-025]: (1) This paragraph, as well as some of those that follow, is so evidently based upon the information given by Sir Edward Michelborne in his interview with the Company, that it has been thought well to give *in extenso* the interesting account entered on the Court Minutes of 26th Jan., 1607/8:— “Att this Courte S<sup>r</sup> Edward Michelborne as form<sup>r</sup>lie he had promysed appeareing, “declared that for the desier he had to ymparte his knowledge vnto them for the “Good of the Company, he was now come hither, whoe signiefied as followeth. “ffirst that by experience he had found that mens healthes were best p<sup>r</sup>served by “labor and refreshinge out of the shipps & in the hotest places by plentie of meate “and drinke then espetiallie to be yealded them, keepeth their Bodies freest from “diseases. “Then that much perrill and small hope of trade may be expected at Aden, yt “being a Garrison Towne of Souldiers, rather then of Marchauntes, yett neare to “Aden aboute some 10 miles of, there is a Towne (as yt seemeth he is informed) “called Moccha, gou<sup>r</sup>ned w<sup>th</sup> m<sup>r</sup>chauntes onelie, and a place of spetiall trade right “ou<sup>r</sup> against w<sup>ch</sup> there is an Iland called Kedgee, wherein is good Harbor & watering “yf need require. “Then that by noe meanes o<sup>r</sup> shipps and men can goe saffelie to Suratt, or theare “expect any quiett trade for the many dangers likelie to happen vnto them by the “Portugalls, Cheeff Comanders of *Diu* and *Demon* & places there aboute very stronge “& hath the sole Comand of those Seas, all the people theare paying them tribute & “the kinge of Cambaia recydeth twoe monnethes iorney from Suratt & the Barr “shallow. “But he saith there is a place not farr thence, twoe daies saileinge from Suratt, “called Lawrie [*see* p. 251] in the Bay of the River Syndus, wheare is good Harbor in “saffetie; Twoe miles from w<sup>ch</sup> vp in the Bay there is a greate Cittie like London called “Nigertuttie [*see* p. 252], where is plentie of Indico Callico & diu<sup>r</sup>s m<sup>r</sup>chandize, the “people there are free onelie gou<sup>r</sup>ned by kinge Acabar whoe resideth at Agree some “ffortie miles from Nigertuttie at w<sup>ch</sup> the Portugalls haue nothing to doe but onelie “come thither for m<sup>r</sup>chandize as other Strangers, where he conceiueth yf o<sup>r</sup> People “doe goe thither behaueing them selues well they will find ample and proffitable “trade aswell of their Comodities as for vent of o<sup>rs</sup>, at w<sup>ch</sup> place Cloth is in greate “request, of the particulars whereof, he will be readie to informe m<sup>r</sup> Sharpie & “m<sup>r</sup> Rowles more at lardge. “He alsoe declared that Iecketta is afitt place to right o<sup>r</sup> selues of such of those “people that should offer vs any wronge, the w<sup>ch</sup> place is scituate in the River Syndus “but for the fittest tyme of the yeare to that purpose, he is vnwillinge to declare.”

[^sec-07-fn-030]: (2) Lahori Bandar, on the south or left bank of the Baghiár or western branch of the Indus, 20 miles from the Piti mouth. Though formerly the principal port of [p. 252] Sind, it has now fallen into complete decay, in consequence of the channel on which it is situated having ceased to be navigable. Hamilton in his *New Account of the East Indies* (1727) describes it as a village of about 100 houses, built of crooked sticks and mud, with a large stone fort mounting four or five guns. The harbour was accessible to ships of 200 tons burden, and a brisk trade was carried on.

Hamilton, who visited it in 1699, speaks of it as "the emporium of the province, a very large and rich city;" and he estimates its dimensions at that time as about three miles long, and one and a half broad. The East India Company had for some time a factory there.

[^sec-07-fn-059]: (1) Immediately after the ships of the *Fourth Voyage* had been despatched, preparations were made for the equipment of a *Fifth*. The *Merchant Royal* of Hull was mentioned at a court held on 22nd March, 1607/8, as a suitable vessel, and three members of the Company, including Mr. Humphrey Smyth, were requested to make the necessary enquiries. On the 19th April, it was agreed that Robert Earle should be sent to Hull to view the ship, and to "deale therein accordinge to o<sup>r</sup> instruccons "giuen him & as he shall be directed by m<sup>r</sup> Humfrey Smyth vnto whome we purpose "to direct o<sup>r</sup> lres to that effect: as by o<sup>r</sup> Register (of such thinges) at lardge appereth." On the 14th June, 15*l*. was voted to Mr. Earle for "his paines & chardges" in going to Hull, but nothing is said as to the result of his mission. The ship was not bought, but this may have been due to the resolution come to that the *Fifth Voyage* should not be sent out by the adventurers in the *Fourth*, as had been intended, but by the adventurers of the *Third Voyage*.

[^sec-07-fn-085]: (3) Vansleb's "Indigo named Serquis," *i.e.* of Sarkhej, 5 miles S.W. from Ahmedabad. *Shirkhist* is the bazaar name for every kind of Manna imported into India ; and is the original Persian name for " Khorassan Manna."
[^sec-07-fn-086]: (4) Vansleb's "Indigo of Balludri" *i.e.* Valabhi [Βυζάντειον of *Ptolemy*, viii. 1, 7], commonly written Ballabi, now an obscure village about 20 miles N.W. from Bhavanagar, but formerly the seat of the famous Valabhi kings, who, in succession to the mysterious Guptas, ruled over Kathiawar <span class="sc">A.D.</span> 318 to 790. The Arab writers of the 9th century name the place Balhara, a dialectic corruption of *bara-rai*, and signifying (the City of) " the Great (Valabhi) King." See E. Thomas in *Numismata Orientalia*, Vol. iii., 1882. But for its close association with "*Serchis*" I should have identified "*Belondri*" here not with Ballabi, but with Vansleb's "Mirabolans surnamed Balludri" ; *i.e. bahira* [Sanskrit and Hindi], *berda* [Mahrati], *bahadrha* [Telugu], *beleyluj* [Arabic], *beleyleh* [Persian], the dry astringent fruit, with its kernel, of *Terminalia Bellerica*, the "Belleric Myrobalan," used in dyeing. The "Chebulic Myrobalan," used in the same way, is the fruit of *T. Chebula*. Neither of these was the μυροβάλανος, or "unguent-nut," of the ancients, which is usually identified with the [p. 288] seeds of *Moringa pterygosperma*; but the acid fruit of *Phyllanthus Emblica*, used in India as a pickle, was their *Μυροβάλανος ἔμπλέτζ* [cp. Sanskrit *amlika*, and *amrita*, and Hindi *aonla*].

[^sec-07-fn-091]: (5) Sophony (Sophonias) Cozuke (the Kazak, *i.e.* as he is also styled in the Court Minutes, “the Russe”), entered the Company’s service, perhaps under the patronage of Sir Thomas Smyth, in March, 1609, on an engagement to stay in the Indies seven years. In 1613 he established a factory at Sukadana, in Borneo, and in the following year attempted to do the same at Landak. Two years later, he took an active part in an expedition sent to establish a factory at Banda, in the Moluccas, but failed to effect his immediate purpose, owing to the opposition of the Dutch. In Oct., 1616, he sailed again, with Capt. Courthop, to make a fresh attempt, and this time the opposing parties came to actual blows. The *Swan* was assailed by a Dutch vessel and captured after a severe fight, in the course of which Sophony was “beaten in pieces with a great shot” (Jan., 1617).

[^sec-07-fn-097]: (1) This is John Davis of Limehouse, who has been so persistently confused with his more famous namesake of Arctic fame. He had been in the *First Voyage* under Lancaster, in Sir Edward Michelborne's expedition of 1604-6, and (first as pilot and afterwards as master) in the *Third Voyage* with Captain David Middleton. After serving in the *Fifth Voyage* (here referred to), he went out again in the *Ninth Voyage* (1612-15), and on the captain's death succeeded to the command and brought the ship home. In 1617 we find him master of the *Swan*, which was captured by the Dutch off Banda, and the crew made prisoners. After his release, he was appointed pilot major of the *James*, which sailed in January, 1621. He was by this time advanced in years, and probably weakened in constitution by his intemperate living; and in December of the same year he died, while the *James* was on a voyage to Jambi in Sumatra. Davis, though an able and intelligent seaman (witness his "Ruter," or sailing directions, printed in *Purchas*), was headstrong and quarrelsome, and much addicted to drink; and this perhaps accounts for the Company's unwillingness (in spite of his experience) to employ him in posts of greater responsibility.

In March, 1614/5, some of the secretary's work was transferred to Atkinson. In August, 1621, he had to submit to a reduction of salary from 150*l*. to 100*l*. He seems to have died in the early part of the following year, and was succeeded by William Hurt.

(*Court Minutes*.)
[^sec-07-fn-116]: (2) A letter to the factors of the *Fourth Voyage*, sent by the ships of the *Sixth Voyage*, under Sir Henry Middleton.
[^sec-07-fn-117]: (1) See page 245.
[^sec-07-fn-118]: (2) Said to have been the largest merchant ship up to that time built in England.
[^sec-07-fn-119]: (3) See page 46, note 3.
[^sec-07-fn-120]: (4) Proposed for "general" in the *Fourth Voyage*, but "spared" until the next expedition. On 13th Nov., 1609, he was appointed a factor for the *Sixth Voyage* at a salary of 200*l*. per annum, with the stipulation that he should remain in the Indies at least three years. He died suddenly, 29th May, 1611, at Mocha, of poison, administered, as was thought, by the Aga, whom he had threatened to report at Constantinople.
[^sec-07-fn-121]: (1) A corresponding letter to the Commanders of the *Fourth Voyage*.
[^sec-07-fn-122]: (1) *i.e.* twenty hundredweight.
[^sec-07-fn-123]: (1) See pages 236 and 285.
[^sec-07-fn-124]: (2) Fair to both sides, just; cp. the prayer in *English Church Liturgy* that those in authority “may truly and *indifferently minister justice*.”
[^sec-07-fn-125]: (1) Not now extant.
[^sec-07-fn-126]: (2) See page 219, note.
[^sec-07-fn-127]: (1) Unsuspecting. It was in his " secure hour " that Hamlet's father was murdered.
[^sec-07-fn-128]: (1) Nicholas Downton was the lieutenant general of the *Sixth Voyage*, and had charge of the *Peppercorn*, with which he returned in safety, though in sore plight, in the autumn of 1613. In the following spring he sailed again, in the *New Year's Gift*, in command of a voyage on account of the *First Joint Stock*. At Surat he had to sustain a formidable attack from a Portuguese fleet, but successfully repulsed them. He next proceeded to Bantam, which was reached in June, 1615; and here he died on the 6th August, "death lying in ambush to intrap," says Purchas, "whom by "open force he could not deuoure."


## Sixth, Seventh & Eighth Voyages, 1609–1611


<!-- page: 411 | folio: 319 -->

### Instrucc̃ons[^sec-08-fn-001] giuen by vs the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>r</sup> & Comittees for the Company of Marchauntę tradinge [into] the East Indies vnto Lawrence ffemale our principall ffactor and the rest of o<sup>r</sup> ffactors now ymployed in this sixt voyadge.

**1  I**NPRIMIS forasmuch as in o<sup>r</sup> generall Comission we haue largelie sett downe what we haue thought necessary to be obserued in o<sup>r</sup> generall busines and doe herew<sup>th</sup> deliver yo<sup>u</sup> a Coppy thereof praying yo<sup>u</sup> as much as in yo<sup>u</sup> lieth to obserue the contentę thereof, we haue thought yt fitt onlie[^sec-08-fn-002] for yo<sup>r</sup> pticulare direcc̃ons to recomend to yo<sup>r</sup> Considerac̃on this o<sup>r</sup> aduise followinge

2   And because we haue beene pswaded to appointe and nominate yo<sup>u</sup> o<sup>r</sup> principall and cheefe ffactor in this voyadge out of the good reportę of diuers yo<sup>r</sup> freindę and o<sup>r</sup> owne opinion of yo<sup>r</sup> honest behavio<sup>r</sup>   And the hope of yo<sup>r</sup> instruccious endevo<sup>r</sup> and skilfull experience in the manadgeing the affaires of m<sup>r</sup>chandize of soe greate ymportance as yo<sup>u</sup> knowe theis to be, we wish yo<sup>u</sup> that wheresoeu<sup>r</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> shall come or settle a ffactory, to inquier and informe yo<sup>r</sup> selfe sufficiently of the Condicons and manners of the people, and gou<sup>r</sup>nm<sup>t</sup> and what Comodity we may send from hence most vendable in those ptę, Espetially concerninge wollen Comodities, and other the natiue Comodities of o<sup>r</sup> owne Country whereby we may be able to dryue a trade w<sup>th</sup>out the transportac̃on of money w<sup>ch</sup> is the cheefe scope of o<sup>r</sup> desires   And of those sortę of Comodities aswell wollen as others the quallity quantity culler and price   And of Cloth whether highe shorne or lowe, strayned or vnstrayned,   And in lyke sorte to aduise of all other Comodities what yo<sup>u</sup> shall imagine needfull for o<sup>r</sup> further direcc̃ons.

3   Alsoe wee desier to vnderstand what comodity yo<sup>u</sup> finde there w<sup>ch</sup> may bee vented to proffitt here or any other place wherevnto o<sup>r</sup> ships shall nauigate in this or in any other succeedinge voyadge.   As alsoe what trade those people haue w<sup>th</sup> other nations either remote or neare confineinge vnto[^sec-08-fn-003] them, [p. 320] And wherein there traffique espetially consiste together w<sup>th</sup> the valua~on of their coynes, Their seu<sup>r</sup>all weightę and measures and what other occurrence needfull for vs to knowe, and thereof to endevo<sup>r</sup> by all possible meanes to giue vs intelligence overland, as by the way of the red sea to Cairo directing yo<sup>r</sup> łres to the ffrench Consull there Resident, To be sent to Mercellus[^sec-08-fn-004] inclosed to Henery Berry or any other Englishman there Resident, Alsoe by the Persian gulfe by any Carauan throughe Persia either bound for Constantinople, Aleppo, or Tripole directing yo<sup>r</sup> łres to the ymbassado<sup>r</sup> or Consull there resident to be Conveyed vnto vs, As alsoe by the Caspyan Sea throughe Muscovia vnto the English Agent there beinge, To w<sup>ch</sup> purpose we giue yo<sup>u</sup> an Alphabett of Characters wherein we wish yo<sup>u</sup> to write for more secrecy.

4 Yf yo<sup>u</sup> should touche at Aden or Machowe[^sec-08-fn-005] in the red sea beinge in yo<sup>r</sup> way before yo<sup>u</sup> come at Suratte we wish yo<sup>u</sup> to inquier whether those of the fourth voyadge haue not setled a factory theare, yf they haue wee desier that they may receiue such comforte from yo<sup>u</sup> as yo<sup>u</sup> may Conveniently afford them and acquainte them of the intelligence we haue had by other mens łres of o<sup>r</sup> ships beinge at Machowe, and of the bartringe for Indico, But not haueinge any łres from them, w<sup>ch</sup> as they knowe wee gaue them in spetiall chardge & to that purpose sent one or twoe to be sent from Aden overland, wee are ignorant whether there be any incourradgm<sup>t</sup> to maintaine trade in those partę, But yf by their łres or by any other meanes we shall vnderstand any hope of good trade, Althoughe yt be but for vent of o<sup>r</sup> english Comodities onelie we shall not omitt to frequent those porte[^sec-08-fn-006] w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> next shippinge, In the meane tyme yf yo<sup>u</sup> may put of in any reasonable sorte either for syluer or gould, any of the Comodities we now send we wishe the same to be done as more att large in o<sup>r</sup> generall Comission is expressed.

5 Att yo<sup>r</sup> comeing to Suratt informe yo<sup>r</sup> selfe whether m<sup>r</sup> W<sup>m</sup>: Hawkins or any other before yo<sup>r</sup> arriuall haue setled Capitula~ons w<sup>th</sup> the greate Magoule of that Country fitt and safe for o<sup>r</sup> quiett trade into his Territorie & yf the same be not done in such sufficient manner as yo<sup>u</sup> deeme expedient, Then wee wishe yo<sup>u</sup> in [p. 321] the meane tyme to procure such safe Conducte from the kinge of Cambaia, & the other cheefe Officers of that Country as may incowrrage yo<sup>u</sup> to negotiate amongst them And w<sup>th</sup>all convenient expedi<span class="sc">c</span>õn to dispeede o<sup>r</sup> Ships from thence, accordinge as in o<sup>r</sup> Comission generall we haue att lardge directed yo<sup>u</sup> And that done then yo<sup>u</sup> may in comely sorte accompanied w<sup>th</sup> such others of o<sup>r</sup> ffactors as yo<sup>u</sup> shall thinke fitt, repair vnto the Courte of the greate Magull to establish further Capitula<span class="sc">c</span>õn for o<sup>r</sup> peaceable trade either at Suratt or any other porte or porte, place or places w<sup>th</sup>in any of his dominions alwaies remembringe the hono<sup>r</sup> of o<sup>r</sup> kinge and Country & the reputacons of o<sup>r</sup> negotia<span class="sc">c</span>õns in those parte & for the greater dignity of yo<sup>r</sup> ymploym<sup>t</sup> vnto him we haue ꝑcured his Ma<sup>ties</sup> lre vnto the Magull, the originall & Coppy whereof we deliu<sup>r</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> wishinge that the deliu<sup>r</sup>y thereof may be w<sup>th</sup> that hono<sup>r</sup> that may be well fittinge soe greate a Monarche, & as the oportunity of the place & other yo<sup>r</sup> Convenience in those pte shall pmitt accompanyinge some honorable present of veluett Plate or whate ells more acceptable both vnto the greate Magull & some spetiall men aboute him as in yo<sup>r</sup> good discree<span class="sc">c</span>õn shall seeme meete.

6 And for yo<sup>r</sup> better instruc<span class="sc">c</span>õns we doe herew<sup>th</sup> deliu<sup>r</sup> yo<sup>u</sup> the Coppy of such priuiledge as S<sup>r</sup> Iames Lancaster obtayned from the kinge of Achine wherevnto yo<sup>u</sup> may ad or diminishe as occasion offereth & the lyke Coppy we haue formerly deliu<sup>r</sup>ed to those of the third and fourth voyadge.

7 ffurther we wish yo<sup>u</sup> diligently to informe yo<sup>r</sup> selfe whether we may not settle a ffactory at Dabull neare Suratt or Negratitte[^sec-08-fn-007] in the Ryver of Syndus or in any other porte towne, where o<sup>r</sup> shippinge may not be subiect to bard[^sec-08-fn-008] hauens as at Suratt nor in soe greate danger of the Portugalls And where we may aswell vent o<sup>r</sup> Comodities and make retornes in the Comodities of those Countries at reasonable rate.

8 Alsoe inquier as much as yo<sup>u</sup> can of the depth, breadth, Ebbs, flowinge, Currante & sholes of the porte & havens thereaboute & what the chardge of transporta<span class="sc">c</span>õn of Comodytie from porte to porte will cost by land as by Sea and whatt customes & [p. 322] duties are payable at each porte aswell for goode and money as ancoradge of shippinge &c:

9 If any Çomodities either of the fourth voyadge shall be prouided at Aden or of the third or fourth voyadge at Suratt or any other poorte wherevnto yo<sup>r</sup> shippinge shall arriue w<sup>ch</sup> are to be sent for England we wish yo<sup>u</sup> to suffer the same to be laden abourd theis o<sup>r</sup> shipps vnder seu<sup>r</sup>all marke aswell w<sup>th</sup>in the Canvas or other Cou<sup>r</sup>ture asw<sup>th</sup>out for the better discou<sup>r</sup>y thereof, And that there be pticular Invoices & bills of ladeinge of all the seu<sup>r</sup>all pcells that shall be laden for each accounte for avoydeinge Confusion in theis pticular accompte alsoe yf any remainders shall be lefte & deliu<sup>r</sup>ed over vnto yo<sup>u</sup> we would haue a true and pfect Inventory thereof kept in a booke Couchant, wherein we will that all busines, either for buyinge sellinge bartringe exchandging shippinge receaueinge transportacõns and what ells needfull to be registred conc<sup>r</sup>ninge o<sup>r</sup> busines and yo<sup>r</sup> ymploym<sup>t</sup> be from tyme to tyme dulie trulie and fairelie kept and written and a true coppy thereof sent vs by eu<sup>r</sup>y shippinge both vnderwritten by o<sup>r</sup> cheefe Agent as alsoe by fower or fyue of those o<sup>r</sup> ffactor<sup>s</sup> w<sup>ch</sup> are in principall places of ymploym<sup>t</sup> vnder him.
