[^sec-08-fn-131]: (1) All along the well-wooded narrow Konkan Coast, and through all the wide extended fertile plains of Southern Gujerat, the Hindu women of Western India, of the higher castes, have, or had in my time, 22 to 37 years ago, a marked partiality for robes (*saris*) of a single coloured text, contrasted with a pretext (παρυφή, *clavus*) of the complementary, or, indeed, any other harmonising colour; the Hindu weavers being able to bring any two colours, even pea-green and purple, and scarlet and purple, into perfect unison. In the Southern Konkan particularly, I found that, besides robes of Cardinal white bordered with gold (χρυσοπάρυφος, *chrysoclavus*), the most commonly worn were of marigold or saffron yellow (κροκωτός) edged with Mazarine blue and buff, or primrose yellow edged with pale blue, both universally favourite combinations, and of pea green with purple (παραλουργής), and blazing [p. 406] scarlet (*κοκκοβαφής*) with pistachio green, and lastly of carnation, with a pretext of either apple green, interthreaded with gold, or deep blue separated from the text of carnation by a strip of gold, a chromatic concordance of exquisite refinement. And beyond doubt it was the great charm of these Indian stuffs that first made carnation a fashionable colour in England. It takes its English name from "the Carnation" [in German *das Incarnat*], or Double Clove Pink, otherwise known as "the Whitsuntide [in German *Pfingsten*] Gilliflower," the *Dianthus* [*Διὸς ἄνθος*, flos Jovis] *Caryophyllus* of botanists; and this name was not given to it on account of its colour, but is corrupted from its earlier English name of "Coronation," given to it on account of the use of its flowers for festive chaplets. Thus Spenser in *The Shepheardes Calender*, April, 134-145:—

    "Bring hither the Pincke [*Dianthus hortensis*] and purple Cullambine With Gelliflowres [single 'Clove Pink']; Bring <span class="sc">coronations</span> and Sops in wine [scented 'Clove Pink'] Worne of Paramoures; Strowe me the ground with Daffadowndillies, And Cowslips, and Kingcups, and loved Lillies: The pretie Pawnce ['Pansy'], And the Chevisaunce [*Cheiranthus Cheiri*, the 'Wallflower'], Shall match with the fayre floure Delice [Fleur de Lys (*i.e.* Louis VII.), the 'Iris']."

    But already the proper English name of the double *Dianthus Caryophyllus* was being contracted to "Carnation." Lyte, in his *Niewe Herbal*, 1578, of the tautologically named "Clove Gillofers," writes, B. ii., ch. 7:—"The greatest and bravest sort of them are called *Coronations* or *Cornations*"; and, again, Shakespeare in *Love's Labour Lost* (1592), III., 1:—"Pray you sir, how much *Carnation* ribbon may a man buy for a remuneration": that is, as I take it, "ribbon (*red* strips or fillets of silk) for chaplets," or other "head gear"; although even at this early stage of the decay of the name it may have acquired the meaning of red, from its erroneous association with, and, indeed, express derivation from, the Italian *incarnadino* and *incarnatino* (Florio, 1598), literally, "raw-meat-coloured," or "incarnadined"; a word which, until it obtained a poetical significance through its erroneous association with "the Coronation,"

[^sec-08-fn-137]: (1) The story of William Adams, who lived in Japan for twenty years, and was “in “such favor with two emperors of Japan as never was any Christian,” has often been told, and may be found admirably summarized in the *Dictionary of National Biography*. He sailed in 1598 as pilot to a Dutch fleet bound for the Indies, but his vessel got separated from her consorts, and with difficulty reached the coast of Japan in April, 1600. Adams was sent up to the court, where he speedily succeeded in gaining much influence over the emperor. In October 1611, he placed himself in communication with the Company’s factors at Bantam; but his story was already known through the Dutch, and, as we see, the Company at home had some months [p. 413] before made arrangements to open up trade with Japan. On Saris's arrival, in June, 1613, Adams accompanied him to court, and assisted in procuring the necessary privileges. He did not, however, avail himself of the opportunity of returning home in the *Clove*, but took service with the Company as second in command of the factory established by Saris at Firando. He made several voyages to Siam and other places in the Company's interests, and even after he had quitted their service in 1616, he made himself useful in many ways to his countrymen. He died on the 16th May, 1620, and was buried on one of the hills overlooking Yedo harbour, where his grave may still be seen.
[^sec-08-fn-138]: (1) See page 376, note.
[^sec-08-fn-139]: (1) The works of the Rev. William Perkins (1558-1602), Fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge, whose name is now almost forgotten, enjoyed at this time considerable popularity both in England and abroad, and he was regarded as one of the ablest exponents of the Calvinism then so much in vogue. His collected works were four times reprinted during the ten years succeeding his death. The "Book of Martyrs" is of course John Foxe's "Actes and Monuments," of which a sixth edition had just appeared.

    Had Femell survived, and succeeded in establishing a permanent factory at Surat, as the Company hoped, these books would doubtless have formed the nucleus of a library there, such as was actually established at a later date. That the Company's agents were not indifferent to literature, and especially to theological literature, is shewn by the following extract from a letter addressed to the Court by the President (Sir George Oxinden) and Council of Surat, under date 25th September, 1666:—

    "Your Library here is carefully looked after and preserved, and wee could wish it "were better furnished with Boòkes. It consists for the maine of English Treatises "and is almost totally disfurnisht of the workes of the Ancient Writers; wee finde "not of all the ffathers workes, any more then the Epistles of Clemens Romanus "published by M<sup>r</sup> Patrick Young. here are the Epistles of Ignatius. The workes "of Epiphanius & S<sup>t</sup> Augustine, with some few imperfect peeces of other ffathers,


## Seventh, Tenth & Twelfth Voyages, 1611–1612

### *The lres caryed by ye Dutchmē*[^sec-09-fn-001]

> _[Margin: To the kinge of Tedore.]_

<span class="sc">James</span> by the grace of Almightie God, kinge of greate Brittaine ffraunce and Ireland defendor of the Christian faith : To the To the highe and mightie kinge the kinge of Tedore &c : greetinge. The good treatm<sup>t</sup> w<sup>ch</sup> o<sup>r</sup> Subiectę haue from tyme to tyme receiued in their trade w<sup>th</sup>in yo<sup>r</sup> Countreys (of w<sup>ch</sup> they haue not ceast to make the best rela<span class="sc">c</span>õn w<sup>th</sup>all due acknowledgm<sup>t</sup> of yo<sup>r</sup> benigne & favorable dispotition towardę them) hath incourradged them againe, to make an other voyadge thither, by occasion whereof wee hould ytt not ymptenent but to expresse o<sup>r</sup> gratious acceptaunce of yo<sup>r</sup> loue & Amity shewed to o<sup>r</sup> said Subiectę, & to intreate the Contynuance thereof, towardę all others of o<sup>rs</sup> as shall from tyme to tyme resorte vnto yo<sup>u</sup>; and more pticularlie to recomend vnto yo<sup>u</sup> the bearers hereof *Peter Flores Lucas Antheumes Robert Browne* and others, whoe nowe w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> good likeinge and pmission doe repaire vnto yo<sup>u</sup> in the good shipp called the Globe, Not doubting but as the effectę of their Comerce cannot but redound to the good and aduancem<sup>t</sup> of yo<sup>r</sup> Countrey and people soe yo<sup>u</sup> will afford them yo<sup>r</sup> Royall ptec<span class="sc">c</span>õn w<sup>th</sup>all the respectę of Courtesie and freindshipp w<sup>ch</sup> wee will be readie to affoord towardę any of yo<sup>rs</sup> yf they shall arriue into any of o<sup>r</sup> Territories. And soe wee pray Almightie God to prosp yo<sup>u</sup> and to make yo<sup>u</sup> victorious against yo<sup>r</sup> Enemies. ffrom o<sup>r</sup> Royall Pallace att Westminster this.

> _[Margin: A letter to all princes, gournors, &c in the East Indies for the secure trade of the Marchauntes]_

<span class="sc">James</span> by the grace of Almightie God kinge of greate Brittaine ffraunce and Ireland defender of the Christian faith &c: As there is nothinge w<sup>ch</sup> Increaseth more the glorie and dignitie of Sou<sup>r</sup>eigne [p. 422] Princes vpon earth then to extend their renownę vnto farr dissident Nations, Soe haueing vnderstoode of late yeares from some of o<sup>r</sup> loueinge subiectę, that haue traded into diu<sup>r</sup>s Countries neare adioyneinge vnto yo<sup>rs</sup> of the reputacõn & greatnes of yo<sup>r</sup> power and dominion, wee haue incourradged o<sup>r</sup> said Subiectę to vndertake a voyadge into yo<sup>r</sup> Countrey, aswell to solicitt yo<sup>r</sup> freindshipp and amity w<sup>th</sup> vs, as to enterchaundge such Comodities of each others Countreys, as may be most of vse the one to the other, beinge nothinge doubtfull, but such will be yo<sup>r</sup> Princelie magnanimitie and disposition as to be ready to embrace this o<sup>r</sup> desier, & not onlie to receaue o<sup>r</sup> people w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>r</sup> accustomed benignitie and favo<sup>r</sup>, butt for their better incourradgem<sup>t</sup>, to afford them yo<sup>r</sup> Ryall proteccõn for the setlinge of a ffactory there, w<sup>th</sup> such securitie & lib̃tie of Comerce as shall be most convenient for the aduancm<sup>t</sup> of the mutuall proffitt and Comodities of each others Subiectę; Wherein for o<sup>r</sup> parte wee doe willingly offer o<sup>r</sup> selfe & the lib̃tie of o<sup>r</sup> kingdomes and Countries, whensoeu<sup>r</sup> any of yo<sup>r</sup> subiectę shall vndertake to haue com̃unication w<sup>th</sup> vs. And soe wee pray vnto Almightie God to blesse and prosp yo<sup>u</sup>, and make yo<sup>u</sup> victorious against yo<sup>r</sup> Enemies. ffrom o<sup>r</sup> Pallace at Westminster this of Ianuary in the eight yeare of o<sup>r</sup> Reigne of greate Brittaine ffraunce & Ireland.[^sec-09-fn-002]


![Decorative woodcut initial letter I](../figures/fig-021_p0514.webp)

> _[Margin: To the Emperor of Iapan.]_

JAMES[^sec-09-fn-003] by the grace of Almightie God kinge of greate Brittaine ffraunce and Ireland, defendor of the Christian faithe &c: to the highe and mightie Prince the Emperour of Iapan &c: greetinge. Most highe and mightie Prince As there is nothinge w<sup>ch</sup> increaseth more the glorie and dignitie of Sou<sup>r</sup>eigne Princes vpon earth, then to extend their renownę vnto farr discident Nations; Soe haueing vnderstoode of late yeares from [p. 423] some of o<sup>r</sup> loueinge Subiecte that haue traded into diu<sup>r</sup>s Countries neere adioyneinge vnto yo<sup>rs</sup>, of the reputac̃on and greatnes of yo<sup>r</sup> power & dominion: Wee haue incourradged o<sup>r</sup> said subiecte to vndertake a Voyadge into yo<sup>r</sup> Countrey, aswell to solicitt yo<sup>r</sup> freindshipp and Amity w<sup>th</sup> vs, as to enterchange such Comodities of each others Countreys as may be most of vse the one to the other, beinge nothinge doubtfull, but such will be your princelie magnanimitie and disposition as to be readie to ymbrace this o<sup>r</sup> desier, & not onlie to receiue o<sup>r</sup> people w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>r</sup> accustomed benignitie and favor, butt for their better encouradgm<sup>t</sup>, to affourd them yo<sup>r</sup> Royall ptec̃on for the setlinge of a ffactorie there, w<sup>th</sup> such securitie and libtie of Comerce, as shall be most convenient for the aduancem<sup>t</sup> of the mutuall proffitt and Comoditie of each others Subiecte; Wherein for o<sup>r</sup> parte, wee doe willinglie offer o<sup>r</sup> selues and the libtie of o<sup>r</sup> kingdomes and Countres whensoeu<sup>r</sup> any of yo<sup>r</sup> Subiecte shall vndertake to haue comunicac̃on w<sup>th</sup> vs. And soe wee pray Almightie God to blesse and prosp yo<sup>u</sup>, and to make yo<sup>u</sup> victorious against your Enemies: ffrom o<sup>r</sup> Pallace at Westminster, this of Ianuary in the Eight yeare of o<sup>r</sup> Reigne of Greate Brittaine ffraunce and Ireland.


![Historiated decorated initial capital 'I' with floral motif.](../figures/fig-022_p0515.webp)

> _[Margin: To the kinge of Bantam]_

IAMES by the grace of Almightie God kinge of greate Brittaine ffraunce and Ireland defendor of the Christian faith &c: To the highe and mightie Prynce the kinge of Bantam &c: Greetinge. The good treatm<sup>t</sup> w<sup>ch</sup> our Subiecte haue receiued in your Countreis, as yt incourradgeth them to continue their trade and entercourse w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>r</sup> people, soe yt giueth vs occasion more and more to ymbrace yo<sup>r</sup> freindshipp, and to offer the like reciprocasion from vs towarde any of yo<sup>rs</sup>, that will happelie vndertake soe longe a voyadge hetherwarde. In the meane time, theis o<sup>r</sup> subiecte resortinge vnto you in their good shipp called the Cloue,[^sec-09-fn-004] We haue thought good to recomend them vnto yo<sup>r</sup> [p. 424] fauorable saueguard and pteccoñ, to the end they may enioye the same libtie and safetie in yo<sup>r</sup> dominions, & receiue such incourradgm<sup>t</sup> for the aduancem<sup>t</sup> of their trade and traffique, as some others of o<sup>rs</sup> haue heretofore enioyed, to the good contentm<sup>t</sup> and furtheraunce of the Comon vtilitie of each others Countries, wherein because wee hope yo<sup>u</sup> will not be backward, wee will forbeare to trouble yo<sup>u</sup> any further, Prayinge Almightie God to blesse and prosp yo<sup>u</sup>, & to make yo<sup>u</sup> victorious against yo<sup>r</sup> Enemies. ffrom o<sup>r</sup> pallace att Westminster this of Ianuary in the eight yeare of o<sup>r</sup> Raigne of greate Bryttaine ffraunce and Ireland.

> _[Margin: To the kinge of Gresecke.]_

<span class="sc">James</span> by the grace of Almightie God kinge of greate Brittaine ffraunce and Ireland, defendor of the Christian faith, To the highe and mightie kinge of Gresicke[^sec-09-fn-005] &c: Greetinge. The reporte we haue heard from o<sup>r</sup> loueing subiecte, that haue traded in the East Indies, both of yo<sup>r</sup> power and greatnes, and of yo<sup>r</sup> Princelie and favorable disposition to cherish and interteyne all sortes of Strangers, that doe resorte into yo<sup>r</sup> Countries, hath incouradged the bearers hereof *Peeter Flores* Lucas Antheumes Robt Browne and others w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> good approbacõn and likeinge, to vndertake a voyadge thither, aswell to sollicitt yo<sup>r</sup> freindshipp and Amitie w<sup>th</sup> vs, as to enterchaunge such Comodities as may be most of vse to each others Countreys, being Confident that yo<sup>u</sup> will be readie to ymbrace this o<sup>r</sup> desire, and not onelie receaue o<sup>r</sup> people w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>r</sup> accustomed favor to others, butt for their better encourradgm<sup>t</sup> to affourd them yo<sup>r</sup> Royal pteccon, for the setlinge of their trade & Comerce in those partes, w<sup>th</sup> such Condicõns of securitie and safetie as shall be most convenient for the aduancem<sup>t</sup> of the mutuall proffitt & vtilitie of each others Countries: We haue geuen in chardge to o<sup>r</sup> people to demeane them selues w<sup>th</sup> all respecte of Courtesie [p. 425] and freindshipp towarde o<sup>r</sup>[^sec-09-fn-006] people, not doubtinge but that there pceedinge will proue as acceptable to you as heretofore they haue beene to yo<sup>r</sup> neighbour kinges and Countries, w<sup>th</sup> whome the haue traded to their good contentm<sup>t</sup> & that in Conformitie thereof you will expreslie chardge and Comand yo<sup>r</sup> Gou<sup>r</sup>nors and Vassalls to ayde and assiste them in their neede & necessities, as wee will be ready to doe the like to yo<sup>rs</sup>, yf happilie they shall arriue into any our Dominions. And soe wee pray Almightie God to preserue and prosp yo<sup>u</sup>, and to make yo<sup>u</sup> victorious against yo<sup>r</sup> Enemies. ffrom our Royall Pallace at Westminster this  .

> _[Margin: To the Gournor of Bandris.]_

**JAMES** by the grace of Almightie God kinge of greate Brittaine ffraunce and Ireland, defender of the Christian faith, To the highe & excellent Lorde the Gou<sup>r</sup>no<sup>rs</sup> of *Bandris*[^sec-09-fn-007] Greetinge. The reporte wee haue heard from o<sup>r</sup> loueinge Subiecte, that haue traded into the East Indies both of yo<sup>r</sup> power and greatnes, and of yo<sup>r</sup> Princelie and favorable disposition to cherish and interteyne all sortes of Strangers that doe resorte into yo<sup>r</sup> Countries, hath encourradged the bearers hereof *Peter Flores*, Lucas Antheumes Robt Browne and others, w<sup>th</sup> o<sup>r</sup> good approbãcon and likeinge to vndertake a Voyadge thither, aswell to sollicitt yo<sup>r</sup> freindshipp and Amity w<sup>th</sup> vs, as to interchange such Comodities as may be most of vse to each others Countries, being Confident that yo<sup>u</sup> will be ready to ymbrace this o<sup>r</sup> desier, and not onlie to receaue our people w<sup>th</sup> yo<sup>r</sup> accustomed favo<sup>r</sup> to others, butt for their better encourradgm<sup>t</sup>, to afford them yo<sup>r</sup> Royall ptec̃con for the setlinge of their trade and comerce in those partes w<sup>th</sup> such Conditions of securitie and safetie as shall be most convenient for the aduancem<sup>t</sup> of the mutuall proffitt & vtility of each others Countries. Wee haue giuen in chardge to o<sup>r</sup> people to demeane themselues w<sup>th</sup>all respecte of Courtesie [p. 426] and freindshipp towarde yoʳ people, not doubtinge butt that there pceedinge will proue as acceptable to yoᵘ, as they haue beene to yoʳ neighbor kinges and Countries wᵗʰ whome they haue traded to their good Contentmᵗ, and that in conformyty thereof yoᵘ will expreslie Comand yoʳ Gouʳnors & Vassells to ayde & assist them in their neede and necessities as wee will be readie to doe the like to yoʳˢ, yf happilie they shall arriue into any oʳ dominions. And soe wee pray Almightie God to preserue and psp yoᵘ, and to make yoᵘ victorious against yoʳ Enemies. ffrom oʳ Royall Pallace att Westminster this .

<span class="sc">James</span>[^sec-09-fn-008] by the grace of Almightie God kinge of greete Brittaine ffraunce & Ireland defendor of the Christian faith: To the highe & mightie Prince the greate kinge of Iapan &c: Greetinge.

> _[Margin: <span class="sc">To the kinge of Iapan</span>]_

The reporte wee heard from oʳ loueinge subiecte, that haue traded into the East Indies, both of yoʳ power and greatnes, and of yoʳ princelie and favorable dispotition to cherish and enterteyne all sortes of straungers, that doe resorte into yoʳ Countreys, hath incourradged the bearers hereof Peter Flores, Lucas Antheumes, Robt Browne & others wᵗʰ oʳ good approbation and likeinge to vndertake a voyadge thither; aswell to solicitt yoʳ freindshipp and Amity wᵗʰ vs, as to enterchange such Comodities, as may be of most vse to each others Countreys, beinge Confident, that yoᵘ wilbe readie to ymbrace this oʳ desier, and not onlie to receaue oʳ people wᵗʰ yoʳ accustomed favor to others, but for their better incourradgemᵗ, to afford them yoʳ Royall protecc̃on for the setlinge of their trade and Comerce in those partes, wᵗʰ such Conditions of securitie and safetie, as shall be most convenient for the aduancmᵗ of the mutuall proffitt & vtility of each others Countreys. Wee haue giuen in chardge to oʳ people to demeane them selues wᵗʰall respecte of courtesie & freindshipp towarde yoʳ people, not [p. 427] doubtinge butt that their pceedinge will proue as acceptable to yo<sup>u</sup>, as heeretofore they haue beene to yo<sup>r</sup> neighbour kinge & Countreis w<sup>th</sup> whome they haue traded to their good contentm<sup>t</sup>, and that in conformitie thereof, yo<sup>u</sup> will expreslie chardge and com̄aunde yo<sup>r</sup> Gou<sup>r</sup>nors and vassalls to aide and assist them in their neede and necessities, as wee will be readie to doe the like to yo<sup>rs</sup>, yf happily they shall arriue into any o<sup>r</sup> domynions. And soe wee pray Almightie God to preserue & prosp yo<sup>u</sup>, and to make yo<sup>u</sup> victorious against yo<sup>r</sup> Enemies. ffrom o<sup>r</sup> Royall Pallace att Westm̄ this      .


### *A discourse delyuered to M<sup>r</sup> Gouern<sup>r</sup>, by Peter Floris & Lucas Antheumes of ther p'tended voiage.*[^sec-09-fn-009]

> _[Margin: A discourse of y<sup>e</sup> Globes voiage, intended to the Bay of Bengala.]_

SETTING sayle from hence in Nouembr̄ 1610, we hope to arryue at *Mesolopatane*[^sec-09-fn-010] and *Port Polmone*[^sec-09-fn-011] vppō y<sup>e</sup> Coast of *Coromandell* in Iuly or August, or at the longest in Septembr̄. 1611. And ther to employe our Capitall in dyu<sup>r</sup>s sorte of Cotten linnen, to wete, one third part for y<sup>e</sup> Island of *Iaua* and *Bantā*, the oth<sup>r</sup> two third parte for *Patane*, and *Siam*. The said capitall being employed as aforesaid, we purpose to set saile frō the Coast of *Coromandell* in Ianuarye 1612 towarde *Bantā*, (the monsone seruing o<sup>r</sup> turne) so as we may be at Bantā in March) and ther employe o<sup>r</sup> foresaid third p̄t of o<sup>r</sup> capitall, eith<sup>r</sup> in Rialls of 8, Gould, China ware, Sandalū, or otherwise as the time shall affourd, for then wilbe the time for y<sup>e</sup> *China* Iunckes to be ther. And after that we shall haue p̄fourmed o<sup>r</sup> trade ther, we purpose to set sayle the last of May, or beginning of Iune, in the foresaid̄ yeare towarde *Pahan*, *Patane*, and *Siam*, and ther along the Coast, employe o<sup>r</sup> oth<sup>r</sup> two third p̄te of o<sup>r</sup> Capitall in *China ware, Beniamyn, Lignū Aloes*, [p. 428] *Calumback*,[^sec-09-fn-012] *Muske, Gum Lac*, and oth<sup>r</sup> druggꬵ, w<sup>ch</sup> we may come by. And if we should not sell all o<sup>r</sup> com̃odityes, by the moneth of Nouemb̃r, then we purpose to settle a factorye in *Patane* or *Siā*, w<sup>th</sup> the rest of the goodꬵ, ther to trade w<sup>th</sup> the *China* Iunckes, in March next following, and the shippe w<sup>th</sup> the rest of the aduaunced Capitall, shall in the moneth of Nouemb̃r, take her voyage, thorough the Straictꬵ of *Sincapura*, by *Malacca*, and so againe towardꬵ the Coast of *Coromandell*, and ther wyll sell o<sup>r</sup> Comodityes, as gould, mony, and oth<sup>r</sup> thinges, for Cottō lynnen whight and paynted, both to trade againe w<sup>th</sup>all, at *Patane* and *Siam*, as also to bring homewardꬵ for *England*; as also a good pcell of Cottō yarne. And then in the moneth of May A° 1613, we meane to set sayle againe from y<sup>e</sup> Coastꬵ of *Coromandell*, to the Straictꬵ of *Sincapura*, and so againe to *Patane* and *Syam*, and ther traffique vntill the moneth of Nouemb̃r, and then take o<sup>r</sup> course towardꬵ *Bantā*; and from thence in *December* 1613, or in Ianuarye 1614, take o<sup>r</sup> course towardꬵ *England*, wher we hope to arryue in *August* 1614. hauing laden into o<sup>r</sup> shippe so much China silke, Taffataes, Damaskes, and Pursalyne, as we may attayne vnto, or as o<sup>r</sup> Capitall will pmytte, and we thinke may be here vented in *England*, Also a good pcell of *Beniamyn*, a pcell of *Lignū Aloes*, a lyttle *Calumback*, *Muske* frō *Syam*, *Gum Lack*, Also 150 bales of Cottō lynnen, whight and paynted, the w<sup>ch</sup> will serue to vent in *Europe*, but espīallye for the Coast of *Barbarye*, and some for the Coast of *Ginnye*, *Angola*, and oth<sup>r</sup> place, and about 200 bales of Cottō yarne; and for a proofe a pcell of *Indico* frō the coast of *Coromandell*, and some other drugges and wares, the w<sup>ch</sup> we may light vppō, and as o<sup>r</sup> capitall shall pmitte vs to deale in; This is o<sup>r</sup> p<sup>r</sup>sent resoluc̃on for y<sup>e</sup> p<sup>r</sup>tended voyage, yet forasmuch as all thingꬵ are mutable, so must we rule and gou<sup>r</sup>ne ourselues (being in those ptꬵ) as y<sup>e</sup> time, & occasiō shall pmitte.[^sec-09-fn-013]


<!-- page: 521 | folio: 429 -->

### *To the right hon<sup>l</sup> y<sup>e</sup> Earle of Salisbuirye Lord high Thrēr of England The humble peticōn of y<sup>e</sup> M<sup>r</sup>chants of London, trading the East Indyes.*[^sec-09-fn-014]


![Decorative drop capital S](../figures/fig-023_p0521.webp)

> _[Margin: Peticon to my Lo. Threr complayning y<sup>e</sup> wrongs sustayned in y<sup>e</sup> E. Indyes by y<sup>e</sup> Hollanders.]_

<span class="sc">Sheweth</span>, That yo<sup>r</sup> supp<sup>t</sup>ę, hauing long and patientlye endured, sundry notorious wrongę & iniuryous Courses at the handę of the *Hollanders* (in ther trade to the *East Indyes*) are enforced at last to breake sylence, and complayne their greifes; That the *Hollanders* hauing gottē into ther possessiō, dyuers of the cheif place of traffique in those p̄tę, and forciblye appropriating some, w<sup>ch</sup> do of right belong vnto the *English*, to trade ther before any oth<sup>r</sup> Natiō whatsoeu<sup>r</sup>, next vnto the *Portugall*, do seeke wholye to debarre yo<sup>r</sup> said supp<sup>t</sup>e, from the said trade, or to drawe sundrye inconuenience vppō them, no way hon<sup>ble</sup> nor p̄fitable for this Land. ffor S<sup>r</sup> ffrancys Drake, (vppō a contract w<sup>th</sup> the king of *Teronata*, for the trade of the Cloues in y<sup>t</sup> Island, and the rest of the Islandę vnder his dominiō) assisted him in his warres, against the king of *Tedore*, and confirm'd that agrem<sup>t</sup>, by delyu<sup>r</sup>ing him a Ring,[^sec-09-fn-015] w<sup>th</sup> a faire *Emerald* stone in y<sup>e</sup> same, (as is well knowne to Yo<sup>r</sup> Lo<sup>pp</sup>.). M<sup>r</sup> Cauendishe afterwardę folowing him, had y<sup>e</sup> like promise at *Balemboa*, in the south p̄t of the Island of *Iaua*, wher he refreshed, conferd w<sup>th</sup> the king or cheif in that place, and had promise of all the pepp ther. Vppō w<sup>ch</sup> assurauncę, the m<sup>r</sup>chantę of Londō, and others, sett out two shippes in trade for that place, vnder the com̄aund of Cap<sup>ne</sup> *Rayman* and Cap<sup>ne</sup> *Lancaster;* In w<sup>ch</sup> accōn *Rayman* was cast away about the Cape *Bonæ spei*, and *Lancaster* p̄fourm'd his voyage, beating along the Coast of *India*, vntill he came to *Sumatra*, wher his men falling sicke, and victualls scanting, durst not aduenture for y<sup>e</sup> *Moluccaes*, but retournd w<sup>th</sup> his lading of pepp, and was wrackt in the *West Indyes*.[^sec-09-fn-016]

After them folowed the *Hollanders* w<sup>th</sup> *English* pylottę, who p̄fourming a succesfull voiage to *Bantā* haue euer since p̄secuted a most ample trade. And p̄sentlye vppō ther retourne, yo<sup>r</sup> [p. 430] supp<sup>te</sup> as well to weaken the *Spanyard*, (then the com̄on enemye) as otherwise, ioyned in a Comp<sup>ie</sup>, and man'd forth, 4 of the best m<sup>r</sup>chant shippes of the kingdome, the *Dragon*, *Hector*, *Susan* and *Ascention*, w<sup>ch</sup> went to *Sumatra* and *Iaua*, and finding peacable trade, setled a factorye at *Bantā*, wher ther men being weake, the Cap<sup>nes</sup> thought fitt not to attempt the *Moluccaes*, (the Monsoune being then past) but hauing fought w<sup>th</sup> the Enemye in the *Straicte of Sincapura*, and takē a Carrycke, they laded ther shippes w<sup>th</sup> spice, and retournd well home, all full laden, (the *Hollander* then being very glad of yo<sup>r</sup> supp<sup>te</sup> companye.) At the retourne of w<sup>ch</sup> shippes, yo<sup>r</sup> supp<sup>te</sup> furnisht them forth againe, (vnder the com̄aund of *S<sup>r</sup> Henry Middletō* Generall) who according to his Com̄ission, attempted the *Moluccaes*, and com̄yng theth<sup>r</sup>, saued the king of *Teranataes* life, w<sup>th</sup> 6 *Hollanders*, w<sup>ch</sup> were in daung<sup>r</sup> and had bene taken by the king of *Tedore*, w<sup>th</sup> 80 men more, and cut in peece, (if he had not bene) as the rest of ther companye were, for which fauo<sup>r</sup> both the king and *Hollanders*, promised to lade ther shippe w<sup>th</sup> Cloues, and to do them any other kindnes that possiblye they could. But vppō newes of the com̄yng of certaine *Holland* shippes, they neith<sup>r</sup> pmitted them trade, according to promise, nor to staie ther, but were absolutelye banisht the Island by the *Hollanders* meanes, (as the king himself tould y<sup>e</sup> *English* the *Hollander* threatning, that if he did not, they would ioyne w<sup>th</sup> the king of *Tedore* his enemye, to driue him out of his Countrye.) *S<sup>r</sup> Henry* thervppō was enforced to pcure his whole lading from the *Portugall*, who vsed him very kindly & respectiuelye, giuing him all the Cloues they had at reasonable prices; And resigned vpp vnto him, a Towne, called *Taffasole*, w<sup>th</sup> a ffort, to the king of *Englands* vse (by y<sup>e</sup> consent of the king of *Tedore* right owner therof) w<sup>ch</sup> now the *Hollanders* kepe, (hauing fortifyed the same) besides many oth<sup>r</sup> place in the Countrye; appropriating to themselues the whole trade of the Islande; keping Men of warre vppō the Coast, and phibyting all oth<sup>r</sup> Nations (as farre as in them lyeth) from any trade ther (maintayning now for Lawe, by strong hand, that w<sup>ch</sup> latelye they estemed vnreasonable: for the *Portugall* to challenge a more spīall ppertie in any of those pte, then themselues or any oth<sup>r</sup> Nation whatsoeu<sup>r</sup>.) And from thence haue pceded to the *Islande of Banda*, (the place wher Nutmege and Mace do growe,) wher at ther com̄yng w<sup>th</sup> 14 sayle of [p. 431] shippes, they found yo<sup>r</sup> supp<sup>te</sup> shippe the *Hector* trading ther, (wherin was Cap<sup>ne</sup> W<sup>m</sup> Keeling,) hauing a house and factorye on shore, and many debtę in the *Islandę*) whome they vsed most vnkindlye, searching his boate disgracefullye both going for fresh water and retourning, and not suffering him to haue any furth<sup>r</sup> trade, nor to gather in his debtę but w<sup>th</sup> a pemptory com̄aund, to be gone, wherunto (thorough necessitye) he submytting himself, was enforced to dept, w<sup>th</sup>out his lading, or any furth<sup>r</sup> trade.

Since that tyme, Cap<sup>ne</sup> *Dauyd Middletō* in the *Expedicō*, seking trade at *Banda*, and vsing his best endeuo<sup>rs</sup>, both by guiftę, psuasions, and Com̄odityes, could not be pmitted by them for any com̄erce, eith<sup>r</sup> w<sup>th</sup> themselues, or the Island<sup>rs</sup>, but w<sup>th</sup> many reprochfull, insolent speches, was forciblye put from all trading in those ptę, but what he gott w<sup>th</sup> strong hand against ther wylles, from oth<sup>r</sup> broken Islandę neare adioyning, w<sup>th</sup> extreame hazard and daung<sup>r</sup>, (they deuising and oftentimes attempting, to surprize consume by fire, and cut off by any indirect meanes, both shippe, Men, and goodę.)

To coulo<sup>r</sup> all w<sup>ch</sup> ther doinge, they do most slanderouslye report, That yo<sup>r</sup> supp<sup>te</sup> haue furnisht the *Spanyard* (as the com̄on enemye,) w<sup>th</sup> great store of Ordinance, and a great quantitye of powder, besides oth<sup>r</sup> implem<sup>te</sup> of warre, And would haue compeld a *Portugall*, (whome they tooke), to haue iustifyed, That *S<sup>r</sup> Hen: Middletō* delyu<sup>r</sup>ed y<sup>e</sup> *Portugalls* 40 bar of powder, and 4 whole Culueringę, w<sup>th</sup> the lending of two of his cheif gunners to do them seruice against the *Hollanders;* w<sup>ch</sup> by the *Portugall* was more conscionablye refusd, then[^sec-09-fn-017] by them vrg'd, and submytted himself rath<sup>r</sup> to haue vndergone death, then father such a vntruth uppō yo<sup>r</sup> supp<sup>te</sup>.

> _[Margin: Capne Wolfard Harman to Mr Ro: Middleton.]_

All w<sup>ch</sup> vncyuell and inhumaine wronge abroad against yo<sup>r</sup> supp<sup>te</sup>, are done by Com̄ission from the m<sup>r</sup>ch<sup>te</sup> and Owners, at home, (as they cannott denye and oth<sup>rs</sup> haue acknowledgd, and hath bene latelye confessed by *some of them*[^sec-09-fn-018]) wherby yo<sup>r</sup> supp<sup>te</sup> hauing the *Spanyarde* and [p. 432] *Holland<sup>rs</sup>* enemyes in the *Indyes*, must of necessitye be enforced to giue ou<sup>r</sup> ther trade ther, (w<sup>ch</sup> is the cheif end the *Hollander* aymeth at).

Yo<sup>r</sup> supp<sup>te</sup> therfore forced by these extremityes, & knowing ther greifes, but hauing no meanes of remedye, do humblye implore yo<sup>r</sup> Lo. hon<sup>ble</sup> assistaunce & mediatiō to the *States* for redresse in these iniuryous courses, and that a reciprocall kindnes may be receyued from ther men, that as yo<sup>r</sup> supp<sup>te</sup> are tyed by a bond of duitye to submytte themselues by com̄aund, not to be offensiue to any whatsoeu<sup>r</sup>; so they might not be iniuriouslye rewarded, but enioye the benefitte and fredome of trade, wher the p<sup>r</sup>rogatiue rather apptaynes to thē then any oth<sup>r</sup>. And yo<sup>r</sup> supp<sup>te</sup> shall (as they haue bene alwayes bound) praie for yo<sup>r</sup> Lo. encrease in all honor and true happynes.

> _[Margin: M<sup>r</sup> Ro: Middleton [^sec-09-fn-019] to certaine Burgom<sup>rs</sup> at *Amsterdam*, by direccon from y<sup>e</sup> Comp:]_

MOST worthie S<sup>rs</sup>. Vppō some speeches had at my being at *Amsterdam*, in opening the wronge, w<sup>ch</sup> I conceyued the *East India Comp<sup>ie</sup> of London* had sustayned by yo<sup>r</sup> people, in those pte, I found yo<sup>r</sup> inclynatiō and readynes to ioyne in conference by some Com̄issioners to be nōīated for eith<sup>r</sup> pt. Wheruppō at my retourne, into *England*, I acquainted o<sup>r</sup> Gouern<sup>r</sup>, Depuitye and Com̄yttees w<sup>th</sup> that motiō. But before my com̄yng, they had exhibyted a petic̃on to my Lo. Thrēr,[^sec-09-fn-020] to acquaint the State w<sup>th</sup> ther wronge, and to craue redresse for the same. Notw<sup>th</sup>standing vppō my relac̃on, I found them wylling to staie any furth<sup>r</sup> pceding, as yet, but to ioyne in any good course, to haue all wronge righted, and all iust cause of offence remou’d betwixt thē and y<sup>u</sup>. That as o<sup>r</sup> Nations haue [p. 433] long contynued, in firme bonde and league of amytye, so we might peacablye pcede to trade ioynctlye togeth<sup>r</sup> (w<sup>th</sup>out troubling of eith<sup>r</sup> *States* (to right conceyued iniuryes) or giuing such an aduauntage to others (who would willinglye take the opportuntye of fishing in the troubled streames of o<sup>r</sup> diuision and dissencõns). So that (vppon conference) they are wylling to ioyne Com̄ission<sup>r</sup>s, w<sup>th</sup> such as y<sup>u</sup> shall substitute here, to salue and put a remedie to all greifes past, and consid<sup>r</sup> of some indifferent course to be contynued betwixt vs heraft<sup>r</sup>, for the good and benefitte of eith<sup>r</sup> pt. Wherin I could not retourne a more spedie resolucoñ, because of some extraordinarye occasions of launching certaine shippes, and oth<sup>r</sup> buysines of great import, w<sup>ch</sup> then hindred them; but haue now w<sup>th</sup> the first opportunitye, acquainted y<sup>u</sup> therw<sup>th</sup>, that if y<sup>u</sup> shall determyne of psecuting the form<sup>r</sup> pposicõn, and appoint some Com̄ission<sup>r</sup>s frō y<sup>u</sup>, it might be done spedilye (for the good I hope of both the Nations) and that I might receiue yo<sup>r</sup> resolucõns herin, w<sup>th</sup> all expedicõn. And so recomēnding the care herof to yo<sup>r</sup> graue consideracõns, and the successe to gode puidence, whome we beseech to direct all o<sup>r</sup> pcedinge to his glorie, (my self being diuoted in all true affeccõn to do all acceptable office I may for the good of both) I take my leaue, and rest,

Yo<sup>rs</sup> to be com̄aunded

Directed To the right Wo<sup>rll</sup>, my most respected friende, Burgom<sup>r</sup> Oatgens, Burgom<sup>r</sup> Pavij, Skepen Hasselare, Skepen Iacop gerson heind, Pentionalis Pavij, Dericke van Os, and Iohn van Harell, at *Amsterdā*, hast yēs.

*London, 5º Octob: 1611.*

ffor aunswer of w<sup>ch</sup> łre, an ord<sup>r</sup> of Court was retournd from thence, w<sup>ch</sup> is recorded in the *Court booke.[^sec-09-fn-021] pag. 271.*


<!-- page: 526 | folio: 434 -->

#### *Laus deo.* 20 *Decēb*: 1611. *In Amsterdam.*

> _[Margin: M<sup>r</sup> Pasfyld to M<sup>r</sup> Ro Middleton about the same buysines.]_

LOUING friend M<sup>r</sup> Middletō &c.  About 2 daies since, I had some speech w<sup>th</sup> Burgom<sup>r</sup> Pavij about the *E. India* matt<sup>rs</sup>; and he wylled me to certifye yo<sup>u</sup>, that they were not vnmyndfull of that matt<sup>r</sup>, y<sup>u</sup> wrote to thē about, though as yet by reason of oth<sup>r</sup> buysines, nothing effected. Yet ther were certaine appointed, (wherof he was one) to moue the States about it, because they could do nothing therin w<sup>th</sup>out ther aduise and consent: and said moreou<sup>r</sup> that they were to go w<sup>th</sup>in 8 or 10 daies to the *Hagh* about it: and that they had giuen exp<sup>r</sup>sse charge to the shippes, y<sup>t</sup> are gone out, y<sup>t</sup> they should carye themselues, in all friendlye manner y<sup>t</sup> was possible, towarde the *English* in the *Indies*, w<sup>th</sup>out offring them the least iniurye that might be;  And y<sup>t</sup> he doubted not, but ere long, ther should so good order be taken, that both Nations should contynue good friende.  Thus much he wylled me to certifye y<sup>u</sup>.  And so not hauing else at instant to enlardge &c.

Yo<sup>r</sup> louing friend *Samuell Pasfyld.*[^sec-09-fn-022]

> _[Margin: Translacon of y<sup>e</sup> Grand Sign<sup>rs</sup> Passe graunted to y<sup>e</sup> East India Merch<sup>ts</sup>.]_

YEE[^sec-09-fn-023] that are my most laudable, fortunate, welthye and great Vizroies and *Beglerbyes*,[^sec-09-fn-024] y<sup>t</sup> are on the way frō my most happie and Imperiall Throne, (both by sea and land) vntill the confynes and lymitte of the *East* [p. 435] *Indyes*; Owners of some part of dignitye, and those vnto whome belongeth to giue ayd, helpe and succo<sup>r</sup> in gode cause and *Musulmanicall* religion, vppō their Empero<sup>rs</sup> beck: the wealth and greatnes of whome, let it contynue for euer. Likewise vnto y<sup>u</sup> my most laudable and valiant *Sangrack-beys*,[^sec-09-fn-025] (that are vnder the abouenam'd *Beglerbeys*) Owners, and hope, of future great<sup>r</sup> dignityes; and those vnto whome belongeth duityfull ayd and helpe in gode cause and religion, vppō their Empero<sup>rs</sup> aduise, the hono<sup>r</sup> and dignitye of whome, be eu<sup>r</sup> contynuing. And vnto yee my most laudable, wise and prudent Iustice of peace, and Iudge,[^sec-09-fn-026] (that are in the p<sup>r</sup>scincte of the said *Sangrack-beyes*) whose iudgmente, iustice, & worde do flowe, as from a myne[^sec-09-fn-027] of all wisdome and prudence; the worthines and greatnes of whose dignitye and functiō, let it contynue for euer. Also to y<sup>u</sup> my laudable, great and most worthie Cap<sup>nes</sup>, and *Reyses*[^sec-09-fn-028] of all o<sup>r</sup> Nauyes, and shippinge, that swym̄e on the face of the sea. Vnto yee my laudable Cap<sup>nes</sup> of the Castles, Cityes and Townes; And vnto y<sup>u</sup> worthie and laudable *Customers*, dwelling vppō the *Sea*,[^sec-09-fn-029] *Ryuers*, *Bridges*, and all oth<sup>r</sup> pte of o<sup>r</sup> Domynions ther adiacent, Vppō the sight of this my most high and Imperiall comaundm<sup>t</sup>, in conformitye of yo<sup>r</sup> most bounden duityes, yee shall arise and do obeysaunce therunto.

And herby yee shall vnderstand that the *English Ambassad<sup>r</sup>*, that here resydeth, in o<sup>r</sup> happye and most high *Port*, hath giuē vs to vnderstand, by his supplicatiō, That forasmuch, as some of his *Ma<sub>tie</sub>* the *King of England* his subiecte, haue w<sup>th</sup> great charge and labo<sup>r</sup>, found out a Trade in the *East Indyes*; and hearing of the fame, and wealth[^sec-09-fn-030] of some parte of our Countrye, in their passage to the *Indyes*, are desirous to visite those place, for y<sup>e</sup> enlarging of the said Trade; and[^sec-09-fn-031] that such men in so good and profitable[^sec-09-fn-032] an enterprize, hauing deserued[^sec-09-fn-033] all fauo<sup>r</sup> ayd and [p. 436] helpe, so farre as may be lawfullye and conuenientlye yeilded, hath requested vs in the name of his *Ma<sup>tie</sup>* the *King of England*, to vouchsaufe them o<sup>r</sup> saufe conduct & com̃endac̃ons. In conformitye of whose request, as also in regard wee and o<sup>r</sup> p<sup>r</sup>decesso<sup>rs</sup>, are and haue bene for the space of many yeares, in strict league and amitye, w<sup>th</sup> the mēconed *King of England* and the Subiecte of that *Kingdome*, that haue long had, and now haue free traffique and trade in merchandizing in o<sup>r</sup> dominions and Countryes, thorough the *Mediterranean* seas. Wee do com̃aund and exp<sup>r</sup>slye charge y<sup>u</sup> all, and eu<sup>r</sup>ye one of y<sup>u</sup> our abouenamed subiecte & officers, that y<sup>u</sup> will not onlye kindlye and louinglye entertayne and receyue the said merchantte subiecte of *England*, com̃yng or passing through, or by any of o<sup>r</sup> Dominions, esp̄iallye intending to trade to the Dominions of *Yemen*, *Aden*, and *Mochon*, and the pte adioyning therunto ; assisting and releyuing them w<sup>th</sup> all thinge nedefull for themselues, their men and their Shippes, but also freelye to pmitte them, by land or by Sea, to go or sayle, to go forward or retourne, euen as their occasion shall require, to remaine in any of o<sup>r</sup> Dominions, Countryes or Cityes, graunting them such libertye of Trafficke and priuiledge, as shalbe reasonable, w<sup>th</sup>out giuing, or suffring any let or hinderaunce, iniurye or molestac̃on to be offered or done vnto thē; yea, y<sup>u</sup> shall yeild vnto thē, such office of beneuolence and humanitye, as shalbe meete and conuenyent to be yeilded vnto honest men, and straung<sup>rs</sup>, vndertaking so long and laboryous a io<sup>r</sup>nye. And if it be so, that wee shall vnderstand that contrarye to the Capitulacõn the Amitye and the League w<sup>ch</sup> is betwene vs and the *King of England*, y<sup>u</sup> do offer them the least wrong, and any way molest and trouble the said m<sup>r</sup>chante in their traffique, or ought els, Knowe yee for certaine that y<sup>u</sup> shall not onlye incurre our high displeasure, but y<sup>u</sup> shalbe punished for example vnto oth<sup>rs</sup>: And therfore in conformitye of this my esp̄iall Imperiall com̃aundm<sup>t</sup>, y<sup>u</sup> shall gouerne yo<sup>r</sup> selues, and gyue creditte to this my Imperiall insigne. Wrytten at o<sup>r</sup> mansion guard *Constantinople*, on the fiuetenth day of the Moone, *Zilkigie* 1019.[^sec-09-fn-034]


<!-- page: 529 | folio: 437 -->
> _[Margin: His Mat<sup>ies</sup> Comission to Cap<sup>ne</sup> Best.]_

[I]AMES[^sec-09-fn-035] by the grace of God king of England Scotland ffraunce and Ireland, Defendor of the Faith &c To our trustie and welbeloved Subiecte Thomas Best[^sec-09-fn-036] and Thomas Aldworth[^sec-09-fn-037] greeting, Whereas diuerse of our loving subiecte, by the name of the Gouernor and company of Merchante of London, trading into the *East Indies*, at theire owne aduentures Coste and chardges for the honor of this our realme of England, and for the increase and advancement of trade and merchandize w<sup>th</sup>in the same haue sett foorth sundry voyages to the *East Indies*, and allreadie discou<sup>r</sup>ed and begun to settle a trade into those parte, and intending the continewing thereof, aswell by frequenting those places allready setled as by further discou<sup>r</sup>y of other ptes, w<sup>ch</sup> may be fitt for the enterchanging, of the Com̄odities of our kingdomes w<sup>th</sup> the Commodities of those places, such as may bee of speciall vse and benefitt, to vs and our Subiecte, having to this purpose nowe prepared and sett foorth thone called the Dragon and the other the Hosiander to the said *East Indies*, and the places adioyning therevnto, And whereas our said Subiecte the aduenturers of those voyages, haue chosen our trusty and welbeloved [p. 438] subiect *Thomas Best* to be the Captaine and cheife Com̄aunder of all the Merchantę Marriners, and other Subiectę w<sup>ch</sup> are or shalbe shipped in the said Twoe shippe  *Wee* gratiously favouring theire intended voyage and approving and allowing of theire choise of yo<sup>u</sup> to the same imployment being willing to furnish yo<sup>u</sup> with all fitt and convenient power, and aucthority to rule and governe all and every our Subiectę implóyed in this voyadge, by a due obedience to be by them yeilded vnto yo<sup>u</sup> in the observing and executing, of all such good orders and constitucõns as yo<sup>u</sup> shall thinke convenyent to ordeine and make, for the furtherance of the said voyage according to such pticuler direccõns and enstruccõns as yo<sup>u</sup> shall receiue from the Gouernor and companie of merchantę the aduenturers in this voyage, w<sup>ch</sup> direccons & instruccons.  Our intencon is, and soe wee doe hereby will and com̃aund. that you doe punctually observe in eu<sup>r</sup>y pticuler, straightly chardging and com̃aunding, all and euery person or psons imployed in this voyadge and shipped in the said Twoe Shipps, to giue all due obedience, and respect vnto yo<sup>u</sup>, during the said voyadge, and to beare themselues one towarde another, in good order and quietnes, for avoyding any occacõn that might bread Mutiny, quarrell or dissensions amongest them, to the hinderaunce of the good successe w<sup>ch</sup> is to be hoped for by Gode providence of this said voyage.  *And* in Default of such duty and obedience to be pformed towarde yo<sup>u</sup>, for the correcting and quenching of all such Mutinyes quarrelle or Dissençõns that maie arise by the euill disposicõn of any pson whatsoeuer  *Wee* do hereby aucthorize the said *Thomas Best*, During the said voyage, or during soe longe time as yo<sup>u</sup> shall liue in the said voyage, to chaistice correct and punish all offendo<sup>rs</sup> and trangresso<sup>rs</sup> in that behalfe according to the quallitie, of theire offences, w<sup>th</sup> such punishmentę as are com̃only vsed in all Armyes at Sea, when they are not Cappitall,  And for Cappitall offences, as Wilfull murther w<sup>ch</sup> is hatefull in the sight of God, or Mutiny, w<sup>ch</sup> is an offence w<sup>ch</sup> maie tend to the overthrowe of the said voyage, the same being duely iustly approved against any of the pson or psons aforesaid, wee doe hereby giue vnto you the said Thomas Best, during all the time of the said voyadge, or during soe long time as yo<sup>u</sup> shall liue in the said voyadge, full power and [p. 439] aucthority, to vse and put in execuc̃on, our Lawe, called Lawe Martiall in that behalfe. And theis our Lres, shall be your sufficient warrant & dischardge for the dooinge and executing of all and singuler the premisses, And forasmuch as at this present time, wee are in amytie, w<sup>th</sup> all Christian princes, and are vnwilling that any of our Subiectę, should giue occac̃on of breach or hinderance thereof towardę any our our Confederates, frindę or Allyes. And because wee are not ignorant, of the emulac̃on and envie. w<sup>ch</sup> doth accompany the discouery of Countries and trades, And of the quarrelle and contenc̃ons, w<sup>ch</sup> doe many times fall out, betweene the subiectę of diuerse Princes when they meete the one w<sup>th</sup> the other, in forraigne and farr remote Countryes, in prosecuting the course of their Discoveries, And being desirous that our subiectę should forbeare to move or beginn any quarrelle or contenc̃on vpon the subiectę of our Confederates frindę or Allies either in theire gooing foorth or retorning from any of theire voyages, Wee therefore doe hereby straightly charge and com̃aund yo<sup>u</sup> the said *Thomas Best*, and all other vnder your Com̃aund, That neither in your voyadge outwardę or homewardę, or in any Country Island Port or Place, where yo<sup>u</sup> shall abide or come, during the time of your being abrade, out of our kingdomes or dominions where yo<sup>u</sup> meete w<sup>th</sup> any the subiectę, of the king of *Spaine* or of any other our confederates frindes or Allies, or of any other nac̃on or people, their Shippe vesselle goodes or merchandizes yo<sup>u</sup> doe not attempt or goe about, to sett vpon take or surprise, theire p̱sons Shippes vesselle goodes or merchandizes, or offer any iniury or discourtesie vnto them, as yo<sup>u</sup> will answere the contrary at your vttermost p̱ille. Except you shalbe by them first therevnto iustly provoked or driven either in the iust defence of your owne persons, shippes vesselle goodes or merchandizes by any there disturbance or hinderance, whatsoever in your quiet course of Trade or for recompence and recovery of the p̱sons shippes goodes or merchandizes, of any our Subiectę that are allready in or neere the *East Indies* or for any other iust cause of your defence. In w<sup>ch</sup> cases soe excepted yf yo<sup>u</sup> attēpte surprize and take the persons Shippe or goode of any Prince or State by whose Subiectę you shall susteine any wrong or losse in manner as aforesaid you shall not for any such act or [p. 440] acte grounded vpon the occac̃ons aboue menc̃oned, be in danger or subiect to the pill and penalties of our lawes, allwayes p<sup>r</sup>supposing, and soe requiring yo<sup>u</sup> to vse, all possible endeavo<sup>rs</sup>, by all meanes whatsoever to suffer noe spoyle to be made of any goodes or merchandizes, nor imbezilling any thing whatsoever, that shalbe recou<sup>r</sup>ed by you, but to see them safely brought home, w<sup>th</sup> the Bille of lading and charter pties to the intent that there maie be restitucõn made by us, soe soone as yo<sup>u</sup> shall receiue satisfaccõn from that State or people by whome yo<sup>u</sup> are dampnified, of what Nacõn soever, And forasmuch as our said Subiecte, the merchante and others the aduenturers of this voyadge out of preiudice[^sec-09-fn-038] and forsight of any Mortallity or otherwise (w<sup>ch</sup> God forbidd) should befall vnto our Subiect *Thomas Best*, haue made choise of our Trustie and loving Subiect Thomas *Aldworth*; to succeede the said Thomas Best, in the chardge and Com̃aund of Captaine and cheife Com̃aunder, of all the psons imployed in this voyadge as aforesaid, wee doe alsoe in case such an accident should happen, allowe and approve of theire choise in that behalfe, And doe hereby giue full power and aucthoritie to you the said Thomas Aldworth, to doe and execute . all and every thing incident to the chardge of Captaine and cheife Com̃aunder of all the psons employed, as is before com̃itted and imposed vppon the said *Thomas Best*; And theis our Lr̄es shalbe, shalbe allsoe sufficient warrant and discharg to the said *Thomas Aldworth* for the dooing and executing of all and singuler the premiss<sup>s</sup> as aforesaid. *In witnes* whereof wee haue caused theis our Lr̄es to be made Pattente. Witnes our selfe at Westm<sup>r</sup> the Sixt day of Ianuary in the Ninthe yeere of our Raigne of England ffraūce and Ireland and of Scotland the ffiue and ffortith.[^sec-09-fn-039] p̄ bre de privato Sigillo *Coppin*.


<!-- page: 533 | folio: 441 -->
JAMES[^sec-09-fn-040] by the grace of God king of England, Scotland ffraūce and Ireland Defendor of the faith &c To our trustie and welbeloved Subiect Thomas Best sendeth greeting signifying vnto all people, that whereas Certaine Shippe of our kingdome of England, at the Aduenture of the Gouernor and company of East *India* merchante, are to take theire voyadge to diuerse parte and porte of the East *Indies* especially to such as are in the kingdome of *Cambaia* or in any other p̄t of the greate *Kinge* of the *Magolles* Dominion, there to mannage a trade and peaceable com̄erce : w<sup>th</sup> the subiecte of the king, wee doe by vertue and aucthority, of theis our present L̄res giue and graunt vnto our said Loving Subiecte *Thomas Best* full power & Aucthoritie aswell to entertaine and prosecute, the said Trade and Com̄erce, as alsoe in our name and in the behalfe of our p̄son, to treate of conclude and ratifie, w<sup>th</sup> the said greate king of the Magolle or any his Deputies, to that purpose sent and lawfully aucthorized a firme and inviolable peace w<sup>ch</sup> (the Condic̃ons by our said Loving subiecte vnto them p̄posed being duly by them kept and observed) shall alsoe remaine on the part of our loving subiecte w<sup>th</sup>out breach.

And if any p̄son or p̄sons whatsoever, shall in contempt of vs our Royall Crowne and Dignity p̄sume to attempt the Contrary to theis present Articles concluded, They shalbe assured to incurr our heavie displeasure and wrathfull Indignac̃on, w<sup>th</sup> all greevous and severe punishment : in bodies, liues, and goode, Witnes our greate Seale of England to the originall annexed.

<span class="sc">Iames</span> by the grace of God king of *England Scotland ffrance and Irland* Defend<sup>r</sup> of the faith &c To our trustie and welbeloued Subiectę *Captaine Christopher Newport*[^sec-09-fn-041] and *Ioseph Saulbanke*[^sec-09-fn-042] Greeting, Whereas Diuerse of our loving subiectę, by the name of Gouern<sup>r</sup> and Company of Merchantę of London, trading into the East Indies, at theire owne aduentures costę and charges for the honour of this our Realme of England, and for the increase and aduancement of Trade and merchandize w<sup>th</sup>in the same, have sett forth sundry voyages to the East Indies, and allready discou<sup>r</sup>ed and begunn to settle a trade into those partę, and intending the contynewing thereof aswell by frequenting those places, allready setled, as by further discou<sup>r</sup>yes of other pte w<sup>ch</sup> maie be fitt for the interchangeing of the Comōdities of those places such as may be of spetiall vse and benefitt to vs and our Subiectę ; having to this purpose, nowe prepared and sett forth the good shipp called the *Expedicōn* of nigh Three hundred tuns. *And* whereas, our said subiectę the aduenturers of those voyages, have chosen, you our said subiect Captaine Christofer Newport, to be the principall Com̄aunder of Merchantę Marriners, and other our subiectę, w<sup>ch</sup> are or shalbe shipped in the said shipp *Wee* gratiously favouring theire intended voyage, and approving and allowing, of theire choise of you to the same Com̄aund, being willing to furnish you w<sup>th</sup> all fitt and convenyent power and aucthoritie to rule and governe all and eu<sup>r</sup>y our Subiectę employed in this voyage, aswell such as belong to the said shipp, as all others that are ffollowers of the *Persian Ambassador*,[^sec-09-fn-043] whome wee haue directed to be transported by you [p. 443] vnto the *Port of Surat*) by a due obedyence to be by them yeilded vnto yo<sup>u</sup>, in the observing and executing of all such good orders and constitucõns as you shall thinke convenyent to ordeine and make, for the furtherance of the said voyage, according to such pticuler direccõns and enstruccõns as yo<sup>u</sup> shall receiue from the said Gouern<sup>r</sup>. and Companye of Merchante the aduenturers in this voyadge, w<sup>ch</sup> direccons our intencõn is, and soe we doe will and require you, that you doe punctually observe in all thinge, Straightly chargeing and com̃aunding, all and eu<sup>r</sup>y person or p̱sons, imployed in this voyage, and shipped in the said shippe to giue all due obedyence, and respect vnto yo<sup>u</sup> during the said voyage, and to beare themselues one towarde another in good order and quietnes, for avoyding any occacõn that might bread Mutiny quarrelle or dissencõn amongst them, to the hinderance of the good successe w<sup>ch</sup> is to be hoped for by gode providence, of this said voyadge, And in defallt of such Duty and obedience to be p̱formed towarde you for the correcting and quenching of all such mutynies quarrelle or dissentions, that maie arise by the evill and disorderly disposicõn, of any p̱son whatsoeuer, wee do hereby aucthorise, the said Captaine Christopher Newport during the said voyadge, or during soe long time as you shall liue in the said voyage to chastice correct and punish all offendo<sup>rs</sup> and transgresso<sup>rs</sup>, in that behalfe, according to the quallity of theire offences, w<sup>th</sup> such punishmente as are com̃only vsed in all armyes at Sea, when they are not cappitall, And for Cappitall offences, as wilfull murther w<sup>ch</sup> is hatefull in the sight of God, or Mutiny w<sup>ch</sup> is an offence w<sup>ch</sup> may tend to the overthrowe of the said voyage the same being duly and iustly approved, against any of the p̱son or p̱sons aforesaid, we doe hereby giue vnto our said subiect Captaine Christofer Newport, during all the time of the said voyadge, or during soe longe time as yo<sup>u</sup> shall Liue, in the said voyadge, full power and aucthority to vse and put in execucõn our [p. 444] Lawe called lawe Martiall in that behalfe, And theis our Lres shalbe your sufficient warrant and dischargdge for the dooing and executing of all and singuler the premiss<sup>s</sup>, And forasmuch as at this present time, wee are in amytie w<sup>th</sup> all Christian Princes, And are vnwilling that any of our subiectę, should giue occac̃on of breach or hinderance thereof, towardę any our confederates frindę or allyes, And because wee are not ignorant of the Emulacon and envy w<sup>ch</sup> doth accompany the discouery of Countryes, and Trades and of the quarrellę and contencons w<sup>ch</sup> do many tymes fall out, betweene the Subiectę of diuerse Princes, when they meete the one w<sup>th</sup> the other in forraigne are[^sec-09-fn-044] farr remote Countryes in p̃secuting the course of theire discoveryes, and being desirous that our Subiectę should forbeare to move or beginn any quarrell or conteñcõn, betwene[^sec-09-fn-045] the Subiectę of our Confederates frindę or Allies either in theire gooing forth or retorning from any of theire voyages Wee therefore doe hereby straightly charge and com̃aund you the said Captaine Christofer Newport, and all other vnder your Com̃aund, that neither in your voyage outward or homeward, or in any Country Iland Port or place, where you shall abide, or come, during your time of being abroad, out of our kingdomes or Dominions, where you meete, w<sup>th</sup> any the subiectę of the king of Spaine, or of any other our Confederatę frindę or Allyes, or of any other Nac̃on or people theire shippes vesselle goodę, or merchandizes, you doe not attempt or goe about to sett vpon take or surprize, theire p̃sons Shippe vesselle goode or merchandizes or offer any iniury or discourtesie vnto them; as you will answere the contrary, at your vttermost pillę Except yo<sup>u</sup> shalbe by them first therevnto iustly provoked, or driven either in the iust defence of your owne p̃sons, Shippe vesselle goode or m<sup>r</sup>chandizes by any their disturbance or hinderance whatsoever in yo<sup>r</sup> quiett course of Trade, or for recompence and recouery of the persons shipe goode or merchandizes of any our Subiectę, that are allready in or neare the *East Indies*, or for any other iust cause of your defence, In w<sup>ch</sup> cases soe excepted, yf you attempt surprize and take, the p̃sons shippe or goode of any *Prince* or *State*, by whose Subiectę yo<sup>u</sup> [p. 445] shall susteyne any wronge, or Losse in manner as aforesaid, you shall not for any such act or acte grounded vpon the occacons aboue meñcõned, be in danger or subiect to the ƀill and penaltyes of our Lawes, Alwayes p<sup>r</sup>supposing and soe requiring you to vse all possible endeavo<sup>r</sup>s, by all meanes whatsoever, to suffer noe spoyle to be made of any goodes or merchandizes, nor imbeazaling of any thing whatsoever, that shalbe recouered by yoᵘ. but to se them safely brought home, with the bille of lading and charter p̄ties to thintent that there may be restituq̃on made by vs, soe soone as you shall receive satisfacc̃on from that State or people, by whome you are dampnifyed of what Nac̃on soever, And forasmuch as our said Subiectę the merchantę and other the aduenturers of this voyadge out of providence and forsight of any mortallitie either by sicknes or otherwise wᶜʰ God forbidd should befall vnto our Subiect the said Captaine Christofer Newport, haue made choise of yoᵘ our trustie and loving subiect, Ioseph Saulbanck to succeede the said Captaine Christofer Newport, in the charge of principall Com̄aunder of all the persons imployed in this voyadge as aforesaid, wee doe alsoe in case such an accident should happen, allowe and approve of theire choise in that behalfe, And doe hereby giue full power and aucthoritie to you the said Ioseph Saulbancke, to doe [and] execute, and[^sec-09-fn-046] and eu<sup>r</sup>y thinge incident to the charge of Principall Com̄aunder of all the ƀsons imployed in that voyadge as aforesaid in as ample mann<sup>r</sup> and forme, and to all intentę and purposes as is before Com̄itted and imposed vpon our subiect Captaine Christofer Newport And theis our L̄res shalbe allsoe sufficient warrant and discharge to the said Ioseph Saulbanck for the dooing and executing of all and singuler of all and singuler the p<sup>r</sup>missę *In witnes* whereof wee haue caused theis our L̄res to be made Pattentę Witnes our selfe at ### Notes

[^sec-09-fn-001]: (1) *i.e.* Floris and Antheumis in the *Seventh Voyage* (see page 363, note). The ships of the *Seventh* and *Eighth Voyages* started within a few months of one another. Hence, probably, the confusion in the present volume between the papers of the two expeditions.

[^sec-09-fn-022]: (1) This well-meant attempt at conciliation seems to have met with scant success. After some delay, the Dutch Company appointed commissioners to treat of the subjects in dispute, who reached London in the spring of 1613. A month was spent in negotiations, but without result. The delegates returned to Holland, and the matter was left to be decided by a future treaty. In 1615, English Commissioners, including Middleton and Abbot as representatives of the Company, proceeded to the Hague, but their efforts to effect a satisfactory settlement proved equally fruitless.

[^sec-09-fn-035]: (1) The Royal Commission for the *Tenth Voyage* (1612-14), consisting of two ships, the *Dragon* and the *Hosiander*, under the command of Thomas Best. There is a docquet of this commission at the Public Record Office, under date 30th December, 1611.
[^sec-09-fn-036]: (2) Thomas Best was a seaman of considerable experience, though he had not been previously in the service of the Company. In this *Tenth Voyage* he particularly distinguished himself by defeating a superior force of Portuguese war vessels, which attacked him off Surat, a victory which made a great impression on the natives, and procured a firman which was practically the foundation of English trade in Western India. On his return in 1614, he was well received by the Company; and for several years his name was brought forward from time to time as that of a fit person to command further expeditions. In November, 1617, all arrangements had been made for his taking command of the fleet then preparing for the Indies, but a quarrel occurred, and Best was dismissed the Company's service. He contrived to make his peace with them, but was not again employed. In 1623, he was in command of a vessel in the Royal Navy, and for the rest of his life was an active servant of the Crown (see *Dict. Nat. Biography*). He is supposed to have died about 1638.
[^sec-09-fn-037]: (3) Thomas Aldworth appears to have been a man of some standing before his entry into the Company's service, and was at one time sheriff of Bristol. He was left at Surat as head of the factory there, and held that post until his death in the autumn of 1615.

Upon his return, he was nominated general of the fleet for the following year, but Keeling was subsequently preferred to that post, with Newport as his vice-admiral in the *Lion*. This was his last voyage, for he died at Bantam in August, 1618.
[^sec-09-fn-042]: (2) See note, page 235.
[^sec-09-fn-043]: (3) Sir Robert Sherley, the youngest of the three celebrated brothers of that name, accompanied his brother Anthony to Persia in 1599, and in 1608 was sent by Shah Abbas on a mission to various European Powers, England among the rest. He was presented to King James at Hampton Court in 1611, and received the honour of knighthood. He [p. 443] was now (1612) returning to Persia. He came again to England in a similar capacity in 1623, but suffered some disgrace through the unexpected appearance of a native ambassador, who roundly declared Sir Robert’s credentials to be forged. King James sent them both back to Persia, together with Sir Dodmore Cotton, accredited as English ambassador to the Shah. Sir Robert reached in safety the country of his adoption, but was badly received by his master, and died soon after in disgrace.

## Sir Thomas Roe, First Joint Stock & Later Documents, 1613–1619


<!-- page: 538 | folio: 446 -->

### <span class="sc">Articles of</span> Agreement made and concluded the Sixteenth daie of November 1614 betwixt the Gou<sup>r</sup>n<sup>r</sup> and Company of merchantę of London trading into the East Indies on the one pte : And S<sup>r</sup> Thomas Rooe knight on thoth[er] parte as followeth.[^sec-10-fn-001]

<span class="sc">Whereas</span> the Gouerno<sup>r</sup> and Company haue nomynated the foresaid *S<sup>r</sup> Thomas Roe* and procured his ma<sup>tie</sup>: to employ him as his Embassador to the Grand *Magore*, for the better establishing and setlinge an absolute trade in any parte, w<sup>th</sup>in the Dominions of the greate *Mogore* aforesaid

<span class="sc">The</span> said Gou<sup>r</sup>ner and company, finding that they cannot convenyently proporcõn any certenty for the expenc[e] of Diett, both for S<sup>r</sup> Thomas Roe and his retinewe, doe leaue the managing thereof, to his Discrecõn care and wisdome, relying vpon his frugallity, wherein he promiseth his vttermost endeavors, And to cause a iust accompt, to be kept of all expences, from the beginning to the End, as alsoe to deliuer vpp a pticuler, of whatsoever shalbe allowed vnto him by the grand *Mogore*, And if it shall soe happen that the Grand Mogore, shall graunt a daylie or yearely allowance, vnto him for his diett and followers, during his abode there to countervaile those expences, That then he shall free the Company from the said chardge

<span class="sc">The</span> said S<sup>r</sup> Thomas Roe doth promise to forbeare all private Trade, for himselfe or any other either directly or indirectly and [p. 447] doth assure the Company by a faithfull promise to hinder it in others (All that he can[]), and to giue intelligence vnto them, of any that he shall take notice of to offend in that nature or shall by any meanes come to the knowledge of and wilbe ready to giue his best assistance vnto theire cheife ffactor, (vpon any occac̃on) to punish all offenders that shall deserue punishment, according to the quallity of theire offences

<span class="sc">And</span> lastly to free himselfe from all iust cause of doubt, concerning theire stock in the Country. Hee is willing not to intermeddle, w<sup>th</sup> any of theire moneys there, as he doth voluntarily offer, And will not desir[e] aboue the value of One hundred pounde vpon any spetiall occac̃ons, to haue it repaid back againe out of his meanes, when they shall growe due. Promising not to haue to doe w<sup>th</sup> any parte of there m<sup>r</sup>chandize, but to Leaue it wholly to the Managing of theire factor<sup>rs</sup>, whome they shall appoint for theis purposes

<span class="sc">In Consideracon</span> of the premiss<sup>s</sup> the said Gouern<sup>r</sup> and Company doe for themselfes and y<sup>r</sup> Successors promise to allowe vnto the said *S<sup>r</sup> Thomas* Roe yerely (for soe long time as he shalbe imployed in this service[]) the som̄e of Six hundred pounde, Three hundred thereof to be paid in the *Country* at fower shillinge sixpence the Riall, for his maintenance of Apparrell and other expences, And thother Three hundred pounde shall yerely be put into the Ioinct stocke, to be ymployed for his benifitt pportionablely w<sup>th</sup> all other aduentures. ffor his better encouragem<sup>t</sup>, whereby to tye his uttermost endeav<sup>rs</sup> to be ymployed for the good of the Company, They were willing to giue him a true Testimony of theire affec̃ons. And therefore bestowed on him freely the some of ffive hundred markes ymprested vpon his Salarie to dispose of as he should thinke fitting

<span class="sc">The</span> said Gouerno<sup>r</sup> and Company desiring to be at a certenty conc<sup>r</sup>ning the wages of all such servantę as shall attend him are contented to allowe him a hundred poundes p Annū for him to giue them satisfacc̃on, besides a preacher and Chirurgion whoe shall haue wages at the Companyes charge, the Preacher 50<sup>li</sup> p Annū, and the Chirurgion Twenty and ffower pounde And did freely bestowe the some of Thirty pounde to be disposed by him [p. 448] for the Liueryes of his said followers, In considerac̃on whereof, he promiseth to entertayne none to attend him, but such as the Company shall approve of.

THE said Gouerner and Company are likewise contented to deliuer vnto *S<sup>r</sup> Thomas Roe* the som̄e of ffifteene[^sec-10-fn-002] poundes in hand, being the one halfe of the yerely allowaūce, giuen by the Compn̄ towarde the entertainem<sup>t</sup> of his followers, and alsoe ffiue and Twenty poundes, for the halfe of the yearely allowance given by them vnto the Preacher, and Twelue pounde for the like halfe yeares allowance vnto the Chirurgion, And for the time ensewing, it is agreed to haue them[^sec-10-fn-003] halfe of theire said yearely allowance to be paid vnto *S<sup>r</sup> Thomas Roe* in the Country for theire dischardge

AND lastly the said Gouernor and company are contented to lend vnto the said *S<sup>r</sup> Thomas Roe*, the som̄e of one hundred poundes to buy plate for his Table, w<sup>ch</sup> some he promiseth to repaie back againe, at his retorne or deliu<sup>r</sup> the value thereof in *Plate* Or to haue it answered out of his Aduenture if he die

MEMORANDUM whereas *S<sup>r</sup> Thomas Roe Kt.* hath receyved the som̄e of Three hundred thirtie and three poundes six shillinge and Eight pence[^sec-10-fn-004] pte of the *Salary* w<sup>ch</sup> is to bee allowed him for the ymployment according to former agreement whereby there cannot be soe much put into the Iointe stock, the first yeare as is formerly menc̃oned, The said S<sup>r</sup> Thomas Roe doth therefore Couenant to haue one hundred markes more of his salarie to make vpp the full of ffower hundred poundes to be paid heare to such as he shall consigne it vnto. and onely Twoe hundred pounde put into the ioynt stock, for his vse in this his first yeare, of ymployment, The second yeare Three hundred poundes as was formerly resould[^sec-10-fn-005] of and the like for the Third, w<sup>ch</sup> in theis Three yeares will arise to the som̄e of Eight hundred poundes to be disposed for his benefit in the Ioinct stock accordinge to former Couenant and agreement

IN WITNES of w<sup>ch</sup> agreement and Coven̄nte concluded the [p. 449] said Gou<sup>r</sup>nor and Company haue for themselues and there Successo<sup>rs</sup> caused theire Common Seale to be fixed to one pte thereof, And the said *S<sup>r</sup> Thomas Roe*, hath to the other pte put his hand and Seale the day and yeare first aboue written

<span class="sc">James</span>[^sec-10-fn-006] by the grace of god king of England Scotland ffraunce and Ireland, defendo<sup>r</sup> of the ffaith &c: TO our trusty and welbeloued Subiect, Cap<sup>ne</sup> Nicholas Downton, WHERAS divers of o<sup>r</sup> lovinge Subiecte by the name of the Gou<sup>r</sup>ner and Companye of M<sup>r</sup>chante of London tradinge into the East Indies at their owne adventures coste and charge for the honor of this o<sup>r</sup> Relme of England, and for the encrease and advauncement of trade and M<sup>r</sup>chandize w<sup>th</sup>in the same, haue sett fourth sundrye voyage to the said East Indyes and haue already discou<sup>r</sup>ed, and beginne to settle a trade in those pte, And intending the continuinge therof, aswell by frequenting those place alreadi settled, as by further discou<sup>r</sup>yes of oth<sup>r</sup> pte w<sup>ch</sup> may be fit for interchanging of the Comodityes of o<sup>r</sup> kingdomes w<sup>th</sup> the Comodities of those place, such as may be of spetiall vse and benefitt to vs and o<sup>r</sup> subiecte, Having to this purpose now p<sup>r</sup>pared and sett fourth ffoure good shippes called the *Newyeares guift*. *Hector Hope & Solomon*, to the said East Indyes, and the place adioyninge thervnto. And wheras o<sup>r</sup> said subiecte the adventurers of those voyage haue chosen the said Cap<sup>ne</sup> Nicholas Downtō to be the principall Commander or Gen<sup>r</sup>all of all the m<sup>r</sup>chante Maryn<sup>r</sup>s and other o<sup>r</sup> Subiecte w<sup>ch</sup> are or shalbe shipped in the said ffoure shippes We gratiously favouring their intended voyage, and approuing and allowing of [p. 450] their choise of y<sup>u</sup> [to] the same place of Commaund, being willing to furnish y<sup>u</sup> w<sup>th</sup> all fitt and convenient pow<sup>r</sup> and authoritye to rule & gou<sup>r</sup>ne all and euerye of o<sup>r</sup> Subiectę imployed in this voyage, by a due obedience to be by them yeilded vnto yo<sup>u</sup> in the observing and executing of all such goodę orders and constitučōns as yo<sup>u</sup> shall thinke convenient to ordayne or make for the furtheraunce of the said voyage accordinge to such pticuler direcčōns and instrucčōns as yo<sup>u</sup> shall receive from the said Gou<sup>r</sup>ner and Company of M<sup>r</sup>chauntę the adventurers in this voyage w<sup>ch</sup> direccons and instrucčōns o<sup>r</sup> intention is,  And soe we will and require yo<sup>u</sup> that yo<sup>u</sup> punctuallye observe in all thingę. WEE do therfore stracklye charge and command all and eu<sup>r</sup>y pson or psons ymployed in this voyage and shipped in those said ffoure shippes to give all due obedience and respect vnto yo<sup>u</sup>, during the said voyage, and to beare themselues one towardę an oth<sup>r</sup> in good order and quietnes, for the avoyding any occacion, that might breede mutynie quarrelle or dessentions amongst them to the hinderaunce or good successe w<sup>ch</sup> is to be hoped for, by Godę prouidence of the said voyage,  And in default of such dutye and obedience to be pformed towardę yo<sup>u</sup> for the correcting and quenching of all such mutynies quarrelle or dessentions that may arrise by the euill and disorderly disposičōns of any psons whatsoeu<sup>r</sup>.  WEE do hereby authorize yo<sup>u</sup> the said Cap<sup>ne</sup> Nicholas Downton during the said voyadge or during so longe tyme as you shall liue in the said voyage.  To chastice correct and punish all offendo<sup>rs</sup> transgresso<sup>rs</sup> in that behalfe, according to the quallitye of their offence w<sup>th</sup> such punishmentę as are commonly vsed in all Armyes at Sea, when they are not capitall, And for capitall offence as wilfull murthe<sup>r</sup> w<sup>ch</sup> is hatfull in the sight of god, or Mutynie w<sup>ch</sup> is an offence that may tend to the ou<sup>r</sup>throw of the said voyage, the same being duly and iustly proued, against any of the pson or psons aforesaid  WEE do hereby giue vnto you the said Cap<sup>ne</sup> Nicholas Downtō during all the tyme of the said voyage or during so long as you shall liue in the said voyage, full power and authoritye to vse and put in execution our law called Martiall lawe in that behalfe.  But that therin you doe expresly vse the advise and counsell of the two principall Masters and of the two principall M<sup>r</sup>chauntę appoynted for the tyme [p. 451] being, or of any two of them. And theis o<sup>r</sup> letters shalbe vnto you sufficient warrant and discharge for the doeing and executing of all and singuler the p<sup>r</sup>misses. <span class="sc">And</span> forasmuch as at this p<sup>r</sup>sent tyme wee are in amitye w<sup>th</sup> all Christian Princes, And are vnwilling that any o<sup>r</sup> Subiecte should giue occacion of breach or hinderance therof towarde any o<sup>r</sup> Confederate freinde or Allyes And because we are not ignorant of the emulation and envye, w<sup>ch</sup> doth companye the discou<sup>r</sup>ye of Countryes and trade and of the querrelle and contencõns w<sup>ch</sup> doe many tymes fall out betweene the Subiecte of divers Princes, when they meete the one w<sup>th</sup> the other in forreyne and farre remote Countryes in prosecuting the course of their discou<sup>r</sup>ings; And being desirous that our Subiecte should forbeare to moue or beginne any quarrell or contencõns vppon the subiecte of o<sup>r</sup> Confederate friende or Allyes eythe<sup>r</sup> in their going fourth or retouring from any of their voyage <span class="sc">Wee</span> therfore doe hereby straicly charge and commaund yo<sup>u</sup> the said Cap<sup>ne</sup> Nicholas Downton, and all other vnder yo<sup>r</sup> gou<sup>r</sup>ment, that neyther in yo<sup>r</sup> voyage outwarde or homewarde or in any Countrye Island Port or place wher yo<sup>u</sup> shall abide or come during the tyme of yo<sup>r</sup> being abroade out of o<sup>r</sup> kingdomes or dominions wher you meete w<sup>th</sup> any the Subiecte of the king of *Spayne* or of any other o<sup>r</sup> confederate, friende or Allyes or of any other nation, or people, their shippes vesselle goode or M<sup>r</sup>chandize yo<sup>u</sup> doe not attempt or goe about to sett vpon take or surprize, their ꝑsons, shippes, vesselle goode or M<sup>r</sup>chandizes Or offer any iniurye or discourtesie vnto them (except y<sup>u</sup> shalbe by them, first thervnto iustlye prouoked or driuē, eyther in the iust defence of yo<sup>r</sup> owne ꝑsons, shippes vessells goode or M<sup>r</sup>chandizes by any their disturbances or hinderance whatsoeu<sup>r</sup> in yo<sup>r</sup> quiet course of Trade Or for recompence and recou<sup>r</sup>ye of the ꝑsons, Shippes goode or M<sup>r</sup>chandizes of any o<sup>r</sup> Subiecte that are already in or neare the *East India* or for any other iust cause of yo<sup>r</sup> defence In w<sup>ch</sup> causes so excepted, of y<sup>u</sup> attempt surprize and take the ꝑsons Shippes and goode of any Princes or State, by whose Subiecte y<sup>u</sup> shall sustayne any wronge or losse in mann<sup>r</sup> as aforesaid y<sup>u</sup> shall not for any such act or acte grounded vppon the occasions aboue mencõned be in
